All five U.S.-listed stocks with clear exposure fell on a day of broad tech selling. By then, the S&P 500 had already dropped about 9% since November 4. He also told communities to make developers pay them instead of stopping projects. For example, he said developers of a Louisiana project paid teachers $50,000 to win approval. Several basic questions went unanswered. He did not say whether a tax would reach foreign subsidiaries or only U.S. parent companies, whether rented space would count the same as owned buildings, or whether existing overseas sites would be exempt. In September 2026, Google announced at least $15 billion for data centers and digital infrastructure in Finland, which it called its largest capital commitment in Europe. But I haven’t even said that to my people,” Trump said, flanked by Vice President JD Vance and Secretary of State Marco Rubio. You know, they allowed that to happen with chips and everything else, and it was very destructive to our country. It’s where we started going behind. > So I just, I don’t know if that’s a breaking story. But I haven’t even said that to my people, but I’m telling them now. extraction.body: The president gave no details at a White House briefing Friday, said he had not told his own team, and named a Google project in Finland as one he will not allow President Donald Trump said Friday that U.S. companies will not be allowed to build artificial intelligence data centers outside the country, and he threatened a "tremendous tax" on firms that go ahead anyway. He made the remarks at a White House briefing shortly after returning from Asia, in a policy statement that came with almost no detail. "We're not going to allow our companies to build data centers outside of our country," Trump told reporters. "Because China will take all of them, and we're not allowing that to happen." He added that "we're going to put tremendous penalties on companies that try and do it." He framed the policy as part of a contest with China over AI, saying the United States is leading in data center construction and will not let China overtake it. Neither the size of the tax nor the method of enforcement was described. Trump said he had not yet told his own team, remarking, "I haven't even said that to my people. But I'm telling them now, they're here." Google announced a 13 billion euro investment in Finnish AI infrastructure in September, about $15 billion, including funding for three data centers, and Trump said of a Finland project, "They want to build now one in Finland, and we're not allowing that to happen." Building work on two of the Google sites was halted last month after plans to clear over 300 hectares of woodland drew concern. Meta has broken ground on a data center in Alberta, Canada, and Anthropic has agreed to lease a planned facility in Nova Scotia under a long-term deal. Many Democratic candidates promised tougher regulation of new data centers in this month's midterm elections, and Trump told communities to take advantage of the facilities and "make them pay you, make them pay your community." Hart Research Associates, working with Public Opinion Strategies, polled 1,000 voters nationwide Oct. 14 to 18 and found that 63 percent oppose an AI data center built within 10 miles of where they live, while 13 percent support one. Roughly half the sample got that question, so its uncertainty runs 4.38 points either way. The Pew Research Center counted about 3,000 data centers nationwide in April, with roughly 1,500 more moving through approval or construction. A Turner & Townsend report on 62 global markets found that U.S. data center construction costs rose 13 percent year over year, more than double the global rate and about three times the ten-year average, as demand for AI capacity outran available land with power and skilled labor. The Commerce Department's interim final rule on where advanced chips can go, announced Nov. 16 and effective Nov. 19, requires export licenses for advanced chips shipped to Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand and Brazil, which the department describes as carrying a higher risk of diversion. Commerce said the Treasury Department and the National Security Council wrote the rule and gave the direction for it. It also requires a license when an overseas data center provides large volumes of compute to a company headquartered in China, and existing providers have 90 days to apply. U.S.-headquartered companies in the five named countries are exempt if they meet reporting requirements. No rate, legal mechanism or timeline has been announced, and Google was contacted for comment on the remarks. Companies already planning foreign sites, from the Finland investment to the Alberta and Nova Scotia projects, face that presidential threat on top of the Commerce Department's new licensing rule, and the October poll of 1,000 voters put opposition at 63 percent, with 13 percent in support, for an AI facility sited fewer than 10 miles from where those voters live. extraction.body: The president gave no details at a White House briefing Friday, said he had not told his own team, and named a Google project in Finland as one he will not allow President Donald Trump said Friday that U.S. companies will not be allowed to build artificial intelligence data centers outside the country, and he threatened a "tremendous tax" on firms that go ahead anyway. He made the remarks at a White House briefing shortly after returning from Asia, in a policy statement that came with almost no detail. "We're not going to allow our companies to build data centers outside of our country," Trump told reporters. "Because China will take all of them, and we're not allowing that to happen." He added that "we're going to put tremendous penalties on companies that try and do it." He framed the policy as part of a contest with China over AI, saying the United States is leading in data center construction and will not let China overtake it. Neither the size of the tax nor the method of enforcement was described. Trump said he had not yet told his own team, remarking, "I haven't even said that to my people. But I'm telling them now, they're here." Google announced a 13 billion euro investment in Finnish AI infrastructure in September, about $15 billion, including funding for three data centers, and Trump said of a Finland project, "They want to build now one in Finland, and we're not allowing that to happen." Building work on two of the Google sites was halted last month after plans to clear over 300 hectares of woodland drew concern. Meta has broken ground on a data center in Alberta, Canada, and Anthropic has agreed to lease a planned facility in Nova Scotia under a long-term deal. Many Democratic candidates promised tougher regulation of new data centers in this month's midterm elections, and Trump told communities to take advantage of the facilities and "make them pay you, make them pay your community." Hart Research Associates, working with Public Opinion Strategies, polled 1,000 voters nationwide Oct. 14 to 18 and found that 63 percent oppose an AI data center built within 10 miles of where they live, while 13 percent support one. Roughly half the sample got that question, so its uncertainty runs 4.38 points either way. The Pew Research Center counted about 3,000 data centers nationwide in April, with roughly 1,500 more moving through approval or construction. A Turner & Townsend report on 62 global markets found that U.S. data center construction costs rose 13 percent year over year, more than double the global rate and about three times the ten-year average, as demand for AI capacity outran available land with power and skilled labor. The Commerce Department's interim final rule on where advanced chips can go, announced Nov. 16 and effective Nov. 19, requires export licenses for advanced chips shipped to Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand and Brazil, which the department describes as carrying a higher risk of diversion. Commerce said the Treasury Department and the National Security Council wrote the rule and gave the direction for it. It also requires a license when an overseas data center provides large volumes of compute to a company headquartered in China, and existing providers have 90 days to apply. U.S.-headquartered companies in the five named countries are exempt if they meet reporting requirements. No rate, legal mechanism or timeline has been announced, and Google was contacted for comment on the remarks. Companies already planning foreign sites, from the Finland investment to the Alberta and Nova Scotia projects, face that presidential threat on top of the Commerce Department's new licensing rule, and the October poll of 1,000 voters put opposition at 63 percent, with 13 percent in support, for an AI facility sited fewer than 10 miles from where those voters live. coreStoryFacts.text: Meta, Snap, TikTok and YouTube settled an earlier lawsuit with a school district in Kentucky in May, in which YouTube agreed to pay slightly more than $2 million.
The video platform was also found negligent in a personal-injury lawsuit in Los Angeles in March and agreed to settle a separate personal-injury lawsuit in June .
The settlement "will likely take a few months to officially finalize" and is contingent on a majority of districts agreeing.
The deal will reportedly also include "additional product safeguards for teens."
Engadget has asked YouTube to comment on the school district settlement.

Like Meta, Snap and TikTok, YouTube is facing a growing number of lawsuits alleging that its platform is designed to be addictive, and that it knew using it could produce negative outcomes for younger users.

YouTube and many other Google products are heavily used in classrooms, so reaching a settlement would allow the company to avoid drawn-out legal battles during what's already a contentious moment between Google and schools .
YouTube is preparing to pay $3 billion to thousands of school districts to settle claims that its “addictive design” harmed kids, according to Bloomberg.
In March, both YouTube and Meta were found negligent in a separate legal battle over social media addiction.
As part of the agreement, Meta will only shell out the remaining $5.3 billion of its $17.1 billion settlement if YouTube and TikTok roll out similar changes and pay matching amounts.
Sources tell the publication that YouTube reached the agreement “in principle,” and that the deal would also include new safeguards for teens.
The settlement would allow Google to avoid a wave of lawsuits filed by US school districts that accuse YouTube, Meta, Snap, and TikTok of negatively impacting the mental health of teen users.

The Google-owned video platform could pay about $3 billion to thousands of school districts that accuse it of designing an addictive service that harmed students’ mental health, a Bloomberg report claimed, citing people familiar with the matter.

The proposed agreement also includes additional safeguards for teenagers who use YouTube.​The agreement depends on a majority of the districts signing on and could take several months to finalise, the report claims.

They say the companies knew about the risks to young users and failed to change their products to reduce those risks.​The cases bring together claims from multiple school districts so that common issues can be handled before trial, while each district’s case is decided separately.
A settlement would allow YouTube to resolve claims from participating districts.

Thousands of individual personal injury lawsuits against the company remain active.​What happened in the Kentucky case​The first school district case set to go to trial involved Breathitt County, Kentucky, a district with fewer than 2,000 students.

YouTube, Meta, Snap and TikTok settled with the district for a combined $27 million about a month before the trial was due to begin.​YouTube agreed to pay slightly more than $2 million and provide training programs to the district, according to documents released under Kentucky’s open records law.

Google spokesperson José Castaneda and the plaintiffs’ attorneys co-leading the federal school district cases have yet to comment.​Why school districts sued YouTubeThe districts allege that features such as autoplay and endless scrolling encourage students to spend more time on social media.
YouTube has reached a preliminary settlement with US schools.
The districts are seeking reimbursement for expenses they say stem from social media addiction, including the cost of expanding counselling and mental health services for students.

The decision is documented in Meta’s filing and the court verdict .
Both companies challenged the ruling, which Cryptopolitan covered .

This agreement is currently in its preliminary stage. The agreement still needs several approvals before it can move forward. A majority of the school districts involved in the lawsuits must accept YouTube’s proposed settlement, which includes about $3 billion in compensation and additional safeguards for teenagers. Judge Yvonne Gonzalez Rogers must then approve the agreement. The process could take months. The federal lawsuit, case 22-md-03047-YGR , focuses on allegations that how YouTube was designed hurts students’ mental health. YouTube is denying the allegations. According to the school districts, the autoplay, personalized recommendations, and infinite scrolling features of YouTube encourage students to linger on the platform longer than intended. They claim that this has necessitated schools to increase their spending on mental health services and to enforce phone restrictions. Limiting YouTube use during school hours is not straightforward because teachers also rely on the platform for lessons. Students, however, do not always use it for educational purposes. A Fordham Institute survey found that more than 30% of surveyed high-school students watched YouTube for entertainment during school hours. YouTube is not alone in facing these allegations. Thousands of lawsuits filed by individuals, school districts and government agencies accuse social media companies, including Meta, TikTok and Snap, of designing platforms that encourage addictive behavior among young people. According to the American Psychological Association , these cases focus on features such as autoplay and infinite scrolling, rather than the content users post. However, researchers have yet to agree on how much harm these features cause. Johns Hopkins researcher Johannes Thrul estimates that social media addiction affects roughly 5% of people worldwide. The research did not officially acknowledge the condition as a diagnosis. The researchers also were not able to determine whether the autoplay and infinite scrolling features play a role in the development of mental health issues. When viewed in the light of YouTube’s advertising earnings, the proposed $3 billion settlement appears to be small. Alphabet reported YouTube advertising revenue of $11.207 billion in the third quarter of 2026. If this amount is maintained throughout the year, the annual revenue would be around $44.8 billion. The proposed settlement represents 6.7% of that annualized estimate or 7.4% of YouTube’s real advertising revenue of $40.367 billion in 2025. But how much would individual schools receive? Dividing $3 billion equally among all 19,183 operating US public school districts would give each roughly $156,000 . This is only an illustration, however. Actual payments would depend on which districts participate and how the money is distributed. The settlement could have consequences beyond the money YouTube pays. Changes to autoplay and personalized recommendations could affect how viewers discover videos, potentially reducing advertising opportunities for content creators. The stakes are growing. WARC expects social video to account for 51.7% of global video advertising spending in 2026. Any changes to how platforms keep audiences watching could therefore affect advertisers and creators worldwide. Meanwhile, European regulators are addressing similar concerns. The European Commission’s July 2025 guidelines recommend switching off autoplay and push notifications by default for minors. Although the guidelines are voluntary, regulators can use them when assessing compliance with the Digital Services Act. YouTube’s proposed settlement comes after other legal setbacks for social media companies. In March 2026, a Los Angeles jury awarded $6 million in an addiction case against Meta and YouTube. The decision is documented in Meta’s filing and the court verdict . Both companies challenged the ruling, which Cryptopolitan covered . Five months later, states announced a separate Meta settlement worth up to $17.1 billion over ten years. The agreement includes additional protections for young users but still requires court approval. The legal battles are not over. Another trial involving the Tucson school district and other social media platforms is scheduled for February 2027. Reuters, citing a Bloomberg News report, said YouTube has agreed in principle to pay about $3 billion, but the deal is not finalized: a majority of school districts must sign on, and US District Judge Yvonne Gonzalez Rogers must approve it, with finalization expected to take a few months. The districts argue that autoplay, infinite scrolling, and recommendation algorithms were built to keep young people hooked and worsened anxiety, depression, and eating disorders, claims the companies deny. No. Johns Hopkins researchers said problematic social media use is associated with loneliness, anxiety, and depression, but a causal link is still debated, and social media addiction is not a recognized clinical diagnosis. The decision is documented in Meta’s filing and the court verdict .
Both companies challenged the ruling, which Cryptopolitan covered .
The agreement still needs several approvals before it can move forward.
A majority of the school districts involved in the lawsuits must accept YouTube’s proposed settlement, which includes about $3 billion in compensation and additional safeguards for teenagers.
Judge Yvonne Gonzalez Rogers must then approve the agreement.
They claim that this has necessitated schools to increase their spending on mental health services and to enforce phone restrictions.
If this amount is maintained throughout the year, the annual revenue would be around $44.8 billion.
This agreement is currently in its preliminary stage.
Limiting YouTube use during school hours is not straightforward because teachers also rely on the platform for lessons.
Students, however, do not always use it for educational purposes.
The federal lawsuit, case 22-md-03047-YGR , focuses on allegations that how YouTube was designed hurts students’ mental health.
YouTube is not alone in facing these allegations.

Thousands of lawsuits filed by individuals, school districts and government agencies accuse social media companies, including Meta, TikTok and Snap, of designing platforms that encourage addictive behavior among young people.
According to the American Psychological Association , these cases focus on features such as autoplay and infinite scrolling, rather than the content users post.
The settlement could have consequences beyond the money YouTube pays.
Changes to autoplay and personalized recommendations could affect how viewers discover videos, potentially reducing advertising opportunities for content creators.
Johns Hopkins researcher Johannes Thrul estimates that social media addiction affects roughly 5% of people worldwide.
Another trial involving the Tucson school district and other social media platforms is scheduled for February 2027.

extraction.body: Meta is “re-evaluating” 2030 sustainability goals. Will others follow? Meta’s executives are rethinking the company’s original goal of achieving net-zero emissions by 2030. That revelation in Meta’s latest sustainability report comes as the company reported a record percentage increase in greenhouse gas emissions that exceeds any other Big Tech competitor racing to build new AI data centers. The company’s 2026 sustainability report claims that “our long-term ambitions haven’t changed, but our operating environment has,” according to an introduction from Rachel Peterson, vice president of data centers at Meta, and Blair Swedeen, global head of net zero and sustainability at Meta. In the November 19, 2026, report, they attributed the changing conditions and the need for a rethink to how “demand for AI infrastructure has grown faster than almost anyone projected.” “We are re-evaluating our timelines, sequencing, and interim milestones—including the 2030 timeframe for our net zero emissions goal and our near-term intensity targets—so our approach reflects current operating realities while keeping progress transparent year over year,” Peterson and Swedeen wrote in the report. Meta’s statement about re-evaluating its 2030 emissions goal is a significant public acknowledgment, given that Amazon, Google, and Microsoft have all stuck by their original sustainability goals so far. But all the companies have acknowledged challenges in balancing their original sustainability goals against the breakneck buildout of hyperscale data centers . Despite efforts to invest in more renewable energy projects, Meta and its rivals are still often pushing forward on AI data centers that rely on burning natural gas to generate electricity. Meta’s report described the company’s total emissions as surging from 15.6 million metric tonnes of carbon dioxide equivalent in 2024 to more than 21.7 million metric tonnes in 2025. That would make Meta’s annual carbon footprint roughly comparable to total emissions for the state of Idaho, while surpassing the total emissions of states such as Hawaii, Maine, South Dakota, and New Hampshire. The company attributed much of this emissions increase to “capital goods,” like as data center servers. That also represents a nearly 40 percent increase in Meta’s carbon footprint between 2024 and 2025, which is the highest percentage year-over-year increase for total emissions reported by any of the four major US tech giants. For comparison, Microsoft reported a 25 percent increase in its overall carbon footprint, Google reported an 18 percent increase, and Amazon’s report described a 16 percent increase between 2024 and 2025. However, Meta still likely has one of the smallest total carbon footprints among the Big Tech companies. Meta’s approach to achieving net-zero emissions has included developing new renewable energy projects to match emissions and using carbon removal technology. But even when factoring in such efforts, Meta still reported net emissions increasing from more than 8.1 million metric tonnes to more than 11.8 million metric tonnes for 2025. That represents a 45 percent increase. From a water consumption standpoint , Meta reported progress in reducing facility consumption from 825 million gallons in 2024 to 790 million gallons in 2025. Yet that positive trend is tempered by the fact that Meta also described an increase in water consumption from “areas with water stress,” rising from 198 million gallons in 2024 to 246 million gallons in 2025. Meta also reported a sharp increase in water consumption related to purchased electricity—the amount of water consumed by related power generation—from 19 billion gallons in 2024 to more than 26 billion gallons in 2025. This once again highlights that, for data centers, the far bigger water usage comes from the power plants that supply electricity to data centers as opposed to data centers directly using water for cooling. Still, some minor credit is due. The publication Data Center Dynamics pointed out that “Meta is the only hyperscaler to report indirect water use, a growing concern as data centers shift to closed-loop cooling systems that, despite using less water at source, require more electricity to run.” It would very much be in the public interest for other Big Tech companies to follow suit on the reporting front—and public pressure continues to build after the AI backlash impact on US midterm election results. passages: Meta is “re-evaluating” 2030 sustainability goals. Will others follow?

Meta’s executives are rethinking the company’s original goal of achieving net-zero emissions by 2030. That revelation in Meta’s latest sustainability report comes as the company reported a record percentage increase in greenhouse gas emissions that exceeds any other Big Tech competitor racing to build new AI data centers.

The company’s 2026 sustainability report claims that “our long-term ambitions haven’t changed, but our operating environment has,” according to an introduction from Rachel Peterson, vice president of data centers at Meta, and Blair Swedeen, global head of net zero and sustainability at Meta. In the November 19, 2026, report, they attributed the changing conditions and the need for a rethink to how “demand for AI infrastructure has grown faster than almost anyone projected.”

“We are re-evaluating our timelines, sequencing, and interim milestones—including the 2030 timeframe for our net zero emissions goal and our near-term intensity targets—so our approach reflects current operating realities while keeping progress transparent year over year,” Peterson and Swedeen wrote in the report.

Meta’s statement about re-evaluating its 2030 emissions goal is a significant public acknowledgment, given that Amazon, Google, and Microsoft have all stuck by their original sustainability goals so far.

But all the companies have acknowledged challenges in balancing their original sustainability goals against the breakneck buildout of hyperscale data centers . Despite efforts to invest in more renewable energy projects, Meta and its rivals are still often pushing forward on AI data centers that rely on burning natural gas to generate electricity.
Meta’s report described the company’s total emissions as surging from 15.6 million metric tonnes of carbon dioxide equivalent in 2024 to more than 21.7 million metric tonnes in 2025.

That would make Meta’s annual carbon footprint roughly comparable to total emissions for the state of Idaho, while surpassing the total emissions of states such as Hawaii, Maine, South Dakota, and New Hampshire. The company attributed much of this emissions increase to “capital goods,” like as data center servers.

That also represents a nearly 40 percent increase in Meta’s carbon footprint between 2024 and 2025, which is the highest percentage year-over-year increase for total emissions reported by any of the four major US tech giants.

For comparison, Microsoft reported a 25 percent increase in its overall carbon footprint, Google reported an 18 percent increase, and Amazon’s report described a 16 percent increase between 2024 and 2025. However, Meta still likely has one of the smallest total carbon footprints among the Big Tech companies.
Meta’s approach to achieving net-zero emissions has included developing new renewable energy projects to match emissions and using carbon removal technology.

But even when factoring in such efforts, Meta still reported net emissions increasing from more than 8.1 million metric tonnes to more than 11.8 million metric tonnes for 2025. That represents a 45 percent increase.
From a water consumption standpoint , Meta reported progress in reducing facility consumption from 825 million gallons in 2024 to 790 million gallons in 2025.

Yet that positive trend is tempered by the fact that Meta also described an increase in water consumption from “areas with water stress,” rising from 198 million gallons in 2024 to 246 million gallons in 2025.

Meta also reported a sharp increase in water consumption related to purchased electricity—the amount of water consumed by related power generation—from 19 billion gallons in 2024 to more than 26 billion gallons in 2025. This once again highlights that, for data centers, the far bigger water usage comes from the power plants that supply electricity to data centers as opposed to data centers directly using water for cooling.

Still, some minor credit is due. The publication Data Center Dynamics pointed out that “Meta is the only hyperscaler to report indirect water use, a growing concern as data centers shift to closed-loop cooling systems that, despite using less water at source, require more electricity to run.”

It would very much be in the public interest for other Big Tech companies to follow suit on the reporting front—and public pressure continues to build after the AI backlash impact on US midterm election results.

passages: Meta Platforms is reportedly reassessing its commitment to achieving net-zero carbon emissions by 2030, as highlighted by recent record emissions stemming from AI data center operations.
The company had initially set a comprehensive net-zero target in 2020, covering both its operations and supply chain.
However, the increased demand for AI-related data centers has led to a 45% rise in emissions, prompting a reevaluation of its timeline and interim goals.
This reassessment does not mean a withdrawal from its overall sustainability ambitions but indicates that the current pathway might need revision.
Observers will be closely monitoring any legislative developments in Oklahoma, where discussions around a data center moratorium are ongoing.
Key actors, such as the Oklahoma Legislature and Governor Kevin Stitt, could influence the outcome.
The market’s response to these developments could provide insights into the evolving landscape of environmental regulations surrounding data centers.

extraction.body: Meta is “re-evaluating” 2030 sustainability goals. Will others follow? Meta’s executives are rethinking the company’s original goal of achieving net-zero emissions by 2030. That revelation in Meta’s latest sustainability report comes as the company reported a record percentage increase in greenhouse gas emissions that exceeds any other Big Tech competitor racing to build new AI data centers. The company’s 2026 sustainability report claims that “our long-term ambitions haven’t changed, but our operating environment has,” according to an introduction from Rachel Peterson, vice president of data centers at Meta, and Blair Swedeen, global head of net zero and sustainability at Meta. In the November 19, 2026, report, they attributed the changing conditions and the need for a rethink to how “demand for AI infrastructure has grown faster than almost anyone projected.” “We are re-evaluating our timelines, sequencing, and interim milestones—including the 2030 timeframe for our net zero emissions goal and our near-term intensity targets—so our approach reflects current operating realities while keeping progress transparent year over year,” Peterson and Swedeen wrote in the report. Meta’s statement about re-evaluating its 2030 emissions goal is a significant public acknowledgment, given that Amazon, Google, and Microsoft have all stuck by their original sustainability goals so far. But all the companies have acknowledged challenges in balancing their original sustainability goals against the breakneck buildout of hyperscale data centers . Despite efforts to invest in more renewable energy projects, Meta and its rivals are still often pushing forward on AI data centers that rely on burning natural gas to generate electricity. Meta’s report described the company’s total emissions as surging from 15.6 million metric tonnes of carbon dioxide equivalent in 2024 to more than 21.7 million metric tonnes in 2025. That would make Meta’s annual carbon footprint roughly comparable to total emissions for the state of Idaho, while surpassing the total emissions of states such as Hawaii, Maine, South Dakota, and New Hampshire. The company attributed much of this emissions increase to “capital goods,” like as data center servers. That also represents a nearly 40 percent increase in Meta’s carbon footprint between 2024 and 2025, which is the highest percentage year-over-year increase for total emissions reported by any of the four major US tech giants. For comparison, Microsoft reported a 25 percent increase in its overall carbon footprint, Google reported an 18 percent increase, and Amazon’s report described a 16 percent increase between 2024 and 2025. However, Meta still likely has one of the smallest total carbon footprints among the Big Tech companies. Meta’s approach to achieving net-zero emissions has included developing new renewable energy projects to match emissions and using carbon removal technology. But even when factoring in such efforts, Meta still reported net emissions increasing from more than 8.1 million metric tonnes to more than 11.8 million metric tonnes for 2025. That represents a 45 percent increase. From a water consumption standpoint , Meta reported progress in reducing facility consumption from 825 million gallons in 2024 to 790 million gallons in 2025. Yet that positive trend is tempered by the fact that Meta also described an increase in water consumption from “areas with water stress,” rising from 198 million gallons in 2024 to 246 million gallons in 2025. Meta also reported a sharp increase in water consumption related to purchased electricity—the amount of water consumed by related power generation—from 19 billion gallons in 2024 to more than 26 billion gallons in 2025. This once again highlights that, for data centers, the far bigger water usage comes from the power plants that supply electricity to data centers as opposed to data centers directly using water for cooling. Still, some minor credit is due. The publication Data Center Dynamics pointed out that “Meta is the only hyperscaler to report indirect water use, a growing concern as data centers shift to closed-loop cooling systems that, despite using less water at source, require more electricity to run.” It would very much be in the public interest for other Big Tech companies to follow suit on the reporting front—and public pressure continues to build after the AI backlash impact on US midterm election results. Meta’s executives are rethinking the company’s original goal of achieving net-zero emissions by 2030. That revelation in Meta’s latest sustainability report comes as the company reported a record percentage increase in greenhouse gas emissions that exceeds any other Big Tech competitor racing to build new AI data centers.

The company’s 2026 sustainability report claims that “our long-term ambitions haven’t changed, but our operating environment has,” according to an introduction from Rachel Peterson, vice president of data centers at Meta, and Blair Swedeen, global head of net zero and sustainability at Meta. In the November 19, 2026, report, they attributed the changing conditions and the need for a rethink to how “demand for AI infrastructure has grown faster than almost anyone projected.”

“We are re-evaluating our timelines, sequencing, and interim milestones—including the 2030 timeframe for our net zero emissions goal and our near-term intensity targets—so our approach reflects current operating realities while keeping progress transparent year over year,” Peterson and Swedeen wrote in the report.

Meta’s statement about re-evaluating its 2030 emissions goal is a significant public acknowledgment, given that Amazon, Google, and Microsoft have all stuck by their original sustainability goals so far.

But all the companies have acknowledged challenges in balancing their original sustainability goals against the breakneck buildout of hyperscale data centers . Despite efforts to invest in more renewable energy projects, Meta and its rivals are still often pushing forward on AI data centers that rely on burning natural gas to generate electricity.
Meta’s report described the company’s total emissions as surging from 15.6 million metric tonnes of carbon dioxide equivalent in 2024 to more than 21.7 million metric tonnes in 2025.

That would make Meta’s annual carbon footprint roughly comparable to total emissions for the state of Idaho, while surpassing the total emissions of states such as Hawaii, Maine, South Dakota, and New Hampshire. The company attributed much of this emissions increase to “capital goods,” like as data center servers.

That also represents a nearly 40 percent increase in Meta’s carbon footprint between 2024 and 2025, which is the highest percentage year-over-year increase for total emissions reported by any of the four major US tech giants.

For comparison, Microsoft reported a 25 percent increase in its overall carbon footprint, Google reported an 18 percent increase, and Amazon’s report described a 16 percent increase between 2024 and 2025. However, Meta still likely has one of the smallest total carbon footprints among the Big Tech companies.
Meta’s approach to achieving net-zero emissions has included developing new renewable energy projects to match emissions and using carbon removal technology.

But even when factoring in such efforts, Meta still reported net emissions increasing from more than 8.1 million metric tonnes to more than 11.8 million metric tonnes for 2025. That represents a 45 percent increase.
From a water consumption standpoint , Meta reported progress in reducing facility consumption from 825 million gallons in 2024 to 790 million gallons in 2025.

Yet that positive trend is tempered by the fact that Meta also described an increase in water consumption from “areas with water stress,” rising from 198 million gallons in 2024 to 246 million gallons in 2025.

Meta also reported a sharp increase in water consumption related to purchased electricity—the amount of water consumed by related power generation—from 19 billion gallons in 2024 to more than 26 billion gallons in 2025. This once again highlights that, for data centers, the far bigger water usage comes from the power plants that supply electricity to data centers as opposed to data centers directly using water for cooling.

Still, some minor credit is due. The publication Data Center Dynamics pointed out that “Meta is the only hyperscaler to report indirect water use, a growing concern as data centers shift to closed-loop cooling systems that, despite using less water at source, require more electricity to run.”

It would very much be in the public interest for other Big Tech companies to follow suit on the reporting front—and public pressure continues to build after the AI backlash impact on US midterm election results.

In the November 19, 2026, report, they attributed the changing conditions and the need for a rethink to how “demand for AI infrastructure has grown faster than almost anyone projected.”

Meta’s statement about re-evaluating its 2030 emissions goal is a significant public acknowledgment, given that Amazon, Google, and Microsoft have all stuck by their original sustainability goals so far.
Despite efforts to invest in more renewable energy projects, Meta and its rivals are still often pushing forward on AI data centers that rely on burning natural gas to generate electricity.

Meta also reported a sharp increase in water consumption related to purchased electricity—the amount of water consumed by related power generation—from 19 billion gallons in 2024 to more than 26 billion gallons in 2025.

This once again highlights that, for data centers, the far bigger water usage comes from the power plants that supply electricity to data centers as opposed to data centers directly using water for cooling.

That would make Meta’s annual carbon footprint roughly comparable to total emissions for the state of Idaho, while surpassing the total emissions of states such as Hawaii, Maine, South Dakota, and New Hampshire.
The company attributed much of this emissions increase to “capital goods,” like as data center servers.
However, Meta still likely has one of the smallest total carbon footprints among the Big Tech companies.

Meta reported that its net emissions rose 45% in 2025 to 11.8 million tonnes of carbon dioxide equivalent, and the report was signed by Rachel Peterson and Blair Swedeen. Meta said its electricity use climbed 35% in 2025 as new data centers came online, and the company did not say what it will change or when it will decide.

Meta said it reached net zero in its own operations in 2020 by cutting emissions 94% from a 2017 baseline, mostly by buying renewable power. Meta also said it would post updates on its sustainability website, while Reuters reported that the cuts would hit non-AI teams as 2026 capital spending rises to as much as $135 billion.

Rachel Peterson and Blair Swedeen wrote that "The reality has been far more complex" after Meta set its net zero goal, and they tied the shift to demand for AI infrastructure. Meta said delivering on its vision "requires building the infrastructure that powers AI," and the company described the resulting buildout as outpacing what it had anticipated. Meta’s sustainability reporting also pointed to accounting methods that climate advocates view with scepticism, and Al Jazeera said the figure is based on those methods.

Meta’s report said its electricity use increased 35% in 2025 as additional data centers came online, and it attributed much of the emissions increase to capital goods like data center servers. Meta’s executives said they anticipated steady growth and falling clean energy costs when they set the goal, but they said the broader system did not enable progress at the pace they envisioned.

Meta’s reassessment arrived as Al Jazeera described a broader corporate retreat from climate pledges, naming General Motors, Walmart, Google, Coca-Cola and Pepsi as companies that had adjusted or weakened climate commitments. Al Jazeera said Google has watched its own emissions rise as AI workloads grew, and it said Google faces the same arithmetic as Meta. Meta’s report also set up a near-term test, because Meta did not announce a revised target date and said it would disclose updates later on its sustainability website.

Meta’s electricity and emissions figures were framed against data center scale, with a study cited by Al Jazeera finding 403 of the most powerful data centers in the United States accounted for about 2% of the country’s electricity use. Al Jazeera also said corporate emissions accounting methods, including renewable energy certificates, are ones climate advocates view with scepticism, and it warned that the physical grid impact could be worse than Meta’s reported number.

passages: Bitcoin has suffered nearly identical sell-offs ahead of two of the biggest public offerings this year, leaving investors wondering if competing demand for investor capital could be weighing on the cryptocurrency and perhaps delaying its recovery.
The price of the bitcoin dropped 22.7% in the 30 days before Anthropic's IPO and fell 22.3% in the month leading up to SpaceX's June 12 listing.
"Liquidity events can elevate correlations across asset classes quickly," Matthew Sheffield, chief investment officer at the ether treasury firm Sharplink , told CNBC.
"The first 15 min of [Thursday's] Anthropic IPO put that on full display.
Tech stocks, value stocks, oil, gold, crypto all sold off as traders sold assets to buy shares in the secondary market."
Bitcoin's next critical test is between $60,000 and $62,000, according to Nicolai Sondergaard, a research analyst at Nansen.
Throughout November, bitcoin has been struggling from a combination of dollar strength, institutional selling, and ongoing leveraged bitcoin liquidations.
Still, the post-IPO price action may offer a data point in understanding where bitcoin's price goes next.
With Anthropic now public, investors are watching to see whether bitcoin and ether find a floor, and if institutional demand returns.

"[After] the SpaceX IPO, bitcoin didn't truly find its final bottom until after the IPO was completed, and it didn't actually reverse the downtrend until 70 days later," said Matt Cole, CEO and chairman of Strive Asset Management , a bitcoin treasury firm.
Bitcoin is in the early stages of forming a bottom, according to Cole.

Retail fear is elevated amid recent outages, quantum concerns and other short-term uncertainties, but bitcoin should continue to benefit from macro forces like rising debt and weakening fiat currencies, which should drive price higher, he said.

extraction.body: Bitcoin has suffered nearly identical sell-offs ahead of two of the biggest public offerings this year, leaving investors wondering if competing demand for investor capital could be weighing on the cryptocurrency and perhaps delaying its recovery. The price of the bitcoin dropped 22.7% in the 30 days before Anthropic's IPO and fell 22.3% in the month leading up to SpaceX's June 12 listing. Ether declined 25.3% in the 30 days preceding Anthropic's debut, and 28% in the same window ahead of SpaceX. "Liquidity events can elevate correlations across asset classes quickly," Matthew Sheffield, chief investment officer at the ether treasury firm Sharplink , told CNBC. "The first 15 min of [Thursday's] Anthropic IPO put that on full display. Tech stocks, value stocks, oil, gold, crypto all sold off as traders sold assets to buy shares in the secondary market." "Stores of value function as such over long horizons, but in the short term are still liquidity driven," Sheffield said. "We saw this in early Covid when the market fled to cash. Stock, bonds, commodities ... it didn't matter, you were being sold for cash." While investors appear to be rotating capital out of crypto to make room for history-making IPO investments, that can't be said with precise certainty. Crypto has also been under pressure from ETF outflows, leverage, macro uncertainty and broader risk-off sentiment. Still, the post-IPO price action may offer a data point in understanding where bitcoin's price goes next. With Anthropic now public, investors are watching to see whether bitcoin and ether find a floor, and if institutional demand returns. "[After] the SpaceX IPO, bitcoin didn't truly find its final bottom until after the IPO was completed, and it didn't actually reverse the downtrend until 70 days later," said Matt Cole, CEO and chairman of Strive Asset Management , a bitcoin treasury firm. "My view is that [for] bitcoin, the most likely scenario is that it chops around here." The expiration of IPO allocation restrictions can influence the timing of capital flows into digital assets, Sheffield said. "Post SpaceX we saw the wealth effect in full force," Sheffield said. "Many brokers make traders wait 15-30 days before they are allowed to flip shares they received as allocations. … If you went long ETH versus SpaceX on the day of the IPO, on day 31 was when you would have become profitable." Bitcoin's next critical test is between $60,000 and $62,000, according to Nicolai Sondergaard, a research analyst at Nansen. On Friday, it was sitting at about $62,000. As of Friday, bitcoin was hovering at the upper end of a critical $60,000 to $62,000 support range. Its next move could determine whether it can stabilize or if it will face another leg lower and revisit its July low of $57,737.35. Throughout November, bitcoin has been struggling from a combination of dollar strength, institutional selling, and ongoing leveraged bitcoin liquidations. The declines began in late October, as concerns over artificial intelligence valuations and spending fueled a broad tech sell-off. They were compounded by the $6.3 billion Binance hack and weakening institutional ETF demand. Bitcoin is in the early stages of forming a bottom, according to Cole. Retail fear is elevated amid recent outages, quantum concerns and other short-term uncertainties, but bitcoin should continue to benefit from macro forces like rising debt and weakening fiat currencies, which should drive price higher, he said. "Capital markets are open, … retail fears are high, and when you combine those things it's much more likely to be a dip-buying opportunity across the board, including bitcoin, than the start of a great financial crisis," said Cole. "It'll likely age as a volatile time to consider allocating to risk, not the opposite." "The winter for bitcoin is basically at the end, but after winter does not come summer, it comes early spring," he added. "Anytime anyone's been around early spring, what you notice is it gets really cold still, it still rains – it's not necessarily great weather, and I think that's the environment we're in for bitcoin." Bitcoin's next critical test is between $60,000 and $62,000, according to Nicolai Sondergaard, a research analyst at Nansen. On Friday, it was sitting at about $62,000.

As of Friday, bitcoin was hovering at the upper end of a critical $60,000 to $62,000 support range. Its next move could determine whether it can stabilize or if it will face another leg lower and revisit its July low of $57,737.35.

Throughout November, bitcoin has been struggling from a combination of dollar strength, institutional selling, and ongoing leveraged bitcoin liquidations. The declines began in late October, as concerns over artificial intelligence valuations and spending fueled a broad tech sell-off. They were compounded by the $6.3 billion Binance hack and weakening institutional ETF demand.

Bitcoin is in the early stages of forming a bottom, according to Cole. Retail fear is elevated amid recent outages, quantum concerns and other short-term uncertainties, but bitcoin should continue to benefit from macro forces like rising debt and weakening fiat currencies, which should drive price higher, he said.

"Capital markets are open, … retail fears are high, and when you combine those things it's much more likely to be a dip-buying opportunity across the board, including bitcoin, than the start of a great financial crisis," said Cole. "It'll likely age as a volatile time to consider allocating to risk, not the opposite."

"The winter for bitcoin is basically at the end, but after winter does not come summer, it comes early spring," he added. "Anytime anyone's been around early spring, what you notice is it gets really cold still, it still rains – it's not necessarily great weather, and I think that's the environment we're in for bitcoin."

That is an almost identical dip the OG crypto recorded around the time of the SpaceX IPO in June, and given that it then went on a run that took it above $80,000, some market watchers are wondering whether the same can happen again. The comparisons were made in a November 19 post on X by CryptosRus, who shared a chart measuring peak-to-trough losses across the weeks before each company’s stock market debut. It showed that before SpaceX w ent public around June 12, BTC’s price had dropped by almost 29% from a peak close to $83,000 in early May to near $59,000 in the first week of June. After that, the asset made a recovery, eventually going as high as $87,000 in September. Something similar is also happening ahead of the Anthropic listing. After Bitcoin went to $87,400 on September 21, it started a steady decline that has it changing hands just above $63,000 at the time of writing, representing a drawdown of nearly 28% across 8 weeks. “Same setup, same opportunity,” CryptosRus wrote, suggesting that the earlier recovery could offer a reference point for the current market. That BTC drop near $63,000 triggered liquidations approaching $500 million, with positions worth more than $100 million wiped out in one hour. Data from CoinGecko shows the asset is nearly 2% lower than 24 hours ago, with the losses stretching to just over 14% across seven days and 21% in the last two weeks. In the previous month, the number one cryptocurrency has seen its price drop by almost 23%, while the plunge year-on-year stands at around 30%. The timing of the asset’s weakness and the Anthropic IPO prompted speculation that investors may have been moving their capital into AI companies. With Anthropic closing its first trading day up 17% at $97.17, crypto analysts are now watching to see if digital assets find a floor or if the liquidity drain deepens as more AI unicorns prepare to go public. The crypto market just delivered an eerie sense of déjà vu. Bitcoin and ether both experienced sharp sell-offs in the weeks leading up to Anthropic's public debut, mirroring almost exactly the same pattern that played out before SpaceX went public earlier this year. The correlation is raising uncomfortable questions for crypto bulls about whether institutional money views digital assets as a liquidity source to fund allocations in hot tech IPOs. As Anthropic priced its IPO at $83, topping its expected range on surging institutional demand, bitcoin slid from recent highs while ether underperformed even more dramatically. The pattern matches what happened in the lead-up to SpaceX's listing, when both cryptocurrencies shed double-digit percentages before finding support only after the IPO priced. When a massive IPO looms, institutional investors appear to be liquidating portions of their crypto holdings to free up capital for new allocations. It's a liquidity rotation that hits hardest in the two to three weeks before pricing, precisely when underwriters are locking in final commitments from large buyers. Anthropic's debut certainly commanded attention. But here's where it gets interesting for crypto traders. After SpaceX priced its IPO, bitcoin and ether both stabilized within days and then mounted modest recoveries over the following weeks. The theory goes that once institutional allocations are locked and IPO euphoria fades, some of that capital rotates back into crypto as investors rebalance portfolios. With Anthropic's first trading day in the books and the initial pop already priced in, crypto markets are testing whether they can find a floor. Bitcoin has shown some signs of stabilization, though trading volumes remain thin, suggesting many institutional players are still on the sidelines. What makes this pattern particularly concerning for crypto advocates is that it suggests digital assets are being treated as secondary holdings, something to liquidate when "real" opportunities like AI IPOs emerge. That's a far cry from the narrative of bitcoin as digital gold or a portfolio hedge that trades independently of traditional markets. The institutional demand picture is murkier than it was during previous crypto rallies. While bitcoin ETFs have attracted steady inflows this year, the pace has slowed considerably. Meanwhile, the pipeline of major tech IPOs remains robust, with several AI and enterprise software unicorns reportedly preparing listings for early 2027. If the SpaceX-Anthropic pattern holds, crypto investors should watch for a potential stabilization phase over the next week or two, followed by a test of whether institutional buyers return. The key variable is whether another blockbuster IPO gets announced soon, which could trigger a repeat of the cycle. Some crypto analysts argue the sell-off is actually healthy, shaking out weak hands and establishing clearer support levels. Others worry it exposes how dependent crypto markets have become on the same institutional money that chases every hot tech trend. The difference in perspective often comes down to whether you view crypto as a mature asset class or still an emerging one fighting for legitimacy. Bitcoin is hovering near technical support levels that held during previous corrections, while ether faces a more uncertain picture given its underperformance. Trading desks report that institutional inquiry has picked up slightly since Anthropic's debut, but no one is ready to call a bottom yet. The broader implication is that crypto's fate may be more intertwined with the tech IPO calendar than many investors realized. As long as venture-backed unicorns keep going public at premium valuations, institutional investors may continue using crypto as a source of liquidity to fund those allocations. That's not necessarily bearish long-term, but it does suggest crypto markets could face periodic pressure whenever the IPO window heats up. The identical sell-off pattern before both the SpaceX and Anthropic IPOs reveals an uncomfortable truth about institutional crypto holdings: they're being used as a liquidity pool to fund hot tech allocations. Whether bitcoin and ether can establish a floor now that Anthropic's debut is complete will signal if the SpaceX playbook repeats, with capital gradually rotating back into digital assets. But with more AI unicorns eyeing 2027 listings, crypto investors may need to accept that their markets are now tethered to the tech IPO calendar in ways that challenge the independence narrative. The next few weeks will show if institutional demand returns or if crypto faces another cycle of liquidation as the next blockbuster listing approaches.

Anthropic's debut certainly commanded attention.
But here's where it gets interesting for crypto traders.
After SpaceX priced its IPO, bitcoin and ether both stabilized within days and then mounted modest recoveries over the following weeks.
The theory goes that once institutional allocations are locked and IPO euphoria fades, some of that capital rotates back into crypto as investors rebalance portfolios.
With Anthropic's first trading day in the books and the initial pop already priced in, crypto markets are testing whether they can find a floor.
Bitcoin has shown some signs of stabilization, though trading volumes remain thin, suggesting many institutional players are still on the sidelines.

What makes this pattern particularly concerning for crypto advocates is that it suggests digital assets are being treated as secondary holdings, something to liquidate when "real" opportunities like AI IPOs emerge.
That's a far cry from the narrative of bitcoin as digital gold or a portfolio hedge that trades independently of traditional markets.
The institutional demand picture is murkier than it was during previous crypto rallies.
While bitcoin ETFs have attracted steady inflows this year, the pace has slowed considerably.
Meanwhile, the pipeline of major tech IPOs remains robust, with several AI and enterprise software unicorns reportedly preparing listings for early 2027.
If the SpaceX-Anthropic pattern holds, crypto investors should watch for a potential stabilization phase over the next week or two, followed by a test of whether institutional buyers return.
The key variable is whether another blockbuster IPO gets announced soon, which could trigger a repeat of the cycle.
Some crypto analysts argue the sell-off is actually healthy, shaking out weak hands and establishing clearer support levels.
Others worry it exposes how dependent crypto markets have become on the same institutional money that chases every hot tech trend.
The difference in perspective often comes down to whether you view crypto as a mature asset class or still an emerging one fighting for legitimacy.
Bitcoin is hovering near technical support levels that held during previous corrections, while ether faces a more uncertain picture given its underperformance.
Trading desks report that institutional inquiry has picked up slightly since Anthropic's debut, but no one is ready to call a bottom yet.
The broader implication is that crypto's fate may be more intertwined with the tech IPO calendar than many investors realized.
As long as venture-backed unicorns keep going public at premium valuations, institutional investors may continue using crypto as a source of liquidity to fund those allocations.
That's not necessarily bearish long-term, but it does suggest crypto markets could face periodic pressure whenever the IPO window heats up.

The identical sell-off pattern before both the SpaceX and Anthropic IPOs reveals an uncomfortable truth about institutional crypto holdings: they're being used as a liquidity pool to fund hot tech allocations.
Whether bitcoin and ether can establish a floor now that Anthropic's debut is complete will signal if the SpaceX playbook repeats, with capital gradually rotating back into digital assets.
But with more AI unicorns eyeing 2027 listings, crypto investors may need to accept that their markets are now tethered to the tech IPO calendar in ways that challenge the independence narrative.
The next few weeks will show if institutional demand returns or if crypto faces another cycle of liquidation as the next blockbuster listing approaches.

"The first 15 min of [Thursday's] Anthropic IPO put that on full display. Tech stocks, value stocks, oil, gold, crypto all sold off as traders sold assets to buy shares in the secondary market." "Stores of value function as such over long horizons, but in the short term are still liquidity driven," Sheffield said. "We saw this in early Covid when the market fled to cash. Stock, bonds, commodities ... it didn't matter, you were being sold for cash." While investors appear to be rotating capital out of crypto to make room for history-making IPO investments, that can't be said with precise certainty. Crypto has also been under pressure from ETF outflows, leverage, macro uncertainty and broader risk-off sentiment. Still, the post-IPO price action may offer a data point in understanding where bitcoin's price goes next. With Anthropic now public, investors are watching to see whether bitcoin and ether find a floor, and if institutional demand returns. "[After] the SpaceX IPO, bitcoin didn't truly find its final bottom until after the IPO was completed, and it didn't actually reverse the downtrend until 70 days later," said Matt Cole, CEO and chairman of Strive Asset Management , a bitcoin treasury firm. "My view is that [for] bitcoin, the most likely scenario is that it chops around here." The expiration of IPO allocation restrictions can influence the timing of capital flows into digital assets, Sheffield said. "Post SpaceX we saw the wealth effect in full force," Sheffield said. "Many brokers make traders wait 15-30 days before they are allowed to flip shares they received as allocations. … If you went long ETH versus SpaceX on the day of the IPO, on day 31 was when you would have become profitable." Bitcoin's next critical test is between $60,000 and $62,000, according to Nicolai Sondergaard, a research analyst at Nansen. On Friday, it was sitting at about $62,000. As long as venture-backed unicorns keep going public at premium valuations, institutional investors may continue using crypto as a source of liquidity to fund those allocations. That's not necessarily bearish long-term, but it does suggest crypto markets could face periodic pressure whenever the IPO window heats up. The identical sell-off pattern before both the SpaceX and Anthropic IPOs reveals an uncomfortable truth about institutional crypto holdings: they're being used as a liquidity pool to fund hot tech allocations. But with more AI unicorns eyeing 2027 listings, crypto investors may need to accept that their markets are now tethered to the tech IPO calendar in ways that challenge the independence narrative. The next few weeks will show if institutional demand returns or if crypto faces another cycle of liquidation as the next blockbuster listing approaches.

CrowdStrike's deals to this point have been on the smaller side.The company announced plans earlier this month to acquire agentic observability platform Fiddler AI and AI trust platform Dreadnode.

extraction.body: Bloomberg reported on November 20, 2026, that CrowdStrike was in ongoing talks to acquire Zscaler, citing people familiar with the matter, in a report carried by CNBC . Zscaler shares rose 18% in extended trading following the report, while CrowdStrike shares fell more than 8%. No acquisition agreement has been announced. CrowdStrike declined to comment on the report, and Zscaler did not immediately respond to a request for comment. CNBC put CrowdStrike’s market capitalization at $235 billion after its stock roughly doubled during 2026, while Zscaler’s was about $32 billion after a 13% decline during the year. A completed transaction would rank among cybersecurity’s largest, CNBC said. Its comparisons were Google’s $32 billion acquisition of Wiz in 2025, Cisco’s roughly $28 billion purchase of Splunk in 2024 and Palo Alto Networks’ $25 billion acquisition of CyberArk in 2026. Zscaler’s September 2, 2026 partnership announcement details an existing technical relationship between the companies. The expanded partnership is intended to automate security workflows and support real-time, adaptive Zero Trust enforcement by connecting CrowdStrike’s detection and response with Zscaler’s access controls. Zscaler said a planned integration using the OpenID Shared Signals Framework, an industry-standard method for sharing risk context, would let Falcon continuously evaluate user risk and pass that context to Zscaler’s Adaptive Access Engine. When suspicious endpoint behavior is detected, Zscaler can then automatically adjust access to match the current risk posture. The companies are also developing a native Falcon Foundry application built on Zscaler OneAPI. Planned functions include triggering Zscaler enforcement from Charlotte Agentic SOAR, CrowdStrike’s security automation interface, and supporting end-to-end automated remediation without middleware, connectors or separate infrastructure. Zscaler said network-event and AI-event logs are designed to stream into Falcon Next-Gen SIEM , CrowdStrike’s security-event management platform, where they can be correlated with Falcon endpoint, identity and cloud data. The combined telemetry is designed to help analysts reconstruct multi-stage attacks across domains. The AI telemetry includes AI-application interactions, risky chatbot prompts and policy violations, placing AI-specific risks alongside network and user activity in a unified investigation interface. Under the partnership plan, CrowdStrike would also expand Project QuiltWorks, an industry coalition focused on frontier AI risk, to include Zscaler . Zscaler cautioned that unreleased services and features covered by the announcement remained in development and subject to change. On November 3, 2026, CrowdStrike announced a definitive agreement to acquire Fiddler AI to add pre-deployment evaluation, continuous agent observability and explainability to Falcon. A separate agreement to acquire Dreadnode would add automated pre-deployment security testing of AI models, applications and agents. Both proposed acquisitions were expected to close in CrowdStrike’s fourth quarter of fiscal 2027, subject to customary closing conditions. The reported talks sit on top of an existing integration roadmap rather than a relationship built from scratch. The open question is whether that roadmap remains a partner integration or becomes part of a single company; for now, the documented product work and the reported transaction are at different stages, with several of the partnership’s features still in development. No acquisition agreement has been announced. CrowdStrike declined to comment on the report, and Zscaler did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
CNBC put CrowdStrike’s market capitalization at $235 billion after its stock roughly doubled during 2026, while Zscaler’s was about $32 billion after a 13% decline during the year.

A completed transaction would rank among cybersecurity’s largest, CNBC said. Its comparisons were Google’s $32 billion acquisition of Wiz in 2025, Cisco’s roughly $28 billion purchase of Splunk in 2024 and Palo Alto Networks’ $25 billion acquisition of CyberArk in 2026.

Zscaler’s September 2, 2026 partnership announcement details an existing technical relationship between the companies. The expanded partnership is intended to automate security workflows and support real-time, adaptive Zero Trust enforcement by connecting CrowdStrike’s detection and response with Zscaler’s access controls.

Zscaler said a planned integration using the OpenID Shared Signals Framework, an industry-standard method for sharing risk context, would let Falcon continuously evaluate user risk and pass that context to Zscaler’s Adaptive Access Engine. When suspicious endpoint behavior is detected, Zscaler can then automatically adjust access to match the current risk posture.

The companies are also developing a native Falcon Foundry application built on Zscaler OneAPI. Planned functions include triggering Zscaler enforcement from Charlotte Agentic SOAR, CrowdStrike’s security automation interface, and supporting end-to-end automated remediation without middleware, connectors or separate infrastructure.

Zscaler said network-event and AI-event logs are designed to stream into Falcon Next-Gen SIEM , CrowdStrike’s security-event management platform, where they can be correlated with Falcon endpoint, identity and cloud data. The combined telemetry is designed to help analysts reconstruct multi-stage attacks across domains. The AI telemetry includes AI-application interactions, risky chatbot prompts and policy violations, placing AI-specific risks alongside network and user activity in a unified investigation interface.

Under the partnership plan, CrowdStrike would also expand Project QuiltWorks, an industry coalition focused on frontier AI risk, to include Zscaler . Zscaler cautioned that unreleased services and features covered by the announcement remained in development and subject to change.

On November 3, 2026, CrowdStrike announced a definitive agreement to acquire Fiddler AI to add pre-deployment evaluation, continuous agent observability and explainability to Falcon. A separate agreement to acquire Dreadnode would add automated pre-deployment security testing of AI models, applications and agents. Both proposed acquisitions were expected to close in CrowdStrike’s fourth quarter of fiscal 2027, subject to customary closing conditions.

The reported talks sit on top of an existing integration roadmap rather than a relationship built from scratch. The open question is whether that roadmap remains a partner integration or becomes part of a single company; for now, the documented product work and the reported transaction are at different stages, with several of the partnership’s features still in development.

passages: CrowdStrike is in talks to acquire Zscaler, Bloomberg and Reuters reported on Friday, November 20, with Reuters putting its story out at 4:46 pm Eastern.
Both outlets cited people familiar with the discussions, which Reuters described as ongoing.
Neither company had commented when Reuters asked, and nothing has been announced.
Reuters was explicit that no deal is guaranteed and that the talks could end without an agreement.
Zscaler already carries a market value of about $33.5 billion, so a premium would push any CrowdStrike offer past $30 billion.
Zscaler jumped 17% and CrowdStrike fell 8%, according to Reuters.
Frankly, the fit looks better on a slide than it may in practice.

Zscaler and CrowdStrike aren't strangers: they've run a partnership for years, covering product integrations, threat-intelligence sharing and automated response, and customers who want both can already get both.
If the combination works only because it's a single invoice, the premium is hard to defend.
If it works because one team can finally write detection logic that sees the laptop and the network connection in the same data set, that's worth paying for.
CrowdStrike built its name on Falcon, a platform that began with endpoint protection, the software on laptops and servers, and has since grown into identity and cloud security through acquisitions.
What it has never had is a strong network-security product.
Zscaler sells exactly that: cloud-delivered zero-trust access, which decides who and what gets onto a company's applications and network before any traffic moves.
CrowdStrike posted strong fiscal first-quarter 2027 results and announced a four-for-one stock split, but the market reaction showed how high expectations have become for AI-linked software stocks.

The company is making a more concrete AI security case, but investors now want proof in growth, margins and guidance. - why AI security stocks face higher valuation standards - how CrowdStrike's strong earnings disappointed AI-focused investors
Reuters noted the purchase would close CrowdStrike's biggest gap and put it in more direct competition with platform vendors such as Palo Alto Networks.

Large companies have been cutting the number of security vendors they pay, and a buyer that can offer endpoint, identity, cloud and network from one contract has an easier sale than one that has to say "and for the network, call someone else."
That split is the oldest pattern in deal-making.
The target's holders get paid a premium, the buyer's holders get handed the bill and the integration risk.
An 8% drop in a company CrowdStrike's size wipes out a lot of value in a few hours, which is the market saying it wants to see the price and the plan before it believes in either.

sources.title: CrowdStrike is in talks to buy Zscaler, and only one stock liked the news - Startup Fortune
passages: CrowdStrike is in talks to acquire Zscaler, Bloomberg and Reuters reported on Friday, November 20, with Reuters putting its story out at 4:46 pm Eastern.
Both outlets cited people familiar with the discussions, which Reuters described as ongoing.
Neither company had commented when Reuters asked, and nothing has been announced.
Reuters was explicit that no deal is guaranteed and that the talks could end without an agreement.
Zscaler already carries a market value of about $33.5 billion, so a premium would push any CrowdStrike offer past $30 billion.
Zscaler jumped 17% and CrowdStrike fell 8%, according to Reuters.
Frankly, the fit looks better on a slide than it may in practice.

Zscaler and CrowdStrike aren't strangers: they've run a partnership for years, covering product integrations, threat-intelligence sharing and automated response, and customers who want both can already get both.
If the combination works only because it's a single invoice, the premium is hard to defend.
If it works because one team can finally write detection logic that sees the laptop and the network connection in the same data set, that's worth paying for.
CrowdStrike built its name on Falcon, a platform that began with endpoint protection, the software on laptops and servers, and has since grown into identity and cloud security through acquisitions.
What it has never had is a strong network-security product.
Zscaler sells exactly that: cloud-delivered zero-trust access, which decides who and what gets onto a company's applications and network before any traffic moves.
CrowdStrike posted strong fiscal first-quarter 2027 results and announced a four-for-one stock split, but the market reaction showed how high expectations have become for AI-linked software stocks.

The company is making a more concrete AI security case, but investors now want proof in growth, margins and guidance. - why AI security stocks face higher valuation standards - how CrowdStrike's strong earnings disappointed AI-focused investors
Reuters noted the purchase would close CrowdStrike's biggest gap and put it in more direct competition with platform vendors such as Palo Alto Networks.

Large companies have been cutting the number of security vendors they pay, and a buyer that can offer endpoint, identity, cloud and network from one contract has an easier sale than one that has to say "and for the network, call someone else."
That split is the oldest pattern in deal-making.
The target's holders get paid a premium, the buyer's holders get handed the bill and the integration risk.
An 8% drop in a company CrowdStrike's size wipes out a lot of value in a few hours, which is the market saying it wants to see the price and the plan before it believes in either.

sources.title: China attackers deployed AI agents that autonomously found and exploited a 0-day to take over a university server - The Register
passages: On September 10, Amazon's Threat Intelligence Team found a server with a publicly hosted instance of Cairn that provided visibility into the campaign targeting universities in East Asia, outside Mainland China, Moses said in a Friday report shared with The Register .

Before the AI agents found and exploited the zero day, however, they tried to break into another university’s Redis server over about 16 hours and 148 sequential actions, including abusing Redis's replication feature to load unauthorized code, escaping its scripting sandbox, writing to its configuration files, and corrupting its memory.

Meanwhile, a separate operation running for more than 6 hours targeted a university GPU server with another credential-spray attack, compiling a list of 80 real user names found across the school’s public websites, academic papers and other documents.
"The agents identified the application's framework, mapped its API endpoints, and found an upload endpoint with a filename parameter," Moses wrote.

None of these were successful, and when those actions failed, the agents also attempted a Log4Shell injection against a different service, a server-side request forgery (SSRF) attack against a vulnerability in a co-located Qdrant instance, and several credential sprays against PostgreSQL, SSH, and other tools.
PLUS: China upgrades smartphone surveillance tools; Ring eases anti-snooping stance; and more

The China-linked attacker used Cairn, an open source, penetration-testing framework that has become increasingly popular with cybercriminals who use the AI tool to carry out multi-stage intrusions with no human assistance .
