The agents, run through an open-source penetration-testing framework called Cairn, spent nearly two full days probing university networks in East Asia before breaking through, according to a report published Friday by CJ Moses, chief information security officer at Amazon Integrated Security. The activity was detected on Sept. 10, and the intrusions began two days earlier. Moses wrote that an agent capable of finding and exploiting a zero-day within minutes "completes its activity faster than many security operations centers can manually triage an alert." His prescription: organizations should lean on high-confidence detections that trigger automatic containment, with humans watching the results rather than signing off on every step. The breakthrough came against MONAI Label, an open-source application for medical imaging AI. The agents identified the software's framework, mapped its API endpoints and located an upload function that accepted a filename parameter. They then tested that parameter for path traversal, a technique that lets an attacker write files outside the directory an application is supposed to use. Within roughly 11 minutes of mapping the API, the agents could write files anywhere on the server, the report said. In a later session they planted a Python reverse shell in sitecustomize.py, a file Python loads at startup, and obtained root, the highest level of access on the machine. Amazon said it assessed with high confidence that the bug was a zero-day because no patch, advisory or prior public mention existed. The company alerted the project's maintainers, who issued a fix; a GitHub advisory published Nov. 18 rates the path traversal flaw as critical. The operator behind the campaign also pointed the agents at a second university network through a proxy, where a server ran the same vulnerable code. Amazon believes the same flaw was used to compromise that machine and open the tunnel. Before the zero-day fell, the agents made two sustained attempts that did not succeed, and the contrast illustrates how much machine speed has changed the economics of intrusion. Against the Redis in-memory database, which was exposed without a password, the agents tried to abuse replication to inject rogue code, escape the scripting sandbox, rewrite configuration files and corrupt memory. They also fired a Log4Shell exploit at another service on the same host, used a server-side request forgery flaw in a co-located Qdrant database to map the internal Docker network, and sprayed credentials at SSH, PostgreSQL and other services. On the GPU server, they assembled a list of about 80 real usernames from faculty directories, lab sites, archived pages and published papers before running their credential attack. Moses noted that the agents "ran continuously for 16 hours without breaks, sleep, or working-hour constraints." Amazon tied the campaign to a China-linked operator with moderate confidence, citing prompts written in Simplified Chinese, scripts configured to China Standard Time and targets of likely strategic interest to Beijing. Because the victims were not AWS customers, the company passed word through a government partner. The Cairn framework has surfaced in other investigations. Gambit Security's threat intelligence team documented a Chinese operator using it in at least 105 attacks that compromised 27 companies to varying degrees, including a Fortune 500 hospitality company, a major U.S. airline, a large private industrial supplies distributor and an online fashion retailer. Google researchers said on Nov. 17 that they had found Cairn in intrusions at American aerospace companies. Moses said the cases together show the framework is being picked up for both espionage and financial crime. The disclosure lands as defenders debate how much autonomy to hand to security tooling. Moses' argument is that the alternative to automated response is a human queue that an agent can outrun. Security teams that wait for an analyst to confirm each alert are, in effect, giving an intruder a head start measured in minutes, and the MONAI Label episode shows that window is now wide enough to go from first contact to full control of a server. For software maintainers, the case is a reminder that open-source projects serving specialized fields such as medical imaging can sit inside university and hospital networks without anyone watching their upload endpoints. The flaw is now public and patched, but Amazon's account suggests the agents found it by probing, not by reading code, which means similar gaps elsewhere may be discovered the same way. extraction.body: 'Agents kept adapting for nearly a full day without human direction,' Amazon CISO said Suspected Chinese spies deployed AI agents which worked autonomously to find a zero-day in an open source application and then abuse the flaw to break into university networks, gaining full control of a server, according to Amazon CISO CJ Moses. The China-linked attacker used Cairn, an open source, penetration-testing framework that has become increasingly popular with cybercriminals who use the AI tool to carry out multi-stage intrusions with no human assistance . In this case, the agents found and exploited a zero-day MONAI Label, an open-source medical imaging AI application. Amazon notified the project's maintainers of the vulnerability, and they released a fix and a security advisory . On September 10, Amazon's Threat Intelligence Team found a server with a publicly hosted instance of Cairn that provided visibility into the campaign targeting universities in East Asia, outside Mainland China, Moses said in a Friday report shared with The Register . The campaign occurred over a period of 48 hours beginning on September 8, and the prompts were written in Simplified Chinese, with timestamps in executed scripts configured to China Standard Time. Before the AI agents found and exploited the zero day, however, they tried to break into another university’s Redis server over about 16 hours and 148 sequential actions, including abusing Redis's replication feature to load unauthorized code, escaping its scripting sandbox, writing to its configuration files, and corrupting its memory. None of these were successful, and when those actions failed, the agents also attempted a Log4Shell injection against a different service, a server-side request forgery (SSRF) attack against a vulnerability in a co-located Qdrant instance, and several credential sprays against PostgreSQL, SSH, and other tools. Meanwhile, a separate operation running for more than 6 hours targeted a university GPU server with another credential-spray attack, compiling a list of 80 real user names found across the school’s public websites, academic papers and other documents. "Neither operation succeeded, yet together they show that the agents kept adapting for nearly a full day without human direction," Moses wrote. Suspected Chinese spies deployed AI agents which worked autonomously to find a zero-day in an open source application and then abuse the flaw to break into university networks, gaining full control of a server, according to Amazon CISO CJ Moses.

The China-linked attacker used Cairn, an open source, penetration-testing framework that has become increasingly popular with cybercriminals who use the AI tool to carry out multi-stage intrusions with no human assistance .

extraction.body: Amazon's security chief is urging defenders to let machines respond to attacks automatically, after AI agents operating without step-by-step human direction discovered an unknown software flaw and used it to take over a university server. The agents, run through an open-source penetration-testing framework called Cairn, spent nearly two full days probing university networks in East Asia before breaking through, according to a report published Friday by CJ Moses, chief information security officer at Amazon Integrated Security. The activity was detected on Sept. 10, and the intrusions began two days earlier. Moses wrote that an agent capable of finding and exploiting a zero-day within minutes "completes its activity faster than many security operations centers can manually triage an alert." His prescription: organizations should lean on high-confidence detections that trigger automatic containment, with humans watching the results rather than signing off on every step. The breakthrough came against MONAI Label, an open-source application for medical imaging AI. The agents identified the software's framework, mapped its API endpoints and located an upload function that accepted a filename parameter. They then tested that parameter for path traversal, a technique that lets an attacker write files outside the directory an application is supposed to use. Within roughly 11 minutes of mapping the API, the agents could write files anywhere on the server, the report said. In a later session they planted a Python reverse shell in sitecustomize.py, a file Python loads at startup, and obtained root, the highest level of access on the machine. Amazon said it assessed with high confidence that the bug was a zero-day because no patch, advisory or prior public mention existed. The company alerted the project's maintainers, who issued a fix; a GitHub advisory published Nov. 18 rates the path traversal flaw as critical. The operator behind the campaign also pointed the agents at a second university network through a proxy, where a server ran the same vulnerable code. Amazon believes the same flaw was used to compromise that machine and open the tunnel. Before the zero-day fell, the agents made two sustained attempts that did not succeed, and the contrast illustrates how much machine speed has changed the economics of intrusion. Against the Redis in-memory database, which was exposed without a password, the agents tried to abuse replication to inject rogue code, escape the scripting sandbox, rewrite configuration files and corrupt memory. They also fired a Log4Shell exploit at another service on the same host, used a server-side request forgery flaw in a co-located Qdrant database to map the internal Docker network, and sprayed credentials at SSH, PostgreSQL and other services. On the GPU server, they assembled a list of about 80 real usernames from faculty directories, lab sites, archived pages and published papers before running their credential attack. Moses noted that the agents "ran continuously for 16 hours without breaks, sleep, or working-hour constraints." Amazon tied the campaign to a China-linked operator with moderate confidence, citing prompts written in Simplified Chinese, scripts configured to China Standard Time and targets of likely strategic interest to Beijing. Because the victims were not AWS customers, the company passed word through a government partner. The Cairn framework has surfaced in other investigations. Gambit Security's threat intelligence team documented a Chinese operator using it in at least 105 attacks that compromised 27 companies to varying degrees, including a Fortune 500 hospitality company, a major U.S. airline, a large private industrial supplies distributor and an online fashion retailer. Google researchers said on Nov. 17 that they had found Cairn in intrusions at American aerospace companies. Moses said the cases together show the framework is being picked up for both espionage and financial crime. The disclosure lands as defenders debate how much autonomy to hand to security tooling. Moses' argument is that the alternative to automated response is a human queue that an agent can outrun. Security teams that wait for an analyst to confirm each alert are, in effect, giving an intruder a head start measured in minutes, and the MONAI Label episode shows that window is now wide enough to go from first contact to full control of a server. For software maintainers, the case is a reminder that open-source projects serving specialized fields such as medical imaging can sit inside university and hospital networks without anyone watching their upload endpoints. The flaw is now public and patched, but Amazon's account suggests the agents found it by probing, not by reading code, which means similar gaps elsewhere may be discovered the same way. sources.title: Strategy’s valuation falls below its bitcoin reserves for the first time - ForkLog
passages: Strategy’s enterprise mNAV fell below 1, putting its valuation under bitcoin reserves.
As MSTR fell to around $82, the company’s value declined to $50.4 billion.
While the shares traded well above the value of BTC on the balance sheet, the company could issue new stock, buy the asset, and increase its per-share figure.
Separately, Strategy’s board authorized a bitcoin monetization program.
It allows the company to sell bitcoin to top up the dollar reserve by up to $1.25 billion, pay dividends and interest, and repurchase credit instruments and MSTR shares.
He said the company may consider selling bitcoin if mNAV falls below 1 and other sources of capital are exhausted.
The company also raised the annual dividend rate on STRC by 50 basis points to 12%.
Strategy will evaluate the rate monthly, considering the price of STRC, market yields, credit spreads, bitcoin’s price and volatility, dollar-reserve coverage, and the overall capital structure.
As part of the new policy, Strategy increased its dollar reserve to $2.55 billion.
The minimum reserve level is set at 12 months of such obligations.
In 2026, Strategy actively used perpetual preferred securities, including STRC, to finance bitcoin purchases.
On June 23, Strategy filed with the SEC to move STRC to semi-monthly distributions.
On June 29, Saylor presented a capital framework for digital credit instruments.
It is aimed at supporting liquidity, preserving long-term bitcoin exposure, and managing obligations to holders of such securities.
Analysts Support Strategy’s Shift from Pure Bitcoin Reserves
Between May 26 and May 31, Strategy sold 32 BTC for roughly $2.5 million at an average price of $77,135 per coin.
According to the official purchases table , as of June 22 Strategy held 847,363 BTC.
Before that, Strategy bought 1,587 BTC during June 8–14 and 1,550 BTC during June 1–7.
In June, Strategy founder Michael Saylor presented the “digital asset stack” concept.
In his view, bitcoin will evolve from a simple asset into the foundation of global financial architecture.
Michael Saylor Asserts Strategy Will Withstand Bitcoin’s Fall to $8000
Investors accuse JPMorgan of targeting Michael Saylor’s Strategy
Coin Bureau founder Nik Pakrin told Reuters the development is “bad news for overall investor sentiment toward cryptocurrencies and bitcoin.”

The fall came as record outflows from BlackRock's spot Bitcoin ETF, a sharp sell-off in US tech stocks, and the prospect of further Fed rate rises weighed on risk appetite. Bitcoin dropped sharply in the afternoon, sliding from $61,113 to a 24-hour low of $58,678.48. Coinbase daily data show Bitcoin last traded below $60,000 on 2 July, when it touched $59,520.02. passages: Bitcoin slid below $60,000 on Friday, November 20, for the first time since July, Reuters reported, trading at $59,381 and down 3.45% at the time of the report.
Cointelegraph later put it near $58,450, down 6.2% over 24 hours, after an intraday low of $58,811.
The Nasdaq Composite was off 2.73% and the S&P 500 had lost 1.44%, with US indexes on course for their worst week since April 2025.

CoinGlass data shows 101,831 traders got liquidated as bitcoin fell below $84,500 this week, with $487 million of the damage hitting long positions after 90.54% of open BTC bets had leaned bullish going into the drop. - bitcoin price drop liquidations over 550 million - leveraged trading positions wiped out crypto market
Spot bitcoin ETFs lost $582.3 million on Thursday, with BlackRock's IBIT taking $541.1 million of it, while long traders made up more than 80% of bitcoin liquidations.
Bitcoin is now roughly half its October peak as Fed hike bets build.
The Federal Reserve is holding at 3.75% to 4.00%, and Cointelegraph reported that Polymarket traders put the odds of another hike by December 9 at 94%.
Bitcoin pays no yield, so every notch up in borrowing costs makes it harder to justify holding.
James Butterfill of CoinShares told the market that bitcoin has increasingly traded alongside other liquidity-sensitive growth assets.
Frankly, that's the end of the hedge argument for this cycle.
Gold is also weak, so there was no safe haven to flee to on the day, and bitcoin behaved like a Nasdaq name with a 24-hour trading window.
Not everyone thinks the pain has much further to run.
Alexander Blume of Two Prime said sellers and leverage liquidations look largely exhausted and he wouldn't be surprised to see bitcoin find a bottom soon.
That's one view from one trading firm, and a $60,000 level that gave way in a few hours isn't a floor anyone can promise.
That puts bitcoin roughly 50% below its October record, according to figures cited in market coverage, and about 30% below where it traded a month ago.
When bitcoin's price falls, mining revenue drops.

Spot bitcoin ETFs lost $582.3 million on Thursday, with BlackRock's IBIT taking $541.1 million of it, while long traders made up more than 80% of bitcoin liquidations. Bitcoin is now roughly half its October peak as Fed hike bets build.
Bitcoin spent a year being sold as digital gold and has just traded like a leveraged tech stock. If you hold it for protection against a stock crash, Friday was the test, and it failed.

Bitcoin slid below $60,000 on Friday, November 20, for the first time since July, Reuters reported, trading at $59,381 and down 3.45% at the time of the report. Cointelegraph later put it near $58,450, down 6.2% over 24 hours, after an intraday low of $58,811. The Nasdaq Composite was off 2.73% and the S&P 500 had lost 1.44%, with US indexes on course for their worst week since April 2025.

That puts bitcoin roughly 50% below its October record, according to figures cited in market coverage, and about 30% below where it traded a month ago. Cointelegraph counts a 13.8% drop in seven days alone.

Reuters pointed to a pile of worries landing at once: doubts about whether the huge AI infrastructure spending will ever pay for itself, rising borrowing costs, regulatory risk after the Democrats' win in the US midterms, and the departure of Nvidia chief Jensen Huang. None of those is a crypto story. All of them hit the same pool of buyers.

Rates are doing a lot of the work. The Federal Reserve is holding at 3.75% to 4.00%, and Cointelegraph reported that Polymarket traders put the odds of another hike by December 9 at 94%. Bitcoin pays no yield, so every notch up in borrowing costs makes it harder to justify holding.

US spot Bitcoin ETFs shed roughly $450 million between September 8 and 10, the sharpest outflow run since June, just weeks after a three-week streak brought in over $3 billion. ARKB took the biggest hit while BlackRock's IBIT held up better, as Bitcoin slid toward $76,000 ahead of a hot CPI print and the Fed's September 16 rate decision under new... - bitcoin ETF outflows after billion dollar inflow week - fastest bitcoin ETF reversal since June 2026

James Butterfill of CoinShares told the market that bitcoin has increasingly traded alongside other liquidity-sensitive growth assets. Frankly, that's the end of the hedge argument for this cycle. Gold is also weak, so there was no safe haven to flee to on the day, and bitcoin behaved like a Nasdaq name with a 24-hour trading window.

US spot bitcoin ETFs took $582.3 million in net outflows on Thursday, up from $306.5 million on Wednesday, according to Cointelegraph. BlackRock's iShares Bitcoin Trust accounted for $541.1 million of that, which Rolling Out described as its largest single-day outflow since launch. Total outflows for November now stand at about $3.47 billion, based on figures reported by crypto.news.

If you bought through an ETF in the autumn, you're likely under water, and these outflows look like holders giving up rather than traders rotating. That matters for the next leg, because ETF buying was the steady bid under this market for two years.

Leverage made it worse. Liquidations ran into the high hundreds of millions of dollars on the day's early figures, with longs making up 82.4% of bitcoin's forced closures, according to Rolling Out. Some trackers later put the 24-hour total higher, near $1.5 billion across all coins, so treat the early number as a floor.

Crypto equities have been taking hits for weeks. Coinbase and Circle each fell about 7.5% on November 16, and 24/7 Wall St. reported that Circle dropped 12% and Coinbase and Strategy about 10% on November 5.

Miners are the more awkward case. Firms such as Core Scientific, IREN and Cipher have spent a year selling themselves as AI landlords, renting power and floor space to the same GPU buyers now being marked down. When bitcoin's price falls, mining revenue drops. When AI sentiment falls, the new business gets repriced. A chart of the two moving together would be hard to argue with.

Not everyone thinks the pain has much further to run. Alexander Blume of Two Prime said sellers and leverage liquidations look largely exhausted and he wouldn't be surprised to see bitcoin find a bottom soon. That's one view from one trading firm, and a $60,000 level that gave way in a few hours isn't a floor anyone can promise.

CoinGlass data shows 101,831 traders got liquidated as bitcoin fell below $84,500 this week, with $487 million of the damage hitting long positions after 90.54% of open BTC bets had leaned bullish going into the drop. - bitcoin price drop liquidations over 550 million - leveraged trading positions wiped out crypto market
The next hard data point is Monday's ETF flow report. Another $500 million day would say the exit hasn't finished.

coreStoryFacts.text: Nov 20 (Reuters) - Bitcoin, the world's largest cryptocurrency, fell below the $60,000 level on Friday for the first time since July, as lofty valuation concerns weighed on the AI trade and other risk assets.
Ether, the second-largest cryptocurrency, was down 5.23% at $1,648.91.
Strategy’s enterprise mNAV fell below 1, putting its valuation under bitcoin reserves.
As MSTR fell to around $82, the company’s value declined to $50.4 billion.
While the shares traded well above the value of BTC on the balance sheet, the company could issue new stock, buy the asset, and increase its per-share figure.
Separately, Strategy’s board authorized a bitcoin monetization program.
It allows the company to sell bitcoin to top up the dollar reserve by up to $1.25 billion, pay dividends and interest, and repurchase credit instruments and MSTR shares.
He said the company may consider selling bitcoin if mNAV falls below 1 and other sources of capital are exhausted.
The company also raised the annual dividend rate on STRC by 50 basis points to 12%.
Strategy will evaluate the rate monthly, considering the price of STRC, market yields, credit spreads, bitcoin’s price and volatility, dollar-reserve coverage, and the overall capital structure.
As part of the new policy, Strategy increased its dollar reserve to $2.55 billion.
The minimum reserve level is set at 12 months of such obligations.
In 2026, Strategy actively used perpetual preferred securities, including STRC, to finance bitcoin purchases.
On June 23, Strategy filed with the SEC to move STRC to semi-monthly distributions.
On June 29, Saylor presented a capital framework for digital credit instruments.
It is aimed at supporting liquidity, preserving long-term bitcoin exposure, and managing obligations to holders of such securities.
Analysts Support Strategy’s Shift from Pure Bitcoin Reserves
Between May 26 and May 31, Strategy sold 32 BTC for roughly $2.5 million at an average price of $77,135 per coin.
According to the official purchases table , as of June 22 Strategy held 847,363 BTC.
Before that, Strategy bought 1,587 BTC during June 8–14 and 1,550 BTC during June 1–7.
In June, Strategy founder Michael Saylor presented the “digital asset stack” concept.
In his view, bitcoin will evolve from a simple asset into the foundation of global financial architecture.

The market is valuing Strategy below its bitcoin reserves: the company’s enterprise mNAV fell below 1, Reuters reported . In December 2025, the market had already valued the company’s market cap below the value of its BTC reserves, but that was based on basic mNAV. The metric compares a company’s market capitalization with the amount of digital assets on its balance sheet. Enterprise mNAV reflects the entire capital structure: common equity market cap, debt, perpetual preferreds, and the dollar reserve. As MSTR fell to around $82, the company’s value declined to $50.4 billion. With bitcoin near $60,000, Strategy’s bitcoin reserves were valued at roughly $51.1 billion. “At these levels, issuing new shares becomes dilutive, as the company would effectively be selling equity at a price below the value of its underlying assets,” CoinDesk noted. The premium to bitcoin reserves has been central to Strategy’s model. While the shares traded well above the value of BTC on the balance sheet, the company could issue new stock, buy the asset, and increase its per-share figure. When enterprise mNAV drops below 1, the firm still has access to other capital management tools, including debt, preferreds, refinancing, and cash flow from its core business. However, issuing common stock at such levels can increase pressure on shareholders due to dilution. Reuters cited a December statement by Strategy CEO Fong Le. He said the company may consider selling bitcoin if mNAV falls below 1 and other sources of capital are exhausted. Le described this as a last resort rather than a change in policy. Between May 26 and May 31, Strategy sold 32 BTC for roughly $2.5 million at an average price of $77,135 per coin. According to the official purchases table , as of June 22 Strategy held 847,363 BTC. The aggregate acquisition cost was $64.1 billion, with an average purchase price of $75,651 per coin. The latest disclosed purchase was during June 15–21: the company acquired 520 BTC for about $35 million at an average price of $67,068. Before that, Strategy bought 1,587 BTC during June 8–14 and 1,550 BTC during June 1–7. With bitcoin below $60,000, the company’s position is under its average purchase price. Reuters valued Strategy’s reserve at roughly $50.4 billion based on Sunday’s bitcoin close at $59,577.82. The issue is not limited to common shares. In 2026, Strategy actively used perpetual preferred securities, including STRC, to finance bitcoin purchases. Against this backdrop, STRC also came under pressure. On Friday the securities fell to a new low around $71.40, then recovered to $74.72. That is about 26% below the $100 par value. With STRC around $73, the securities’ effective yield approached 15%, increasing expectations of a dividend rate hike, The Block wrote. On June 23, Strategy filed with the SEC to move STRC to semi-monthly distributions. On June 29, Saylor presented a capital framework for digital credit instruments. It is aimed at supporting liquidity, preserving long-term bitcoin exposure, and managing obligations to holders of such securities. As part of the new policy, Strategy increased its dollar reserve to $2.55 billion. According to the company, this covers 17.4 months of expected preferred dividend payments and interest expense. The minimum reserve level is set at 12 months of such obligations. The company also raised the annual dividend rate on STRC by 50 basis points to 12%. The change takes effect in July 2026. Strategy will evaluate the rate monthly, considering the price of STRC, market yields, credit spreads, bitcoin’s price and volatility, dollar-reserve coverage, and the overall capital structure. Separately, Strategy’s board authorized a bitcoin monetization program. It allows the company to sell bitcoin to top up the dollar reserve by up to $1.25 billion, pay dividends and interest, and repurchase credit instruments and MSTR shares. Strategy also approved buyback programs of up to $1 billion each: for credit instruments including STRC, STRF, STRD and STRK, and for Class A common shares. The company emphasized that such repurchases will not be funded from the dollar reserve. As The Block noted, other companies using the bitcoin-treasury model are also under pressure. Japanese Metaplanet’s enterprise mNAV was about 0.9, and Nakamoto, backed by David Bailey, about 0.92. Strive is an exception. According to BitcoinTreasuries , its enterprise mNAV was around 1.24. Coin Bureau founder Nik Pakrin told Reuters the development is “bad news for overall investor sentiment toward cryptocurrencies and bitcoin.” “MSTR was that one digital treasury company investors continued to believe in, but that belief is now eroding. We are already seeing it in the price of bitcoin,” he said. In June, Strategy founder Michael Saylor presented the “digital asset stack” concept. In his view, bitcoin will evolve from a simple asset into the foundation of global financial architecture. At the end of the month, CEO Ripple Brad Garlinghouse called the model harmful for the market ; it finances cryptocurrency purchases by issuing preferred stock. WhatsApp patched three security vulnerabilities, including an Android flaw the company suspects scammers used to make fraudulent messages look credible.
The first flaw, CVE-2026-23871, affects WhatsApp for Android and WhatsApp Business for Android before version 2.26.17.4.
It involves incomplete validation of external ad-reply URLs.
An attacker could send media from an attacker-controlled URL in a crafted Click to WhatsApp ad-reply message.
WhatsApp said someone may have used the flaw with specific spam messages.
The company's security team discovered and reported the issue.
A WhatsApp spokesperson said the team found the flaw while disrupting a scam campaign and believes a scammer used it to make scam messages seem more credible.
WhatsApp did not disclose the scale of the activity or whether those efforts succeeded.
The tap can delete files stored on the device.
An actor positioned inside Meta infrastructure could bypass the hardware root of trust with a Versioned Chip Endorsement Key (VCEK) certificate not signed by the hardware manufacturer's key.
Someone would first need to publish that certificate to the third-party binary transparency ledger that WhatsApp Private Processing uses.
WhatsApp advises users to keep apps and devices updated.
The company said it keeps strengthening its systems and acknowledged the bug bounty community's contributions to platform security.

WhatsApp patched three security vulnerabilities, including an Android flaw the company suspects scammers used to make fraudulent messages look credible. The first flaw, CVE-2026-23871, affects WhatsApp for Android and WhatsApp Business for Android before version 2.26.17.4. It involves incomplete validation of external ad-reply URLs. An attacker could send media from an attacker-controlled URL in a crafted Click to WhatsApp ad-reply message. When WhatsApp displayed that message in a thread, the attacker could learn the target's IP address. WhatsApp said someone may have used the flaw with specific spam messages. The company's security team discovered and reported the issue. A WhatsApp spokesperson said the team found the flaw while disrupting a scam campaign and believes a scammer used it to make scam messages seem more credible. WhatsApp did not disclose the scale of the activity or whether those efforts succeeded. The second flaw, CVE-2026-102769, is an SQL injection vulnerability in WhatsApp for Android before version 2.26.35.74. It occurs when a recipient taps a crafted "order details" message sent from an unofficial client. The tap can delete files stored on the device. An attacker could learn one bit about the user's chat database through an induced-crash delivery receipt timing side channel if the user is online when the malicious message arrives. WhatsApp said it found no evidence that anyone exploited the flaw in the wild. The third flaw, CVE-2026-44908, is a trust-validation vulnerability in WhatsApp's certificate verification mechanism for Meta AI's confidential computing infrastructure. It affects WhatsApp for iOS before version 2.26.24.72, WhatsApp Business for iOS and WhatsApp for Mac Desktop before version 2.26.23.72, WhatsApp for Android before version 2.26.23.74, and WhatsApp Business for Android before version 2.26.23.70. An actor positioned inside Meta infrastructure could bypass the hardware root of trust with a Versioned Chip Endorsement Key (VCEK) certificate not signed by the hardware manufacturer's key. Someone would first need to publish that certificate to the third-party binary transparency ledger that WhatsApp Private Processing uses. WhatsApp said the ledger shows every published VCEK certificate chains to the hardware root of trust, which confirms no exploitation. WhatsApp advises users to keep apps and devices updated. The company said it keeps strengthening its systems and acknowledged the bug bounty community's contributions to platform security. The disclosures, reported on 20 November, cover different parts of the service and do not all carry the same evidence of abuse.
The first issue, CVE-2026-23871, affected the Android editions of WhatsApp and WhatsApp Business before version 2.26.17.4.
The company's advisory says inadequate checks on external ad-reply addresses could cause a device to disclose IP information when a specially prepared message appeared in a conversation.
The November disclosures describe three patched problems, not one sweeping breach.
Only the ad-reply issue comes with suspected real-world abuse, and the scale remains undisclosed.
WhatsApp recommends keeping its apps and devices updated.
The affected-version limits differ by vulnerability and platform, so the Android ad-reply fix alone does not describe every correction in this release of advisories.
The suspected scam-related flaw concerns media in replies to Click to WhatsApp advertisements.
Two other fixes address a malicious order-details message and the checks used to establish trust in Meta AI's confidential computing systems.
WhatsApp says it has not found evidence of attacks exploiting those two issues.
It affected specified WhatsApp and Business releases across Android and iOS, plus the Mac desktop app.
The company says the ledger contains no such invalid certificate, supporting its conclusion that this flaw was not exploited.

extraction.body: Meta-owned messaging platform WhatsApp has patched three security vulnerabilities affecting its Android, iOS and desktop applications, including a flaw suspected of being misused in connection with fraudulent messages. The vulnerabilities could potentially expose users’ IP information, delete locally stored files and weaken certificate verification protections associated with Meta AI infrastructure. One of the vulnerabilities, identified as CVE-2026-23871, was discovered by WhatsApp’s internal security team while investigating a scam campaign. The company suspects that the flaw was being used to make fraudulent messages appear more credible. WhatsApp has not disclosed the scale of the suspected activity or confirmed whether the exploitation attempts were successful. The company has advised users to keep their applications and devices updated to protect against the vulnerabilities. FCRF Launches Certified Chief Risk Officer (CRO) Program for India’s Risk Leaders The first vulnerability, CVE-2026-23871, affects WhatsApp for Android and WhatsApp Business for Android versions earlier than 2.26.17.4. The flaw, assigned a Common Vulnerability Scoring System (CVSS) severity score of 3.5, resulted from incomplete validation of external URLs associated with advertisements that allow users to initiate WhatsApp conversations. According to WhatsApp, an attacker could potentially cause a targeted device to disclose its IP information by sending media from an attacker-controlled URL through a specially crafted Click to WhatsApp advertisement reply message. The exposure could occur when the manipulated message was rendered and displayed in a conversation thread. WhatsApp said the vulnerability may have been abused alongside specific spam messages. The company confirmed that its security researchers identified the issue while disrupting a scam campaign. A spokesperson indicated that the suspected attacker may have used the vulnerability to make scam messages appear more trustworthy to recipients. However, WhatsApp did not provide details about the number of users potentially affected or whether the suspected exploitation resulted in successful fraud. The second vulnerability, CVE-2026-102769, is an SQL injection flaw affecting WhatsApp for Android versions earlier than 2.26.35.74. With a CVSS score of 6.8, the vulnerability could allow a specially crafted order details message sent through an unofficial WhatsApp client to trigger the deletion of locally stored WhatsApp files when the recipient tapped on the message. Researchers also found that the vulnerability could expose a limited amount of information through a timing-based side channel. According to WhatsApp, an attacker could potentially obtain one bit of information relating to a user’s chat database by analysing the timing of delivery receipts associated with an induced application crash. The company stated that there was no evidence of this vulnerability being exploited in real-world attacks. The third flaw, CVE-2026-44908, concerns improper trust validation within the certificate verification mechanism used by Meta AI’s confidential computing infrastructure. The vulnerability carries a CVSS score of 4.8 and affects certain older versions of WhatsApp and WhatsApp Business for Android and iOS, as well as WhatsApp for Mac. Successful exploitation could theoretically have allowed an attacker positioned within Meta’s infrastructure to bypass hardware-based trust verification by using a Versioned Chip Endorsement Key certificate that was not signed by the hardware manufacturer’s key. However, WhatsApp stated that such certificates would first need to appear in a third-party binary transparency ledger used by its Private Processing infrastructure. The company said the ledger showed that all published certificates were properly linked to the hardware root of trust, indicating that the vulnerability had not been exploited. WhatsApp has addressed the vulnerabilities through software updates and advised users to install the latest available versions of its applications. The Android vulnerability associated with scam messages affects versions earlier than 2.26.17.4, while the SQL injection flaw affects versions earlier than 2.26.35.74. The certificate validation issue affects WhatsApp for iOS versions earlier than 2.26.24.72, WhatsApp and WhatsApp Business for Mac versions earlier than 2.26.23.72, WhatsApp for Android versions earlier than 2.26.23.74, and WhatsApp Business for Android versions earlier than 2.26.23.70. The reported weaknesses highlight different areas of application security, ranging from the handling of external web addresses and specially crafted messages to the validation of certificates used in confidential computing environments. Although WhatsApp suspects that one vulnerability was associated with scam-related activity, the company has not confirmed successful exploitation. It has also reported no evidence of real-world exploitation involving the other two flaws. Users are advised to update WhatsApp through official application stores, avoid interacting with suspicious messages and exercise caution when receiving unexpected payment requests or messages containing unfamiliar links. WhatsApp said it continues to strengthen its security systems and acknowledged the contributions of its internal security researchers and the wider bug bounty community in identifying vulnerabilities. WhatsApp patched three security vulnerabilities, including an Android flaw the company suspects scammers used to make fraudulent messages look credible. The first flaw, CVE-2026-23871, affects WhatsApp for Android and WhatsApp Business for Android before version 2.26.17.4. It involves incomplete validation of external ad-reply URLs. An attacker could send media from an attacker-controlled URL in a crafted Click to WhatsApp ad-reply message. When WhatsApp displayed that message in a thread, the attacker could learn the target's IP address. WhatsApp said someone may have used the flaw with specific spam messages. The company's security team discovered and reported the issue. A WhatsApp spokesperson said the team found the flaw while disrupting a scam campaign and believes a scammer used it to make scam messages seem more credible. WhatsApp did not disclose the scale of the activity or whether those efforts succeeded. The second flaw, CVE-2026-102769, is an SQL injection vulnerability in WhatsApp for Android before version 2.26.35.74. It occurs when a recipient taps a crafted "order details" message sent from an unofficial client. The tap can delete files stored on the device. An attacker could learn one bit about the user's chat database through an induced-crash delivery receipt timing side channel if the user is online when the malicious message arrives. WhatsApp said it found no evidence that anyone exploited the flaw in the wild. The third flaw, CVE-2026-44908, is a trust-validation vulnerability in WhatsApp's certificate verification mechanism for Meta AI's confidential computing infrastructure. It affects WhatsApp for iOS before version 2.26.24.72, WhatsApp Business for iOS and WhatsApp for Mac Desktop before version 2.26.23.72, WhatsApp for Android before version 2.26.23.74, and WhatsApp Business for Android before version 2.26.23.70. An actor positioned inside Meta infrastructure could bypass the hardware root of trust with a Versioned Chip Endorsement Key (VCEK) certificate not signed by the hardware manufacturer's key. Someone would first need to publish that certificate to the third-party binary transparency ledger that WhatsApp Private Processing uses. WhatsApp said the ledger shows every published VCEK certificate chains to the hardware root of trust, which confirms no exploitation. WhatsApp advises users to keep apps and devices updated. The company said it keeps strengthening its systems and acknowledged the bug bounty community's contributions to platform security. extraction.body: Meta-owned messaging platform WhatsApp has patched three security vulnerabilities affecting its Android, iOS and desktop applications, including a flaw suspected of being misused in connection with fraudulent messages. The vulnerabilities could potentially expose users’ IP information, delete locally stored files and weaken certificate verification protections associated with Meta AI infrastructure. One of the vulnerabilities, identified as CVE-2026-23871, was discovered by WhatsApp’s internal security team while investigating a scam campaign. The company suspects that the flaw was being used to make fraudulent messages appear more credible. WhatsApp has not disclosed the scale of the suspected activity or confirmed whether the exploitation attempts were successful. The company has advised users to keep their applications and devices updated to protect against the vulnerabilities. FCRF Launches Certified Chief Risk Officer (CRO) Program for India’s Risk Leaders The first vulnerability, CVE-2026-23871, affects WhatsApp for Android and WhatsApp Business for Android versions earlier than 2.26.17.4. The flaw, assigned a Common Vulnerability Scoring System (CVSS) severity score of 3.5, resulted from incomplete validation of external URLs associated with advertisements that allow users to initiate WhatsApp conversations. According to WhatsApp, an attacker could potentially cause a targeted device to disclose its IP information by sending media from an attacker-controlled URL through a specially crafted Click to WhatsApp advertisement reply message. The exposure could occur when the manipulated message was rendered and displayed in a conversation thread. WhatsApp said the vulnerability may have been abused alongside specific spam messages. The company confirmed that its security researchers identified the issue while disrupting a scam campaign. A spokesperson indicated that the suspected attacker may have used the vulnerability to make scam messages appear more trustworthy to recipients. However, WhatsApp did not provide details about the number of users potentially affected or whether the suspected exploitation resulted in successful fraud. The second vulnerability, CVE-2026-102769, is an SQL injection flaw affecting WhatsApp for Android versions earlier than 2.26.35.74. With a CVSS score of 6.8, the vulnerability could allow a specially crafted order details message sent through an unofficial WhatsApp client to trigger the deletion of locally stored WhatsApp files when the recipient tapped on the message. Researchers also found that the vulnerability could expose a limited amount of information through a timing-based side channel. According to WhatsApp, an attacker could potentially obtain one bit of information relating to a user’s chat database by analysing the timing of delivery receipts associated with an induced application crash. The company stated that there was no evidence of this vulnerability being exploited in real-world attacks. The third flaw, CVE-2026-44908, concerns improper trust validation within the certificate verification mechanism used by Meta AI’s confidential computing infrastructure. The vulnerability carries a CVSS score of 4.8 and affects certain older versions of WhatsApp and WhatsApp Business for Android and iOS, as well as WhatsApp for Mac. Successful exploitation could theoretically have allowed an attacker positioned within Meta’s infrastructure to bypass hardware-based trust verification by using a Versioned Chip Endorsement Key certificate that was not signed by the hardware manufacturer’s key. However, WhatsApp stated that such certificates would first need to appear in a third-party binary transparency ledger used by its Private Processing infrastructure. The company said the ledger showed that all published certificates were properly linked to the hardware root of trust, indicating that the vulnerability had not been exploited. WhatsApp has addressed the vulnerabilities through software updates and advised users to install the latest available versions of its applications. The Android vulnerability associated with scam messages affects versions earlier than 2.26.17.4, while the SQL injection flaw affects versions earlier than 2.26.35.74. The certificate validation issue affects WhatsApp for iOS versions earlier than 2.26.24.72, WhatsApp and WhatsApp Business for Mac versions earlier than 2.26.23.72, WhatsApp for Android versions earlier than 2.26.23.74, and WhatsApp Business for Android versions earlier than 2.26.23.70. The reported weaknesses highlight different areas of application security, ranging from the handling of external web addresses and specially crafted messages to the validation of certificates used in confidential computing environments. Although WhatsApp suspects that one vulnerability was associated with scam-related activity, the company has not confirmed successful exploitation. It has also reported no evidence of real-world exploitation involving the other two flaws. Users are advised to update WhatsApp through official application stores, avoid interacting with suspicious messages and exercise caution when receiving unexpected payment requests or messages containing unfamiliar links. WhatsApp said it continues to strengthen its security systems and acknowledged the contributions of its internal security researchers and the wider bug bounty community in identifying vulnerabilities. extraction.body: Bitcoin 's latest sell-off is reviving doubts that it can behave as the "digital gold" market hedge that crypto backers have long envisioned. Coming into 2026, experts said that showing bitcoin could serve as a market hedge rather than a risk-on asset that moves up and down with growth stocks was an important test for the cryptocurrency. Bitcoin was trading under $62,000 on Friday morning, down from an all-time high of more than $126,000 in early October last year. Its downward spiral in recent months and weeks has been precipitated by a confluence of factors. The heavy midterm elections losses for the Republicans, the Binance hack, and a world on edge about the security of all things technology — FAA ground stop, the outage of the National Security Agency's highly classified internal communications system, several online banking outages — have not helped the mood when it comes to putting trust in the digital world. But the market itself may be the biggest factor. Investors are currently in sell everything mode, including tech stocks and gold — the Dow Jones Industrial Average and S&P 500 tumbled into correction territory on Friday, according to CNBC data. Bitcoin's recent price action has also tracked the move in the biggest tech IPOs , SpaceX and Anthropic. Taken together, the cryptocurrency is failing the test again when it comes to showing its worth as a market hedge during times of investor anxiety. In the past month alone, bitcoin had dropped roughly $20,000, as of Friday morning, according to CNBC data. Investors and financial management firms aren't viewing it as safe an investment as in the past, said Ryan Kirkley, co-founder and chief executive of Global Settlement Network, a Miami-based fintech that provides infrastructure for currency settlement, including crypto. "There's a bit more caution than there was a year ago." What is behind bitcoin's fall, and what is in store for its future? Here is what experts say. There have been many theories about how bitcoin would react based on different market and economic conditions. But historically, bitcoin has done best in low-rate environments and when lending opportunities are plentiful, said Juan Xavier Sanchez, head of wealth strategy at Activest Wealth Management in Aventura, Florida. When rates are down and treasuries aren't paying good yields, people tend to be more risk-seeking for higher returns. "Bitcoin for many investors is in that bucket," Sanchez said. Experts have noted that gold, which is now down over 35% from its early 2026 peak, is less attractive when cash accounts are paying 5%. Investments like gold and bitcoin offer no yield. Bitcoin's rising correlation with the Nasdaq-100 since late September suggests the two are increasingly moving in tandem, according to data from Fairlead Strategies, a technical research firm. That's consistent with an environment of higher volatility in which correlations across risk assets tend to increase. However, the correlation remains below its early-2026 highs, the data show. Bitcoin has certain characteristics of digital gold, in that it has a limited supply, no single owner and no CEO or board that can decide to issue more, said Anthony Georgiades, founder and general partner at Innovating Capital in New York, which invests in early-stage crypto, blockchain, digital infrastructure and deep tech companies. But it's also been caught up in monetary policy since its inception. The last decade or so of monetary policy has been extremely rewarding to speculative risk-on assets, Georgiades said. However, in periods of volatility, those types of assets have experienced the most significant drawdowns and have been the most heavily punished, Georgiades said. That means that a shock on one side of the board that might be completely independent of bitcoin could trigger a large volatility event "given how intertwined digital assets have become in the overall financial system," he said. Notably, bitcoin hasn't acted much like digital gold in more recent years, said Abe Sheikh, chief investment officer of Cordoba Advisory Partners in New York. In fact, it has fallen substantially during periods when the stock market has been falling. For example, from October 6 through November 18, the S&P 500 fell about 6.3%, and bitcoin fell around 27%. From January 21, 2025 through April 8, 2025, the S&P dropped around 17.4%, while bitcoin slid 27.8%, he said. Democrats gaining control over both houses is viewed as a negative for crypto from a market perspective. The crypto industry spent more than $200 million to support crypto-friendly candidates, but its role had less of an impact on overall results than in the last election cycle. However, bitcoin's downward trend was already in the works, said Cyrus Amini, chief investment officer at Hyphen Wealth Management in Lafayette, California. In September, the Clarity Act failed in the U.S. Senate, and while its outlook is now dim , according to many political and market experts, some form of crypto legislation is still considered a priority for many Democrats and Republicans, while the Trump-appointed heads of the Commodity Future Trading Commission and Securities and Exchange Commission continue to favor crypto in rulemaking. This fall, investors also started to question the security of encryption technology, leading to more concerns over the security of their bitcoin holdings, said Kirkley of Global Settlement Network. The Binance hack in October muddied the waters further. And the recent stock market jitters and economic concerns piled on doubts, Kirkley said. The last few weeks have been especially rough with data security concerns from multiple fronts, he added. Wall Street's embrace of bitcoin has been a big positive for the cryptocurrency. Kirkley noted that 20% of bitcoin's market price is coming from institutional investors, and that's a conservative estimate. In addition, new research from digital assets company Galaxy shows that a record 40.5% of all 13F-reported spot bitcoin exchange-traded product holdings, and 11.2% of all the bitcoin in the funds, came from advisory and wealth planning firms, such as RIAs and brokerage platforms, as of the third quarter 13F filings with the SEC, which are required of firms with over $100 million in assets to report their holdings. Much of this investment is through bitcoin spot ETFs like the iShares Bitcoin Trust ETF (IBIT) that track its price. These ETFs, first approved by the SEC in January 2024, were supposed to provide a reliable new source of institutional demand. But ETF ownership also makes bitcoin especially easy to sell. Outflows from several of these funds have been substantial in recent months. IBIT, the largest of its peers, had six-month net outflows of $1.65 billion through Nov. 18 and one-month outflows of $1.37 billion, according to ETF Database. The second biggest, Fidelity Wise Origin Bitcoin Fund ( FBTC ) had one-month net outflows of $322.65 million and six-month net outflows of $771.86 million, according to ETF Database. Grayscale Bitcoin Mini Trust ETF ( BTC ) had one-month net outflows of $66.35 million, though it had inflows of $590.04 million over six months. As of September 2026, public companies collectively hold close to 1.29 million bitcoins, which is more than 6% of the 21 million coins in existence, according to bitcoin.com . Most public companies invest their corporate treasury portfolios in low-risk, highly liquid instruments such as money market funds, Treasury bonds and Treasury bills. That said, there are some well-known companies that have invested in bitcoin. SpaceX, for example, purchased 18,712 bitcoins for a total cost of $661 million, at an average price of $35,324 per coin. The company began accumulating bitcoin in early 2021 and held its position unchanged from mid-2024 until its IPO filing . Digital Asset Treasury companies, known as DATs or DATCOs, have also played a role in bitcoin's volatility . DATs are publicly listed firms whose primary business strategy involves holding significant quantities of digital assets, such as bitcoin or ethereum , on their corporate balance sheets to drive shareholder value. Companies in this space include Strategy , Strive, and Twenty One Capital. "DATs have exacerbated the problem," said Sheikh of Cordoba Advisory Partners. When bitcoin is rising, these companies borrow money in the debt market or raise capital to buy more bitcoin, which magnifies the upswings. They have also sold bitcoin to make their bond coupon payments. "It leads to enormous volatility on the upside and downside," Sheikh said. As of mid-November, Strategy, the largest corporate holder of bitcoin, holds 850,849 BTC, according to a regulatory filing . That represents roughly 4% of bitcoin's total supply. The company acquired these holdings at a total cost of approximately $64.2 billion, with an average purchase price of roughly $75,452 per coin, according to the filing. Bitcoin has been trending lower since the peak in October 2025. A trading range has taken hold and the bottom of the range is just below 60,000, said Katie Stockton, founder and managing partner of Fairlead Strategies. "It appears to be trying to find a footing," she said. Oversold conditions on the heels of recent lows in June and July, in addition to long-term momentum, suggest bitcoin can support an upturn, she said. But that depends on whether the crypto can hold at a current range around $60,000, she said. "At the end of the day, bitcoin is exceptionally volatile. It's still an area that people might go to sell when they think that risk is higher in other areas." By mid-morning Friday, the price of bitcoin had slipped below $60,000, its lowest mark since July. It was on pace for its seventh-straight weekly loss for the first time since May 2022, according to CNBC data.

Sunday Guardian Live By: Zaini Majeed Last Updated: November 21, 2026 00:24:26 IST Bitcoin has plunged below the psychologically critical $60, 000 threshold to hit its weakest level since July, undermining long-standing claims that the world’s largest cryptocurrency functions as “digital gold” during periods of financial turbulence. Trading around $59, 170 on Friday, Bitcoin has shed roughly $20, 000 over the past month alone and now sits approximately 53 per cent below its October 2025 record high near $126, 000. Far from shielding investor portfolios from equity volatility, the digital asset broke lower shortly after the US market open alongside sharp losses in technology shares, with the Nasdaq Composite falling 2. 4 per cent and chipmaker Nvidia dropping 6 per cent. “The market appears to be trying to find a footing, ” Fairlead Strategies founder Katie Stockton said in a market note cited by financial outlets, pointing out that Bitcoin’s trading range has compressed to a floor just below $60, 000 as its correlation with the Nasdaq-100 climbed steadily since late September. Proponents of cryptocurrency have argued for years that Bitcoin’s capped supply of 21 million coins makes it an uncorrelated store of value capable of insulating investors from inflation and stock market drawdowns. Recent cross-asset trading, however, indicates that institutional desks continue to treat Bitcoin as a high-beta risk asset rather than a defensive refuge. Market data from Fairlead Strategies underscores that Bitcoin has moved largely in tandem with high-growth technology stocks throughout the autumn downturn. Even physical bullion faced acute liquidity pressure this week, with spot gold sliding more than 3 per cent to drop below $3, 700 per ounce as investors raised cash across asset classes to cover losses and margin requirements. Corporate treasury buyers that fuelled earlier rallies are also magnifying the downward volatility. Cordoba Advisory Partners chief investment officer Abe Sheikh told market analysts that companies such as Strategy, which holds 850, 849 BTC, roughly 4 per cent of total supply, borrow capital to accumulate Bitcoin during upswings and face pressure to offload holdings to service debt obligations when prices retreat. Institutional retreat from US spot Bitcoin exchange-traded funds has removed a vital pillar of market support. According to figures compiled by Farside Investors, investors withdrew $582. 3 million from US spot Bitcoin funds on Thursday alone—including $541. 1 million from BlackRock’s flagship iShares fund—marking a third consecutive day of redemptions and pushing total November outflows to $3. 47 billion. Broader macroeconomic headwinds have further tightened global liquidity. Hotter-than-expected US consumer inflation readings have pushed the 10-year US Treasury yield past 5 per cent and prompted bond traders to price in the risk of renewed Federal Reserve interest rate increases rather than cuts. At the same time, shifting capital flows across the technology sector have drained speculative liquidity from digital tokens. FalconX co-head of markets Joshua Lim noted in commentary reported by Bloomberg that nearly $20 billion in stablecoin outflows over the past month, alongside investors raising cash for major artificial intelligence listings such as Anthropic’s market debut, have weighed heavily on crypto valuations. Derivatives markets reflect widespread defensive positioning as leveraged long bets unwind. More than $528 million in leveraged Bitcoin positions were liquidated during the latest leg down, while the crypto Fear and Greed Index dropped to 12, signalling extreme investor anxiety. Technical analysts warn that a sustained break below the $59, 800 to $60, 500 support band could expose Bitcoin to a test of its July 1 yearly low near $57, 877, with deeper weekly support sitting closer to $55, 000. Until Treasury yields stabilise and institutional exchange-traded fund outflows reverse, analysts expect Bitcoin to remain tethered to the broader trajectory of global equities.

extraction.body: Bitcoin fell sharply on Thursday, dropping below $85,000 for the first time in nearly two months, as a broad pullback in risk assets swept through global markets and intensified pressure on cryptocurrencies. The world’s largest digital asset slid as much as 5.7% to $84,233, its lowest level since Dec. 1. The decline marked a significant breakdown after weeks of sideways trading and underscored the fragility of sentiment across the crypto market. Losses were even steeper among smaller tokens, with Ether, XRP, Dogecoin, Cardano and Solana all falling by 6% or more. The sharp move lower in prices triggered a wave of forced selling across crypto derivatives markets. Around $785 million worth of digital assets were liquidated over the past 24 hours, according to data compiled by Coinglass. More than half of those liquidations occurred in just the last four hours, reflecting the speed at which losses cascaded as key technical levels were breached. The latest drop extended a broader downturn that has persisted in crypto markets since early October. Bitcoin prices had largely stagnated in recent weeks, even as technology stocks and precious metals such as gold and silver rallied. That divergence broke down abruptly, however, as cryptocurrencies began to mirror a wider selloff in risk assets. Technology stocks led the decline, with Microsoft shares collapsing more than 11%, a move that would rank as their worst one-day fall since March 2020. The selloff followed the company’s report of slowing growth in its cloud business and dragged the Nasdaq Composite lower by roughly 1.5%, reinforcing a risk-off tone across markets. The pressure was not limited to equities. Precious metals, which had surged to record highs, also reversed violently. Gold, which had briefly climbed above $5,600 per ounce earlier in the session — having never traded above $5,000 before Sunday night — plunged nearly 10% within minutes during US morning trade, falling back below $5,200. Silver followed a similar trajectory, sliding from around $121 per ounce to $108. Bitcoin exchange-traded funds have also come under strain. So far this week, bitcoin ETFs have recorded $160.1 million in net outflows, according to data from SoSoValue, extending a pattern of capital leaving the products amid market turbulence. Julio Moreno, head of research at CryptoQuant, said the recent pullback represents the first meaningful stress test for bitcoin ETFs since their rapid growth last year. Moreno noted that cumulative ETF flows peaked at $72.6 billion on Oct. 10, 2025, and have since seen $6.1 billion in net outflows. That reduction has cut ETF holdings to about $66.5 billion, representing an 8.4% drawdown from the peak. “If price holds above ETF realized price, it gives this cohort a reason to stay invested. If it fails, ETF flows risk shifting from passive consolidation into active distribution. Right now, Bitcoin is trading at the line where ETF conviction is tested,” Moreno wrote. passages: Bitcoin fell sharply on Thursday, dropping below $85,000 for the first time in nearly two months, as a broad pullback in risk assets swept through global markets and intensified pressure on cryptocurrencies.
The world’s largest digital asset slid as much as 5.7% to $84,233, its lowest level since Dec. 1.
The decline marked a significant breakdown after weeks of sideways trading and underscored the fragility of sentiment across the crypto market.
Losses were even steeper among smaller tokens, with Ether, XRP, Dogecoin, Cardano and Solana all falling by 6% or more.
The sharp move lower in prices triggered a wave of forced selling across crypto derivatives markets.
Around $785 million worth of digital assets were liquidated over the past 24 hours, according to data compiled by Coinglass.
More than half of those liquidations occurred in just the last four hours, reflecting the speed at which losses cascaded as key technical levels were breached.
The latest drop extended a broader downturn that has persisted in crypto markets since early October.
Bitcoin prices had largely stagnated in recent weeks, even as technology stocks and precious metals such as gold and silver rallied.
That divergence broke down abruptly, however, as cryptocurrencies began to mirror a wider selloff in risk assets.
Technology stocks led the decline, with Microsoft shares collapsing more than 11%, a move that would rank as their worst one-day fall since March 2020.
The selloff followed the company’s report of slowing growth in its cloud business and dragged the Nasdaq Composite lower by roughly 1.5%, reinforcing a risk-off tone across markets.
The pressure was not limited to equities. Precious metals, which had surged to record highs, also reversed violently.

Gold, which had briefly climbed above $5,600 per ounce earlier in the session — having never traded above $5,000 before Sunday night — plunged nearly 10% within minutes during US morning trade, falling back below $5,200.
Silver followed a similar trajectory, sliding from around $121 per ounce to $108.
Bitcoin exchange-traded funds have also come under strain.
So far this week, bitcoin ETFs have recorded $160.1 million in net outflows, according to data from SoSoValue, extending a pattern of capital leaving the products amid market turbulence.
Julio Moreno, head of research at CryptoQuant, said the recent pullback represents the first meaningful stress test for bitcoin ETFs since their rapid growth last year.
Moreno noted that cumulative ETF flows peaked at $72.6 billion on Oct. 10, 2025, and have since seen $6.1 billion in net outflows.
That reduction has cut ETF holdings to about $66.5 billion, representing an 8.4% drawdown from the peak.

“If price holds above ETF realized price, it gives this cohort a reason to stay invested. If it fails, ETF flows risk shifting from passive consolidation into active distribution. Right now, Bitcoin is trading at the line where ETF conviction is tested,” Moreno wrote.

coreStoryFacts.text: But the market itself may be the biggest factor.
Investors are currently in sell everything mode, including tech stocks and gold — the Dow Jones Industrial Average and S&P 500 tumbled into correction territory on Friday, according to CNBC data.
Bitcoin's recent price action has also tracked the move in the biggest tech IPOs , SpaceX and Anthropic.
Taken together, the cryptocurrency is failing the test again when it comes to showing its worth as a market hedge during times of investor anxiety.
Bitcoin 's latest sell-off is reviving doubts that it can behave as the "digital gold" market hedge that crypto backers have long envisioned.
Bitcoin was trading under $62,000 on Friday morning, down from an all-time high of more than $126,000 in early October last year.
Its downward spiral in recent months and weeks has been precipitated by a confluence of factors.
By mid-morning Friday, the price of bitcoin had slipped below $60,000, its lowest mark since July.
Notably, bitcoin hasn't acted much like digital gold in more recent years, said Abe Sheikh, chief investment officer of Cordoba Advisory Partners in New York.
Bitcoin has been trending lower since the peak in October 2025.
"It appears to be trying to find a footing," she said.
Bitcoin's rising correlation with the Nasdaq-100 since late September suggests the two are increasingly moving in tandem, according to data from Fairlead Strategies, a technical research firm.
That's consistent with an environment of higher volatility in which correlations across risk assets tend to increase.
However, the correlation remains below its early-2026 highs, the data show.
When rates are down and treasuries aren't paying good yields, people tend to be more risk-seeking for higher returns.
"Bitcoin for many investors is in that bucket," Sanchez said.
Investments like gold and bitcoin offer no yield.
But ETF ownership also makes bitcoin especially easy to sell.

Bitcoin has plunged below the psychologically critical $60, 000 threshold to hit its weakest level since July, undermining long-standing claims that the world’s largest cryptocurrency functions as “digital gold” during periods of financial turbulence.
More than $528 million in leveraged Bitcoin positions were liquidated during the latest leg down, while the crypto Fear and Greed Index dropped to 12, signalling extreme investor anxiety.

Technical analysts warn that a sustained break below the $59, 800 to $60, 500 support band could expose Bitcoin to a test of its July 1 yearly low near $57, 877, with deeper weekly support sitting closer to $55, 000.

Investors and financial management firms aren't viewing it as safe an investment as in the past, said Ryan Kirkley, co-founder and chief executive of Global Settlement Network, a Miami-based fintech that provides infrastructure for currency settlement, including crypto. "There's a bit more caution than there was a year ago." What is behind bitcoin's fall, and what is in store for its future? Here is what experts say. But historically, bitcoin has done best in low-rate environments and when lending opportunities are plentiful, said Juan Xavier Sanchez, head of wealth strategy at Activest Wealth Management in Aventura, Florida. When rates are down and treasuries aren't paying good yields, people tend to be more risk-seeking for higher returns. "Bitcoin for many investors is in that bucket," Sanchez said. Experts have noted that gold, which is now down over 35% from its early 2026 peak, is less attractive when cash accounts are paying 5%. Investments like gold and bitcoin offer no yield. Bitcoin's rising correlation with the Nasdaq-100 since late September suggests the two are increasingly moving in tandem, according to data from Fairlead Strategies, a technical research firm. That's consistent with an environment of higher volatility in which correlations across risk assets tend to increase. However, the correlation remains below its early-2026 highs, the data show. Bitcoin has certain characteristics of digital gold, in that it has a limited supply, no single owner and no CEO or board that can decide to issue more, said Anthony Georgiades, founder and general partner at Innovating Capital in New York, which invests in early-stage crypto, blockchain, digital infrastructure and deep tech companies. But it's also been caught up in monetary policy since its inception. The last decade or so of monetary policy has been extremely rewarding to speculative risk-on assets, Georgiades said. However, in periods of volatility, those types of assets have experienced the most significant drawdowns and have been the most heavily punished, Georgiades said. That means that a shock on one side of the board that might be completely independent of bitcoin could trigger a large volatility event "given how intertwined digital assets have become in the overall financial system," he said. Notably, bitcoin hasn't acted much like digital gold in more recent years, said Abe Sheikh, chief investment officer of Cordoba Advisory Partners in New York. In fact, it has fallen substantially during periods when the stock market has been falling. For example, from October 6 through November 18, the S&P 500 fell about 6.3%, and bitcoin fell around 27%. Democrats gaining control over both houses is viewed as a negative for crypto from a market perspective. The crypto industry spent more than $200 million to support crypto-friendly candidates, but its role had less of an impact on overall results than in the last election cycle. This fall, investors also started to question the security of encryption technology, leading to more concerns over the security of their bitcoin holdings, said Kirkley of Global Settlement Network. The Binance hack in October muddied the waters further. And the recent stock market jitters and economic concerns piled on doubts, Kirkley said. The last few weeks have been especially rough with data security concerns from multiple fronts, he added. Wall Street's embrace of bitcoin has been a big positive for the cryptocurrency. Kirkley noted that 20% of bitcoin's market price is coming from institutional investors, and that's a conservative estimate. In addition, new research from digital assets company Galaxy shows that a record 40.5% of all 13F-reported spot bitcoin exchange-traded product holdings, and 11.2% of all the bitcoin in the funds, came from advisory and wealth planning firms, such as RIAs and brokerage platforms, as of the third quarter 13F filings with the SEC, which are required of firms with over $100 million in assets to report their holdings. Much of this investment is through bitcoin spot ETFs like the iShares Bitcoin Trust ETF (IBIT) that track its price. These ETFs, first approved by the SEC in January 2024, were supposed to provide a reliable new source of institutional demand. But ETF ownership also makes bitcoin especially easy to sell. Outflows from several of these funds have been substantial in recent months. IBIT, the largest of its peers, had six-month net outflows of $1.65 billion through Nov. 18 and one-month outflows of $1.37 billion, according to ETF Database. The second biggest, Fidelity Wise Origin Bitcoin Fund ( FBTC ) had one-month net outflows of $322.65 million and six-month net outflows of $771.86 million, according to ETF Database. Grayscale Bitcoin Mini Trust ETF ( BTC ) had one-month net outflows of $66.35 million, though it had inflows of $590.04 million over six months. As of September 2026, public companies collectively hold close to 1.29 million bitcoins, which is more than 6% of the 21 million coins in existence, according to bitcoin.com . Most public companies invest their corporate treasury portfolios in low-risk, highly liquid instruments such as money market funds, Treasury bonds and Treasury bills. That said, there are some well-known companies that have invested in bitcoin. SpaceX, for example, purchased 18,712 bitcoins for a total cost of $661 million, at an average price of $35,324 per coin. The company began accumulating bitcoin in early 2021 and held its position unchanged from mid-2024 until its IPO filing . Digital Asset Treasury companies, known as DATs or DATCOs, have also played a role in bitcoin's volatility . DATs are publicly listed firms whose primary business strategy involves holding significant quantities of digital assets, such as bitcoin or ethereum , on their corporate balance sheets to drive shareholder value. Companies in this space include Strategy , Strive, and Twenty One Capital. "DATs have exacerbated the problem," said Sheikh of Cordoba Advisory Partners. When bitcoin is rising, these companies borrow money in the debt market or raise capital to buy more bitcoin, which magnifies the upswings. They have also sold bitcoin to make their bond coupon payments. "It leads to enormous volatility on the upside and downside," Sheikh said. As of mid-November, Strategy, the largest corporate holder of bitcoin, holds 850,849 BTC, according to a regulatory filing . That represents roughly 4% of bitcoin's total supply. The company acquired these holdings at a total cost of approximately $64.2 billion, with an average purchase price of roughly $75,452 per coin, according to the filing. Bitcoin has been trending lower since the peak in October 2025. A trading range has taken hold and the bottom of the range is just below 60,000, said Katie Stockton, founder and managing partner of Fairlead Strategies. "It appears to be trying to find a footing," she said. Oversold conditions on the heels of recent lows in June and July, in addition to long-term momentum, suggest bitcoin can support an upturn, she said. But that depends on whether the crypto can hold at a current range around $60,000, she said. "At the end of the day, bitcoin is exceptionally volatile. It's still an area that people might go to sell when they think that risk is higher in other areas." By mid-morning Friday, the price of bitcoin had slipped below $60,000, its lowest mark since July. It was on pace for its seventh-straight weekly loss for the first time since May 2022, according to CNBC data.
