The sharp move lower in prices triggered a wave of forced selling across crypto derivatives markets. Around $785 million worth of digital assets were liquidated over the past 24 hours, according to data compiled by Coinglass. More than half of those liquidations occurred in just the last four hours, reflecting the speed at which losses cascaded as key technical levels were breached. The latest drop extended a broader downturn that has persisted in crypto markets since early October. Bitcoin prices had largely stagnated in recent weeks, even as technology stocks and precious metals such as gold and silver rallied. That divergence broke down abruptly, however, as cryptocurrencies began to mirror a wider selloff in risk assets. Technology stocks led the decline, with Microsoft shares collapsing more than 11%, a move that would rank as their worst one-day fall since March 2020. The selloff followed the company’s report of slowing growth in its cloud business and dragged the Nasdaq Composite lower by roughly 1.5%, reinforcing a risk-off tone across markets. The pressure was not limited to equities. Precious metals, which had surged to record highs, also reversed violently. Gold, which had briefly climbed above $5,600 per ounce earlier in the session — having never traded above $5,000 before Sunday night — plunged nearly 10% within minutes during US morning trade, falling back below $5,200. Silver followed a similar trajectory, sliding from around $121 per ounce to $108. Bitcoin exchange-traded funds have also come under strain. So far this week, bitcoin ETFs have recorded $160.1 million in net outflows, according to data from SoSoValue, extending a pattern of capital leaving the products amid market turbulence. Julio Moreno, head of research at CryptoQuant, said the recent pullback represents the first meaningful stress test for bitcoin ETFs since their rapid growth last year. Moreno noted that cumulative ETF flows peaked at $72.6 billion on Oct. 10, 2025, and have since seen $6.1 billion in net outflows. That reduction has cut ETF holdings to about $66.5 billion, representing an 8.4% drawdown from the peak. “If price holds above ETF realized price, it gives this cohort a reason to stay invested. If it fails, ETF flows risk shifting from passive consolidation into active distribution. Right now, Bitcoin is trading at the line where ETF conviction is tested,” Moreno wrote. extraction.body: Bitcoin’s price plunged below $59,000 on Friday as the November cryptocurrency market rout showed no signs of letting up. The plunge came just days after crypto market maker Wintermute warned that bitcoin’s bear market was not over and flagged the risk of a further slide into the $50,000 range. Bitstamp data shows bitcoin briefly dropped to $58,701, a level last seen in early July, when a bearish trend threatened to push the price toward $50,000. Earlier Friday, however, bitcoin appeared to be holding comfortably above $61,000, with $62,000 acting as its immediate resistance level. Between 11 a.m. and noon EST, bitcoin shed nearly $3,000 amid heightened selling pressure and a lack of buyers. Although a relief rally briefly lifted the price above $59,300, the cryptocurrency was still down approximately 5% over 24 hours and more than 13% over seven days. After narrowing its year-to-date losses to single digits by the end of September, bitcoin has steadily declined since the beginning of October. The latest sell-off leaves the cryptocurrency down more than 30% since Jan. 1. Meanwhile, bitcoin’s sharp decline was particularly devastating for traders betting on higher prices. According to Coinglass data, the price collapse wiped out more than $220 million in leveraged long positions in just one hour, compared with less than $10 million in short positions. Over 24 hours, bitcoin liquidations exceeded $543 million, including more than $494 million in long positions. With most major altcoins mirroring bitcoin’s decline, long liquidations across the broader cryptocurrency market surpassed $1.38 billion over 24 hours, while short liquidations totaled approximately $142 million—a total of $1.53 billion in liquidations across the market. In its Nov. 16 market update, Wintermute argued that bitcoin’s recent rebounds were primarily driven by short covering rather than fresh spot buying. Without renewed demand from spot bitcoin exchange-traded funds (ETFs), which have recorded roughly $1.9 billion in net outflows in 2026, and corporate bitcoin treasury companies, the prospects for a sustained recovery remain slim. Wintermute said bitcoin would need to reclaim $68,000 on a sustained basis, accompanied by a clear return to net spot ETF inflows, before the market maker would reconsider its bearish outlook. The cryptocurrency market sell-off came on the heels of Anthropic’s record-breaking initial public offering (IPO), which raised more than $81 billion. However, the blockbuster listing failed to revive investor confidence in technology stocks, which have been battered by mounting concerns over artificial intelligence valuations, the profitability of massive AI infrastructure investments and the prospect of further U.S. interest rate hikes. The pressure intensified Friday as Anthropic shares plunged almost 13% following their trading debut, while semiconductor stocks extended their losses. Nvidia fell approximately 7% in morning trading, while Advanced Micro Devices (AMD) dropped nearly 12%. Broadcom, Marvell Technology, and Micron Technology each shed more than 9%, underscoring the scale of the sell-off in companies closely tied to the AI boom. The rout also reflected growing doubts about whether the billions of dollars being poured into AI infrastructure will generate sufficient returns to justify elevated technology stock valuations. Nvidia’s recent leadership upheaval, regulatory uncertainty following the U.S. midterm elections and concerns about higher borrowing costs have further undermined investor confidence. Adding to the pressure, hawkish signals from Federal Reserve officials have reinforced expectations of another interest rate hike in December. Higher borrowing costs typically weigh on growth-oriented technology companies by reducing the present value of their expected future earnings and making speculative investments less attractive. The resulting sell-off pushed the Nasdaq down approximately 3.5% on Friday, while the broader S&P 500 fell 2%. The S&P 500 was heading toward its seventh consecutive losing session, while the Nasdaq briefly slipped into negative territory for the year. The simultaneous decline in bitcoin, technology stocks, and other risk-sensitive assets suggests that investors are increasingly reducing exposure to speculative investments amid mounting uncertainty over valuations, monetary policy, and economic growth.

extraction.body: The bitcoin price crashed below $60,000 on Friday for the first time since early July, falling about $1,800 in roughly an hour as a deepening U.S. tech stock selloff dragged risk assets lower. Bitcoin traded near $61,400 at 9:40 a.m. ET and slid to about $59,600 by 10:45 a.m., a drop of nearly 3%, according to Look Into Bitcoin data . The bitcoin price is down about $3,400, or more than 5%, from the same time Thursday, when it traded near $63,000. The break of $60,000 is a key psychological level, and it came with little warning. Bitcoin price had held above $61,000 for most of the morning, even after a third straight daily loss. Wall Street opened sharply lower. The Nasdaq Composite fell more than 2% in morning trading as shares of Anthropic extended losses in its second day since a record Nasdaq debut. Nvidia and AMD also traded lower. Bitcoin has been moving with tech stocks. The market has questioned whether heavy spending on artificial intelligence will pay off, and Friday’s open did nothing to ease that worry. Rate expectations are adding pressure. Traders see a roughly 94% chance the Federal Reserve raises rates in December, CME Group’s FedWatch tool showed . Higher rates tend to hurt bitcoin and other assets that pay no yield. Earlier Friday, South Korea’s Kospi index fell more than 5% and chipmakers sank across Asia. That selling carried into U.S. trading and then into bitcoin. Some analysts had flagged $60,000 as a floor. Katie Stockton of Fairlead Strategies told CNBC the bottom of bitcoin’s trading range sits “just below 60,000,” and that it “appears to be trying to find a footing.” Friday’s drop tests that view. CoinShares head of research James Butterfill said this week the drop is a “continuation of the existing bear market.” His base case is range trading around $60,000 to $90,000 through much of 2027. JUST IN: Bitcoin falls below $60,000 for the first time since June. BTC is now less than 4% away from a new cycle low 👀 pic.twitter.com/GSZkbGdzZz Funds have been sellers. BlackRock’s iShares Bitcoin Trust (IBIT) lost $541.1 million on Thursday, its biggest one-day outflow on record. U.S. spot bitcoin ETFs lost about $582 million in total, extending a streak of heavy withdrawals this week. Leveraged traders were hit as well. More than $700 million in crypto positions were liquidated in the 24 hours before the latest drop, and about 86% were bets on higher prices. The slide below $60,000 likely forced out more of them. The move extends a month-long slump. Bitcoin has dropped roughly $20,000 in the past month, a slide tracked as the price fell under $62,000 on Thursday. Crypto stocks fell even faster. Strategy (MSTR) was down about 7% near $79.85, a day after it tumbled for a sixth straight session . Coinbase (COIN) fell about 3% to $105.36. Shares of Strive (ASST) fell to $15.31 Friday morning, down 21.47%, or $4.19, over the past five days. The stock has slid steadily from near $19.50 as bitcoin price’s sell-off deepened, with its sharpest drop in Friday’s trading. Bitcoin miners took the worst of it. MARA Holdings (MARA) dropped about 11% to $5.55. Riot Platforms (RIOT) lost about 11% to $15.85, and CleanSpark (CLSK) fell about 12% to $5.13. Data center operators that also mine bitcoin were hit hard. IREN fell about 12% to $12.62, and Cipher Digital (CIFR) dropped 14% to $5.58. Both have traded with AI stocks, which are also under pressure. The bitcoin price is now at its lowest since the first days of July. Bitcoin set its record above $126,000 in October 2025, so it has lost more than half its value from that peak. At the time of writing, the bitcoin price is near $59,600. Earlier Friday, South Korea’s Kospi index fell more than 5% and chipmakers sank across Asia. That selling carried into U.S. trading and then into bitcoin.

Some analysts had flagged $60,000 as a floor. Katie Stockton of Fairlead Strategies told CNBC the bottom of bitcoin’s trading range sits “just below 60,000,” and that it “appears to be trying to find a footing.” Friday’s drop tests that view.
CoinShares head of research James Butterfill said this week the drop is a “continuation of the existing bear market.” His base case is range trading around $60,000 to $90,000 through much of 2027.
JUST IN: Bitcoin falls below $60,000 for the first time since June. BTC is now less than 4% away from a new cycle low 👀 pic.twitter.com/GSZkbGdzZz

Funds have been sellers. BlackRock’s iShares Bitcoin Trust (IBIT) lost $541.1 million on Thursday, its biggest one-day outflow on record. U.S. spot bitcoin ETFs lost about $582 million in total, extending a streak of heavy withdrawals this week.

Leveraged traders were hit as well. More than $700 million in crypto positions were liquidated in the 24 hours before the latest drop, and about 86% were bets on higher prices. The slide below $60,000 likely forced out more of them.
The move extends a month-long slump. Bitcoin has dropped roughly $20,000 in the past month, a slide tracked as the price fell under $62,000 on Thursday.

Crypto stocks fell even faster. Strategy (MSTR) was down about 7% near $79.85, a day after it tumbled for a sixth straight session . Coinbase (COIN) fell about 3% to $105.36. Shares of Strive (ASST) fell to $15.31 Friday morning, down 21.47%, or $4.19, over the past five days. The stock has slid steadily from near $19.50 as bitcoin price’s sell-off deepened, with its sharpest drop in Friday’s trading.
Bitcoin miners took the worst of it. MARA Holdings (MARA) dropped about 11% to $5.55. Riot Platforms (RIOT) lost about 11% to $15.85, and CleanSpark (CLSK) fell about 12% to $5.13.

Data center operators that also mine bitcoin were hit hard. IREN fell about 12% to $12.62, and Cipher Digital (CIFR) dropped 14% to $5.58. Both have traded with AI stocks, which are also under pressure.
The bitcoin price is now at its lowest since the first days of July. Bitcoin set its record above $126,000 in October 2025, so it has lost more than half its value from that peak.
At the time of writing, the bitcoin price is near $59,600.

extraction.body: Bitcoin’s price plunged below $59,000 on Friday as the November cryptocurrency market rout showed no signs of letting up. The plunge came just days after crypto market maker Wintermute warned that bitcoin’s bear market was not over and flagged the risk of a further slide into the $50,000 range. Bitstamp data shows bitcoin briefly dropped to $58,701, a level last seen in early July, when a bearish trend threatened to push the price toward $50,000. Earlier Friday, however, bitcoin appeared to be holding comfortably above $61,000, with $62,000 acting as its immediate resistance level. Between 11 a.m. and noon EST, bitcoin shed nearly $3,000 amid heightened selling pressure and a lack of buyers. Although a relief rally briefly lifted the price above $59,300, the cryptocurrency was still down approximately 5% over 24 hours and more than 13% over seven days. After narrowing its year-to-date losses to single digits by the end of September, bitcoin has steadily declined since the beginning of October. The latest sell-off leaves the cryptocurrency down more than 30% since Jan. 1. Meanwhile, bitcoin’s sharp decline was particularly devastating for traders betting on higher prices. According to Coinglass data, the price collapse wiped out more than $220 million in leveraged long positions in just one hour, compared with less than $10 million in short positions. Over 24 hours, bitcoin liquidations exceeded $543 million, including more than $494 million in long positions. With most major altcoins mirroring bitcoin’s decline, long liquidations across the broader cryptocurrency market surpassed $1.38 billion over 24 hours, while short liquidations totaled approximately $142 million—a total of $1.53 billion in liquidations across the market. In its Nov. 16 market update, Wintermute argued that bitcoin’s recent rebounds were primarily driven by short covering rather than fresh spot buying. Without renewed demand from spot bitcoin exchange-traded funds (ETFs), which have recorded roughly $1.9 billion in net outflows in 2026, and corporate bitcoin treasury companies, the prospects for a sustained recovery remain slim. Wintermute said bitcoin would need to reclaim $68,000 on a sustained basis, accompanied by a clear return to net spot ETF inflows, before the market maker would reconsider its bearish outlook. The cryptocurrency market sell-off came on the heels of Anthropic’s record-breaking initial public offering (IPO), which raised more than $81 billion. However, the blockbuster listing failed to revive investor confidence in technology stocks, which have been battered by mounting concerns over artificial intelligence valuations, the profitability of massive AI infrastructure investments and the prospect of further U.S. interest rate hikes. The pressure intensified Friday as Anthropic shares plunged almost 13% following their trading debut, while semiconductor stocks extended their losses. Nvidia fell approximately 7% in morning trading, while Advanced Micro Devices (AMD) dropped nearly 12%. Broadcom, Marvell Technology, and Micron Technology each shed more than 9%, underscoring the scale of the sell-off in companies closely tied to the AI boom. The rout also reflected growing doubts about whether the billions of dollars being poured into AI infrastructure will generate sufficient returns to justify elevated technology stock valuations. Nvidia’s recent leadership upheaval, regulatory uncertainty following the U.S. midterm elections and concerns about higher borrowing costs have further undermined investor confidence. Adding to the pressure, hawkish signals from Federal Reserve officials have reinforced expectations of another interest rate hike in December. Higher borrowing costs typically weigh on growth-oriented technology companies by reducing the present value of their expected future earnings and making speculative investments less attractive. The resulting sell-off pushed the Nasdaq down approximately 3.5% on Friday, while the broader S&P 500 fell 2%. The S&P 500 was heading toward its seventh consecutive losing session, while the Nasdaq briefly slipped into negative territory for the year. The simultaneous decline in bitcoin, technology stocks, and other risk-sensitive assets suggests that investors are increasingly reducing exposure to speculative investments amid mounting uncertainty over valuations, monetary policy, and economic growth.

The studio called it the biggest entertainment launch in history, a record that spans film, music and video games. Rockstar said it sold 32.5 million copies before the game was even out, a preorder record. Before its release, the game had sold almost half as much as the best-selling album in recorded music history, Michael Jackson’s “Thriller.” Critics greeted the game with a 99 out of 100 on Metacritic, making it the highest-rated video game of all time. The Washington Post review called it “ an astonishing American epic. ” The series breaks its own record as the fastest-selling media product of all time. In 2013, “Grand Theft Auto V” hit that record, generating $1 billion in sales after three days. At the worldwide box office, “Avengers: Endgame” took five days to reach $1 billion in 2019. Christopher Nolan’s “The Odyssey” reached that mark in three weeks this summer. “We are incredibly humbled by the response from players around the world and we couldn’t be more excited to share this moment with you,” Sam Houser, the studio’s president and founder, said in a statement. President Donald Trump on Friday defended ousted Nvidia chief Jensen Huang, calling for his reinstatement at the company after news broke that the tech scion had an affair with a woman suspected of being a Chinese spy. “He’s a good man. By the way, he’s a man — while we’re at it. He made some bad decisions, but he is a brilliant person,” Trump said Friday at a news conference following his trip to Asia. “… I would love to see Jensen be given a second chance. You know, we’re a country of second chances.” The Washington Post reported Monday that Nvidia’s board was not considering reinstating Huang. Huang, who has acknowledged the affair, has agreed to testify before Congress next month over whether Nvidia allowed Chinese companies to access its advanced chips despite U.S. export restrictions. Huang has a close relationship with Trump. The president said Friday that it was important for the United States to protect its “brilliant people,” like Huang. “I think the company, if they were smart, they’d take that brilliant man, accept an apology and let him go back to work,” Trump said. He likened his defense of the Nvidia co-founder to his support for Elon Musk, the founder of Tesla, SpaceX and xAI. “You know, I came to Elon’s defense in my first term very strongly,” Trump said, without elaborating on the reason for his intervention. “I’m not sure that Elon would be with us right now if I didn’t. And I said, ‘We have to protect our brilliant people because no country has too many of them.’” A second federal judge on Friday said she would block construction of President Donald Trump’s planned triumphal arch, according to statements from the lawsuit’s parties. U.S. District Judge Leonie Brinkema said from the bench that she intended to issue a preliminary injunction, granting a request from Arlington County to halt work on the project while the case continues in the Eastern District of Virginia, according to Democracy Forward, a legal advocacy nonprofit and party to the case. The White House on Friday said the ruling came from “another activist district court.” “The judiciary should not be abused to politicize a structure designed to unite our nation,” White House spokesperson Davis Ingle said in a statement. Earlier this week, a different federal judge blocked construction of the arch for an additional two weeks while she weighs legal arguments. Brinkema’s injunction, however, would extend until the Virginia-based case is over. Opponents of the arch include the D.C. government, the Commonwealth of Virginia, historic preservationists and some military veterans. In a statement, an attorney with Democracy Forward said they were pleased that the judge ruled to stop what it called a “massive vanity project.” On Thursday afternoon, in the hours after the Cincinnati Zoo announced the sudden death of Fiona — the world-famous, 9-year-old Nile hippopotamus who first became an internet celebrity as a premature newborn calf — legions of her fans took to social media to share their sense of shock and grief. But the discourse has quickly spiraled into outrage, fueled by the spread of unsubstantiated accounts of what led to Fiona’s death. According to the Cincinnati Zoo, a child threw a knit hat into the air while standing in an enclosed observation area; a ceiling fan caught and flung the hat through a narrow opening, into the hippo’s enclosure. In a statement, zoo spokesperson Michelle Curley described the incident as an accident, noting: “We probably couldn’t make [it] happen again if we tried.” This didn’t satisfy those who voiced fury over Fiona’s loss — focusing their ire on the child who threw the hat and the parent (or parents) who were present at the time. Some called for the family to be doxed, “charged,” “prosecuted” or far worse. In the absence of verified details, unconfirmed accounts spread wildly — sharing conflicting reports about the child’s age, their intention in throwing the hat, the conduct of the parents and whether or not zoo officials were notified when the hat entered the enclosure. The death of the beloved hippo soon morphed into a referendum on permissive parenting and the dangers of being too lenient with misbehaving children — even as many others emphasized the impossibility of anticipating such an unlikely tragedy, and expressed concern for the safety and well-being of the child and their family who were involved in the incident. As players worldwide dive into the complex world of “Grand Theft Auto VI” this week, several have noticed a never-heard-before song playing on one of the in-game radio stations: an unreleased track by the late R&B soul visionary D’Angelo. The song “Kamikazi” by D’Angelo — who died last year of cancer at 51 — appears in the official music credits from “Grand Theft Auto” maker Rockstar Games. Some players have posted videos of the song played by the in-game radio station, “WorldWide FM.” This is notable because D’Angelo song releases are major musical events; the elusive godfather of neo-soul would allow years to pass between music releases. His most recent album was 2014’s “Black Messiah.” The new song is credited to “courtesy of RCA.” The record label did not immediately respond to an inquiry on whether “Kamikazi” will be released as a single elsewhere. The Commerce Department approved the sale of almost 580,000 Nvidia artificial intelligence chips to China under a Trump administration plan to allow the sales in exchange for a cut of the revenue. The approvals were outlined in confidential documents released by the House Foreign Affairs Committee on Thursday. The approved customers included two big Chinese tech companies that the Pentagon lists as having ties to the country’s military. The documents date to May and do not reflect actual shipments, but they underscore the size of Nvidia’s potential market in China. In total the company applied to export more than 2.8 million of the chips, known as H200s. The value of the sales is redacted in the documents, but the company said this week that in its most recent quarter it made $2.4 billion from sales under licenses to Chinese customers. The Commerce Department did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

The studio called it the biggest entertainment launch in history, a record that spans film, music and video games. Rockstar said it sold 32.5 million copies before the game was even out, a preorder record. Before its release, the game had sold almost half as much as the best-selling album in recorded music history, Michael Jackson’s “Thriller.” Critics greeted the game with a 99 out of 100 on Metacritic, making it the highest-rated video game of all time. The Washington Post review called it “ an astonishing American epic. ” The series breaks its own record as the fastest-selling media product of all time. In 2013, “Grand Theft Auto V” hit that record, generating $1 billion in sales after three days. At the worldwide box office, “Avengers: Endgame” took five days to reach $1 billion in 2019. Christopher Nolan’s “The Odyssey” reached that mark in three weeks this summer. “We are incredibly humbled by the response from players around the world and we couldn’t be more excited to share this moment with you,” Sam Houser, the studio’s president and founder, said in a statement. President Donald Trump on Friday defended ousted Nvidia chief Jensen Huang, calling for his reinstatement at the company after news broke that the tech scion had an affair with a woman suspected of being a Chinese spy. “He’s a good man. By the way, he’s a man — while we’re at it. He made some bad decisions, but he is a brilliant person,” Trump said Friday at a news conference following his trip to Asia. “… I would love to see Jensen be given a second chance. You know, we’re a country of second chances.” The Washington Post reported Monday that Nvidia’s board was not considering reinstating Huang. Huang, who has acknowledged the affair, has agreed to testify before Congress next month over whether Nvidia allowed Chinese companies to access its advanced chips despite U.S. export restrictions. Huang has a close relationship with Trump. The president said Friday that it was important for the United States to protect its “brilliant people,” like Huang. “I think the company, if they were smart, they’d take that brilliant man, accept an apology and let him go back to work,” Trump said. He likened his defense of the Nvidia co-founder to his support for Elon Musk, the founder of Tesla, SpaceX and xAI. “You know, I came to Elon’s defense in my first term very strongly,” Trump said, without elaborating on the reason for his intervention. “I’m not sure that Elon would be with us right now if I didn’t. And I said, ‘We have to protect our brilliant people because no country has too many of them.’” A second federal judge on Friday said she would block construction of President Donald Trump’s planned triumphal arch, according to statements from the lawsuit’s parties. U.S. District Judge Leonie Brinkema said from the bench that she intended to issue a preliminary injunction, granting a request from Arlington County to halt work on the project while the case continues in the Eastern District of Virginia, according to Democracy Forward, a legal advocacy nonprofit and party to the case. The White House on Friday said the ruling came from “another activist district court.” “The judiciary should not be abused to politicize a structure designed to unite our nation,” White House spokesperson Davis Ingle said in a statement. Earlier this week, a different federal judge blocked construction of the arch for an additional two weeks while she weighs legal arguments. Brinkema’s injunction, however, would extend until the Virginia-based case is over. Opponents of the arch include the D.C. government, the Commonwealth of Virginia, historic preservationists and some military veterans. In a statement, an attorney with Democracy Forward said they were pleased that the judge ruled to stop what it called a “massive vanity project.” On Thursday afternoon, in the hours after the Cincinnati Zoo announced the sudden death of Fiona — the world-famous, 9-year-old Nile hippopotamus who first became an internet celebrity as a premature newborn calf — legions of her fans took to social media to share their sense of shock and grief. But the discourse has quickly spiraled into outrage, fueled by the spread of unsubstantiated accounts of what led to Fiona’s death. According to the Cincinnati Zoo, a child threw a knit hat into the air while standing in an enclosed observation area; a ceiling fan caught and flung the hat through a narrow opening, into the hippo’s enclosure. In a statement, zoo spokesperson Michelle Curley described the incident as an accident, noting: “We probably couldn’t make [it] happen again if we tried.” This didn’t satisfy those who voiced fury over Fiona’s loss — focusing their ire on the child who threw the hat and the parent (or parents) who were present at the time. Some called for the family to be doxed, “charged,” “prosecuted” or far worse. In the absence of verified details, unconfirmed accounts spread wildly — sharing conflicting reports about the child’s age, their intention in throwing the hat, the conduct of the parents and whether or not zoo officials were notified when the hat entered the enclosure. The death of the beloved hippo soon morphed into a referendum on permissive parenting and the dangers of being too lenient with misbehaving children — even as many others emphasized the impossibility of anticipating such an unlikely tragedy, and expressed concern for the safety and well-being of the child and their family who were involved in the incident. As players worldwide dive into the complex world of “Grand Theft Auto VI” this week, several have noticed a never-heard-before song playing on one of the in-game radio stations: an unreleased track by the late R&B soul visionary D’Angelo. The song “Kamikazi” by D’Angelo — who died last year of cancer at 51 — appears in the official music credits from “Grand Theft Auto” maker Rockstar Games. Some players have posted videos of the song played by the in-game radio station, “WorldWide FM.” This is notable because D’Angelo song releases are major musical events; the elusive godfather of neo-soul would allow years to pass between music releases. His most recent album was 2014’s “Black Messiah.” The new song is credited to “courtesy of RCA.” The record label did not immediately respond to an inquiry on whether “Kamikazi” will be released as a single elsewhere. The approvals were outlined in confidential documents released by the House Foreign Affairs Committee on Thursday. The approved customers included two big Chinese tech companies that the Pentagon lists as having ties to the country’s military. The documents date to May and do not reflect actual shipments, but they underscore the size of Nvidia’s potential market in China. In total the company applied to export more than 2.8 million of the chips, known as H200s. The value of the sales is redacted in the documents, but the company said this week that in its most recent quarter it made $2.4 billion from sales under licenses to Chinese customers. The Commerce Department did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

He presented it at the Vatican alongside AI developer Christopher Olah, cofounder of Anthropic, who acknowledged that companies like his need moral guidance to guard against “incentives and constraints that can sometimes conflict with doing the right thing”, the New York Times reported. “Technology is not simply a tool,” read the roughly 42,300-word open letter. “When it becomes the standard by which everything is judged, it begins to dictate what matters and what can be discarded, reducing creation to an object of exploitation and human beings to mere cogs in a system driven toward ever greater efficiency.” It warns that AI is never truly neutral, but “takes on the characteristics of those who devise, finance, regulate and use it”. And it calls for ethical oversight, social justice, protection of workers, responsible governance and peace. The encyclical criticises the use of AI in warfare, calling for imposing the “most rigorous ethical constraints” on weapons developed using AI. As governments invest heavily in autonomous military technologies and AI-assisted defence systems, the “growing ease” of deploying them makes war more likely and “less subject to human control”, it warns. This “violates the principle that armed force should be used only as a last resort in cases of legitimate self-defense”. The letter also criticises the growing concentration of technological power, and systems that reduce people to data or economic functions. It promotes what it calls a “civilisation of love”, centred on human dignity, solidarity, truth, compassion and the common good. Pope Leo’s response to the the AI revolution deliberately references his predecessor Pope Leo XIII’s response to the problems of the Industrial Revolution, Rerum Novarum (“Of New Things”) , in 1891. Though Magnifica Humanitas was released on May 25 2026, it is symbolically dated May 15, the date of Rerum Novarum. An encyclical is not an ordinary papal statement. Traditionally addressed to bishops and the wider Catholic world, it is one of the Catholic church’s most authoritative teaching documents. The pope no longer has the direct political power the papacy held in the 19th century. But papal teaching still carries moral weight across a global Catholic network of schools, universities, charities, hospitals and community organisations. The Vatican cannot regulate AI. It cannot write safety standards, police data centres, or force companies to disclose how their systems work. But it can help shape the moral terms of the debate. For more than a century, Catholic social teaching has influenced public arguments about work, inequality, poverty, human dignity and the ethical limits of economic power. Although popes issued encyclicals long before the modern era, Rerum Novarum made social encyclicals globally influential. It confronted exploitative labour conditions, widening inequality, and conflict between workers and employers. Pope Leo XIII defended workers’ rights and argued that wealth carried social responsibilities. He criticised both unrestricted capitalism and revolutionary socialism. The document influenced debates about labour rights and economic justice well beyond the church. In Australia in 1907, Justice H.B. Higgins drew on Rerum Novarum when establishing principles for a fair living wage. Pope Leo XIV’s encyclical attempts to do for the AI age what Rerum Novarum did for the industrial age: provide a moral framework for a technological transformation reshaping work, power and human relationships. Pope Leo XIV argues human rights are not granted by governments or corporations: they arise from the intrinsic dignity of every person. Technologies should serve humanity rather than reduce people to data, economic units or optimisation problems. He builds on Pope Francis’ critique of “the tendency to let the logic of efficiency, control and profit alone shape personal, social and economic decisions”, in his 2015 encyclical . It, too, warned of the risks of technology. Pope Leo XIV argues moral responsibility can’t be transferred to automated systems, regardless of how sophisticated they become. He also rejects transhumanist ideas that human limitations should be technologically overcome, arguing vulnerability, dependence and imperfection are essential to being human. Relationships, care, solidarity and compassion are not weaknesses. “Humanity flourishes not despite limitations, but often through them.” Running throughout the encyclical is a contrast between a “culture of power” and a “civilization of love”. One treats technology primarily as a tool for domination and control. The other places human dignity, justice and care at the centre of social life. The significance of Magnifica Humanitas lies in its ability to shape public conversation and moral imagination. Moral frameworks matter. They influence what societies fear, what they tolerate, what they defend – and what they refuse to sacrifice. Governments are investing in AI capability while still developing frameworks for transparency, accountability and safe deployment. Businesses are adopting AI tools at speed . Schools and universities are rethinking assessment, authorship and learning. Workers are being asked to adapt to systems they did not design and often cannot challenge. And citizens are increasingly governed, assessed and targeted by automated systems they may never see. Pope Leo XIV’s intervention reminds us the central question is not whether AI will be powerful: it already is. The question is whether that power will be made answerable to human dignity. The future of AI will not just be decided in laboratories, boardrooms or parliaments. It will also be decided by the moral limits societies are willing to set. Pope Leo XIV’s encyclical is an attempt to draw those limits. passages: By Deborah Castellano Lubov Pope Leo XIV welcomed participants in the International Space Forum 2026, which has been reflecting on the theme "The Gate to the Sky: Space for Peace," on Saturday at the Vatican.
sources.body: By Deborah Castellano Lubov Pope Leo XIV welcomed participants in the International Space Forum 2026, which has been reflecting on the theme "The Gate to the Sky: Space for Peace," on Saturday at the Vatican.

extraction.body: By Deborah Castellano Lubov Pope Leo XIV welcomed participants in the International Space Forum 2026, which has been reflecting on the theme "The Gate to the Sky: Space for Peace," on Saturday at the Vatican. The Pope expressed his appreciation for the choice of the Vatican as the venue for this year's Forum, dedicated to the urgent need to safeguard outer space from any kind of use or exploration for non-peaceful purposes. Need for a broader perspective of the world Pope Leo reflected that those who study space help us to adopt a broader perspective on the world. "You invite us to look at it as a whole, and to understand that the interests which lead people to wage war and exploit creation reveal a shortsighted outlook, often shaped by the idols of power and wealth." In this regard, he expressed his gratitude, noting that the Holy See, together with scholars from the Vatican Observatory, continues to contribute to research in the field of astrophysics. Pope Leo XIV concluded by imparting his Apostolic Blessing and wishing them every success in their work. [ Photo Embed: A photo of Pope Leo with those present at the audience]

BGR is pointing readers to it as the one Android privacy setting that can stop apps from reaching the camera, and the setting is documented on Android’s own help pages.
With the switch off, an app that asks for the camera gets a blank feed.
Android does not force-close a video-calling app because you cut the camera.
Open Settings, then Security & privacy, then Privacy, then Privacy controls, then Camera access.
Under Settings, Apps, the app’s name, Permissions, then Camera, you can choose Allow or Don’t allow for that single app.
This analysis walks through where the toggle lives, what it does, what it leaves alone, and how it compares with the other camera safeguards on your phone.
Test your own must-have apps once before relying on the toggle in a live situation.
If the green icon lights up anyway, something is trying to reach hardware, and the blank feed is doing its job.
The toggle addresses one channel, camera access by apps.
How it presents that blank feed depends on the app.
Android documents more than one way to reach camera settings.
Audit per-app permissions once a quarter so the apps you never use lose the camera for good.
Android also shows a green icon in the top-right corner of the screen whenever the camera or microphone is in use, according to the platform documentation.
A visible privacy control can serve as a selling point in a market where buyers weigh cameras heavily.
Swipe down twice to open Quick Settings and tap the Camera tile.
The Permission manager under Privacy shows the same permission across apps.

extraction.body: Android 12 and higher gives users a system-wide switch that turns off camera access for every app at once. BGR is pointing readers to it as the one Android privacy setting that can stop apps from reaching the camera, and the setting is documented on Android’s own help pages. With the switch off, an app that asks for the camera gets a blank feed. That detail matters more than it sounds. The app does not crash and does not see your room. It simply receives nothing useful. For anyone who has wondered what a flashlight app, a shopping app or a game could do with a lens, the toggle offers a blunt answer: take the lens away from all of them. The control sits alongside other phone-hygiene habits, such as the power-off and reboot advice for iPhone and Android we covered earlier. This analysis walks through where the toggle lives, what it does, what it leaves alone, and how it compares with the other camera safeguards on your phone. It sticks to what the published documentation and BGR’s report confirm. Where the sources go quiet, we say so. Add Shattered once in the Google app and our stories show up in your news suggestions. Per the Android documentation, supported devices running Android 12 or higher can disable camera access for all apps through a single system-wide toggle. The toggle appears in Quick Settings and in the Privacy area of Settings. Flip it off and every app on the phone loses the camera at once, whether you installed it yesterday or three years ago. This differs from the permission prompts most people know. A normal permission is a per-app decision. You grant it, deny it, and move on. The system-wide switch sits above those decisions. Think of it as a master breaker for the lens. Your per-app choices stay in place underneath, but while the master switch is off, none of them can deliver an image. The fact sheet we built this story on names two official entities, Android and Google, and no individual spokespeople. No one has gone on record with a statement about why the control exists or how many people use it. We therefore treat this as a documentation story and a how-to story, not a product-launch story. The setting is there, it works as described, and many owners probably have not touched it. Android’s official help pages give a specific menu route. Open Settings, then Security & privacy, then Privacy, then Privacy controls, then Camera access. Turning that control off disables camera access for apps. Menu names can shift a little between phone makers and software versions, so if your screen reads differently, look for the same words in the Privacy section. Android documents more than one way to reach camera settings. The table below lists each path exactly as the official documentation describes it, along with what each one controls. Two of these paths flip the master switch. The other two manage individual apps. The fifth item is not a control at all but a warning light, and it earns its own section below. Speed is the real feature here. A control buried five menus deep gets used once, during setup, and forgotten. A tile that sits in the panel you open for Wi-Fi and Bluetooth gets used in the moments that matter: before a sensitive meeting, while a phone sits on a desk beside a whiteboard, or when you hand your device to a stranger for a minute. Privacy tools succeed when they cost almost nothing to use. A two-swipe gesture sits near that threshold. It also reverses just as fast, so there is little penalty for being wrong. Turn the camera off by mistake, miss a video call prompt, tap the tile again, and the call resumes. That forgiving loop is what separates a habit from a one-time setup chore. If the tile is missing from your panel, the documented Settings route above still works. Many Android versions let you edit which tiles appear, though the exact steps vary by device and are not part of the confirmed facts for this story. The documentation states the outcome plainly. When camera access is disabled system-wide, an app receives a blank camera feed. Two things follow from that design choice. First, the lens stays unreachable in practice. A blank feed carries no pixels from the real world, so a camera-hungry app has nothing to record, upload or analyze. Second, apps keep running. Android does not force-close a video-calling app because you cut the camera. The app opens, asks for the lens, and shows a black or empty frame. You can still talk, type and share your screen on most services, depending on how the app handles the missing video. Expect some friction. An app that assumes a working camera may show an error, a spinning loader or a black rectangle. That is the trade-off for a control that sits above individual apps. The sources do not describe how particular apps respond, so we cannot rank them. Test your own must-have apps once before relying on the toggle in a live situation. Android already offers granular control. Under Settings, Apps, the app’s name, Permissions, then Camera, you can choose Allow or Don’t allow for that single app. The Permission manager, reached through Settings, Security & Privacy, Privacy, then Permission manager and Camera, shows the camera permission across your apps and lets you manage it from one list. So why bother with a master switch? Because the two tools solve different problems. Per-app permissions answer a long-term question: which apps deserve the camera? The system switch answers a short-term one: should any app have the camera right now? The table compares them. Used together, they cover each other’s weak spots. Audit per-app permissions once a quarter so the apps you never use lose the camera for good. Keep the master switch for moments when you want certainty without reviewing a list. Owners of Samsung phones who like layered unlock and trust settings may find the same mindset in our guide to Extend Unlock on a Galaxy phone . Android also shows a green icon in the top-right corner of the screen whenever the camera or microphone is in use, according to the platform documentation. It is a passive control. You cannot tap it to block anything, but it tells you something is happening. That makes the indicator a useful partner for the master switch. Picture a phone sitting idle on a table with the camera switch off. If the green icon lights up anyway, something is trying to reach hardware, and the blank feed is doing its job. If the icon lights up while the switch is on and you did not open a camera app, you have a prompt to open the Permission manager and see which app holds access. The pattern holds across all five groups. They want a quick, visible, reversible way to say no. The Quick Settings tile fits that need better than any permission prompt buried inside a particular app. Headlines that call this a privacy fix can overreach, so precision helps. Our fact sheet marks one category as unconfirmed: any claim that the setting prevents every form of surveillance, protects against all malicious apps, or guarantees complete privacy. None of the sources make those claims, and neither do we. The toggle addresses one channel, camera access by apps. It does not cover the microphone, location, stored photos, account data or the network traffic an app generates. A phone with the camera off can still leak plenty through other doors. Think of the switch as a lock on one door in a house with several. Enterprise IT teams care too. Companies that manage fleets of Android devices have a ready-made answer for staff who work near confidential screens. A short policy note that tells employees to flip the tile before a sensitive discussion costs nothing and needs no new software. Phone makers carry the third stake. A visible privacy control can serve as a selling point in a market where buyers weigh cameras heavily. How each maker places the tile, names the menu and defaults the setting will shape how often people use it. Those choices vary by device, and the confirmed facts here describe the standard Android paths only. The following are our analytical judgments, not reported facts. extraction.body: When you download a new app to your smartphone, you may find that it wishes to access certain features. These can range from accessing your contacts and location to using your camera. But some apps request camera access when they don't even need it. If you want that to stop, one Android privacy setting can prevent apps from accessing your camera. You may find several perfectly fair reasons as to why an app needs access to features on your smartphone. However, if you don't want apps to access your camera, you can turn it off in your Android phone's privacy settings. Go to Settings, Privacy, and Permission Manager. From there, select Camera to bring up a new screen that shows how many apps are accessing the camera. You can turn permissions on or off as you wish. This built-in Android feature shows all the privacy permissions you have or haven't granted to apps. Navigational apps like Google Maps may need your location to get around using GPS, Snapchat may ask to use your camera when you try to access it, and more. Going into app permissions to control what privacy settings and permissions you have enabled is one way to control what apps can access. You can also use a few other tools and methods to better control app permissions. You can do either manually through the app, and one even works automatically as part of a privacy feature on Android phones . You can change app permission settings for individual apps in Settings. On your Android device, go to Settings, and then Apps. Search for any app you have downloaded to your phone, then tap it to see more details. Choose Permissions for the app you want to change, and you will see whether you allowed or denied permissions for the app in question. To change the Permission setting, tap it and choose Allow or Don't allow. Additional prompts may include options like allow all the time, only while using the app, ask every time, and don't allow. If you have an app that works with Android 11 or higher on your smartphone but haven't used it in a while, Android may help you out on its own. The system has a built-in feature that automatically resets runtime permissions you may have granted when using the app. This resets the permissions by denying the app access to certain features. You can prevent your smartphone from spying on you. Using apps that request permission for your camera, location, and data can be helpful, but they have drawbacks. Companies and developers with access may use it to market to you. This can happen through ads that appear after you search for something on your smartphone and later see an ad about it. Your camera can also be used by others if you grant apps permission to access it. Hackers could potentially find a way into the app and use your data to hack into your smartphone's camera. If this happens, the hacker could turn on your camera to snap photos or take videos of your surroundings, you, and anything important nearby. There are ways to see if your Android smartphone's camera or microphone is being used by your phone. When you use any app that requires access to the camera or microphone, a green indicator appears in the top right corner of the phone's display. You can swipe down and select the indicator to see which app is using the camera or microphone. If you don't want the app to use either, go to Permissions to change the settings.

extraction.body: Android 12 and higher gives users a system-wide switch that turns off camera access for every app at once. BGR is pointing readers to it as the one Android privacy setting that can stop apps from reaching the camera, and the setting is documented on Android’s own help pages. With the switch off, an app that asks for the camera gets a blank feed. That detail matters more than it sounds. The app does not crash and does not see your room. It simply receives nothing useful. For anyone who has wondered what a flashlight app, a shopping app or a game could do with a lens, the toggle offers a blunt answer: take the lens away from all of them. The control sits alongside other phone-hygiene habits, such as the power-off and reboot advice for iPhone and Android we covered earlier. This analysis walks through where the toggle lives, what it does, what it leaves alone, and how it compares with the other camera safeguards on your phone. It sticks to what the published documentation and BGR’s report confirm. Where the sources go quiet, we say so. Add Shattered once in the Google app and our stories show up in your news suggestions. The toggle appears in Quick Settings and in the Privacy area of Settings. Flip it off and every app on the phone loses the camera at once, whether you installed it yesterday or three years ago. This differs from the permission prompts most people know. A normal permission is a per-app decision. You grant it, deny it, and move on. The system-wide switch sits above those decisions. Think of it as a master breaker for the lens. Your per-app choices stay in place underneath, but while the master switch is off, none of them can deliver an image. The fact sheet we built this story on names two official entities, Android and Google, and no individual spokespeople. No one has gone on record with a statement about why the control exists or how many people use it. We therefore treat this as a documentation story and a how-to story, not a product-launch story. Menu names can shift a little between phone makers and software versions, so if your screen reads differently, look for the same words in the Privacy section. Two of these paths flip the master switch. The other two manage individual apps. The fifth item is not a control at all but a warning light, and it earns its own section below. Speed is the real feature here. A control buried five menus deep gets used once, during setup, and forgotten. A tile that sits in the panel you open for Wi-Fi and Bluetooth gets used in the moments that matter: before a sensitive meeting, while a phone sits on a desk beside a whiteboard, or when you hand your device to a stranger for a minute. Privacy tools succeed when they cost almost nothing to use. A two-swipe gesture sits near that threshold. It also reverses just as fast, so there is little penalty for being wrong. Turn the camera off by mistake, miss a video call prompt, tap the tile again, and the call resumes. That forgiving loop is what separates a habit from a one-time setup chore. extraction.body: When you download a new app to your smartphone, you may find that it wishes to access certain features. These can range from accessing your contacts and location to using your camera. But some apps request camera access when they don't even need it. If you want that to stop, one Android privacy setting can prevent apps from accessing your camera. You may find several perfectly fair reasons as to why an app needs access to features on your smartphone. However, if you don't want apps to access your camera, you can turn it off in your Android phone's privacy settings. Go to Settings, Privacy, and Permission Manager. From there, select Camera to bring up a new screen that shows how many apps are accessing the camera. You can turn permissions on or off as you wish. This built-in Android feature shows all the privacy permissions you have or haven't granted to apps. Navigational apps like Google Maps may need your location to get around using GPS, Snapchat may ask to use your camera when you try to access it, and more. Going into app permissions to control what privacy settings and permissions you have enabled is one way to control what apps can access. You can also use a few other tools and methods to better control app permissions. You can do either manually through the app, and one even works automatically as part of a privacy feature on Android phones . You can change app permission settings for individual apps in Settings. On your Android device, go to Settings, and then Apps. Search for any app you have downloaded to your phone, then tap it to see more details. Choose Permissions for the app you want to change, and you will see whether you allowed or denied permissions for the app in question. To change the Permission setting, tap it and choose Allow or Don't allow. Additional prompts may include options like allow all the time, only while using the app, ask every time, and don't allow. If you have an app that works with Android 11 or higher on your smartphone but haven't used it in a while, Android may help you out on its own. The system has a built-in feature that automatically resets runtime permissions you may have granted when using the app. This resets the permissions by denying the app access to certain features. You can prevent your smartphone from spying on you. Using apps that request permission for your camera, location, and data can be helpful, but they have drawbacks. Companies and developers with access may use it to market to you. This can happen through ads that appear after you search for something on your smartphone and later see an ad about it. Your camera can also be used by others if you grant apps permission to access it. Hackers could potentially find a way into the app and use your data to hack into your smartphone's camera. If this happens, the hacker could turn on your camera to snap photos or take videos of your surroundings, you, and anything important nearby. There are ways to see if your Android smartphone's camera or microphone is being used by your phone. When you use any app that requires access to the camera or microphone, a green indicator appears in the top right corner of the phone's display. You can swipe down and select the indicator to see which app is using the camera or microphone. If you don't want the app to use either, go to Permissions to change the settings.

extraction.body: Security cameras outside the Bishop Henry Whipple Federal Building at Fort Snelling recorded plain-clothes officers making an ICE re-arrest of two men seconds after they walked out the front doors, freed on orders from federal judges, MPR News reported Nov. 20. The previously unpublished footage, dated Sept. 9 and Sept. 25, puts pictures to a tactic that has divided the federal bench in Minnesota, and at least one judge there is now writing new limits into his release orders to stop it. The legal stakes are larger than two arrests. A habeas corpus petition under 28 U.S.C. 2241 is the main way a detained immigrant can challenge custody in federal court, and its remedy is release. If ICE can hand someone release papers and take him back into custody at the threshold, the government can say it obeyed the order while the person never spent a free minute. Whether a release happened at all is a question of fact, and video is exactly the kind of evidence that settles questions of fact. The Sept. 9 recording shows Pablo Hernandez Franco, 32, of Mexico, whom U.S. District Judge Jeffrey Bryan had ordered released “immediately.” In a sworn statement, Hernandez said his shoulder was dislocated during the arrest; the deportation officer involved stated under oath that Hernandez did not express pain to him, according to MPR. Bryan later found the re-arrest violated his order, reasoning that because ICE “immediately swarmed” Hernandez, he “was not released from custody.” ICE let him go on Sept. 25. That same morning, cameras caught the re-arrest of Alejandro Corro Guzmán, 34, also from Mexico. Chief U.S. District Judge Eric Tostrud refused to order him freed again and called the argument that he had never been released “not persuasive.” Those two outcomes capture the split. MPR has confirmed at least eight men in Minnesota who were re-arrested this way after a judge ordered each released, one of them twice. Bryan and Judge John Tunheim have found violations; Tostrud and Judge Jerry Blackwell have not. Earlier coverage of the Minnesota and Colorado contempt fights traced how the practice spread. Tunheim has shifted from finding violations after the fact to heading them off. In two habeas orders issued the Monday before the footage ran, MPR reported, he wrote that “Respondents SHALL NOT re-detain Petitioner” without adequate notice and a pre-detention bond hearing, citing the station’s reporting. That tracks Colorado, where judges have required advance notice to the court before any re-detention and where U.S. District Judge Charlotte Sweeney held the government in contempt but imposed no sanction after an ICE official testified the practice had stopped. The government’s position deserves to be stated plainly. DHS has said ICE “may seek to rearrest the alien in a way that complies with the judicial decision,” and an ICE official told MPR this month that enforcement options can include re-arresting someone. ICE officials in Minnesota have said agency lawyers review release orders for re-arrest candidates, and that when a judge finds the first arrest was made without a warrant, ICE treats the ruling as room for a “do-over,” according to MPR. That theory has real footing: an order curing an unlawful arrest does not, on its own terms, bar a new and lawful one, and Bryan himself wrote that a release order does not prevent future re-arrest. The fight is over timing and process, not over whether ICE may ever detain these men again. The practical effect is a district where protection depends on the judge and the drafting. A detainee whose order carries Tunheim’s notice and bond-hearing terms has a shield that a detainee before another judge in the same courthouse lacks. Expect lawyers to ask for that language in every petition, and for the government to push back against limits it did not have before. A division this sharp among judges of one district is the kind of question likely to reach the Eighth Circuit. Similar challenges are already moving elsewhere, including a class action over re-detention in Atlanta and at least 20 re-arrest cases nationwide . For one man the debate is not abstract. Tha Im, a Cambodian man representing himself, was re-arrested at Whipple on Oct. 19 and was still held at the Kandiyohi County Jail a month later, MPR reported. The re-arrests come as the paths for immigrants to gain release from ICE detention have narrowed under the second Trump administration.

Previously, immigrants were commonly released on bond if they were detained at all. They would continue to live and work in between regular check-ins with ICE as their immigration case made its way through the court.

Now, many immigrants are being denied bond or even the chance at a bond hearing. Many challenge their detention by filing what’s known as a petition for habeas corpus requiring the government to justify why it's holding someone.
In many cases, federal judges are granting habeas petitions and ordering the government to provide a bond hearing or ordering the person’s release outright.

In each of the eight cases confirmed in Minnesota, an immigrant was ordered released by a federal judge. ICE agents brought them from one of the county jails that are paid to hold detainees for ICE to the Whipple building for processing.
The Whipple building is located in Fort Snelling and houses ICE’s St. Paul field office and the immigration court.
The men were told they were being released, signed release papers and were given back their belongings. However, some men reported belongings were missing. Then the men were pointed toward a door.
Sometimes, the men made it steps outside the building’s front doors. Others were brought out a back door or said they didn't make it outside at all before ICE re-arrested them.
Sometimes ICE told the court what happened. Sometimes it didn’t. Some men had lawyers who could quickly alert the court to the re-arrest. Some didn’t.
For example, a Cambodian man named Tha Im was instantly re-arrested on Oct. 19. He is representing himself in court and is still in custody a month later at Kandiyohi County Jail.
Federal judges in Minnesota are split on the issue. Bryan and U.S. District Judge John Tunheim found the re-arrests violated their release orders.

U.S. District Judge Jerry Blackwell found a re-arrest did not violate his release order. Tostrud denied re-release requests from two re-arrested men and wrote he found Corro’s argument that he had never been released at all “not persuasive.”

In two habeas release orders issued Monday, Tunheim proactively wrote “Respondents SHALL NOT re-detain Petitioner” without “adequate notice” and a pre-detention bond hearing, citing reporting about instant re-arrests by MPR News.

An ICE official in Colorado testified he ordered similar re-arrests there after speaking to “colleagues” in Minnesota . ICE instantly re-arrested at least 18 people in Colorado in about a week, according to court records.

Colorado U.S. District Judge Charlotte Sweeney held the government in contempt for an instant re-arrest and said she wouldn’t take further action only because the ICE official had said under oath that he had stopped the re-arrests.

extraction.body: Security cameras outside the Bishop Henry Whipple Federal Building at Fort Snelling recorded plain-clothes officers making an ICE re-arrest of two men seconds after they walked out the front doors, freed on orders from federal judges, MPR News reported Nov. 20. The previously unpublished footage, dated Sept. 9 and Sept. 25, puts pictures to a tactic that has divided the federal bench in Minnesota, and at least one judge there is now writing new limits into his release orders to stop it. The legal stakes are larger than two arrests. A habeas corpus petition under 28 U.S.C. 2241 is the main way a detained immigrant can challenge custody in federal court, and its remedy is release. If ICE can hand someone release papers and take him back into custody at the threshold, the government can say it obeyed the order while the person never spent a free minute. Whether a release happened at all is a question of fact, and video is exactly the kind of evidence that settles questions of fact. The Sept. 9 recording shows Pablo Hernandez Franco, 32, of Mexico, whom U.S. District Judge Jeffrey Bryan had ordered released “immediately.” In a sworn statement, Hernandez said his shoulder was dislocated during the arrest; the deportation officer involved stated under oath that Hernandez did not express pain to him, according to MPR. Bryan later found the re-arrest violated his order, reasoning that because ICE “immediately swarmed” Hernandez, he “was not released from custody.” ICE let him go on Sept. 25. That same morning, cameras caught the re-arrest of Alejandro Corro Guzmán, 34, also from Mexico. Chief U.S. District Judge Eric Tostrud refused to order him freed again and called the argument that he had never been released “not persuasive.” Those two outcomes capture the split. MPR has confirmed at least eight men in Minnesota who were re-arrested this way after a judge ordered each released, one of them twice. Bryan and Judge John Tunheim have found violations; Tostrud and Judge Jerry Blackwell have not. Earlier coverage of the Minnesota and Colorado contempt fights traced how the practice spread. Tunheim has shifted from finding violations after the fact to heading them off. In two habeas orders issued the Monday before the footage ran, MPR reported, he wrote that “Respondents SHALL NOT re-detain Petitioner” without adequate notice and a pre-detention bond hearing, citing the station’s reporting. That tracks Colorado, where judges have required advance notice to the court before any re-detention and where U.S. District Judge Charlotte Sweeney held the government in contempt but imposed no sanction after an ICE official testified the practice had stopped. The government’s position deserves to be stated plainly. DHS has said ICE “may seek to rearrest the alien in a way that complies with the judicial decision,” and an ICE official told MPR this month that enforcement options can include re-arresting someone. ICE officials in Minnesota have said agency lawyers review release orders for re-arrest candidates, and that when a judge finds the first arrest was made without a warrant, ICE treats the ruling as room for a “do-over,” according to MPR. That theory has real footing: an order curing an unlawful arrest does not, on its own terms, bar a new and lawful one, and Bryan himself wrote that a release order does not prevent future re-arrest. The fight is over timing and process, not over whether ICE may ever detain these men again. The practical effect is a district where protection depends on the judge and the drafting. A detainee whose order carries Tunheim’s notice and bond-hearing terms has a shield that a detainee before another judge in the same courthouse lacks. Expect lawyers to ask for that language in every petition, and for the government to push back against limits it did not have before. A division this sharp among judges of one district is the kind of question likely to reach the Eighth Circuit. Similar challenges are already moving elsewhere, including a class action over re-detention in Atlanta and at least 20 re-arrest cases nationwide . For one man the debate is not abstract. Tha Im, a Cambodian man representing himself, was re-arrested at Whipple on Oct. 19 and was still held at the Kandiyohi County Jail a month later, MPR reported. Previously unpublished security camera footage shows two men being instantly re-arrested by immigration officers steps outside the Bishop Henry Whipple Federal Building after judges ordered their release.

The videos show instant re-arrests made on Sept. 9 and Sept. 25, a tactic several judges have found Immigration and Customs Enforcement has used to circumvent their release orders. MPR News has confirmed at least eight men have been instantly re-arrested this way. One man was re-arrested twice.

In both videos, ICE officers in plain clothes wait outside the front doors of the Whipple building and instantly arrest the men as soon as they step outside. Pablo Hernandez Franco said in a sworn statement that his shoulder was dislocated during his Sept. 9 re-arrest.

ICE deportation officer Mitchell T. Olson was involved in at least four instant re-arrests, according to court records. Court records confirm that Olson carried the new arrest warrant when Hernandez was re-arrested. The video shows Olson holding a piece of paper in front of Hernandez for about a second.
MPR News helps you turn down the noise and build shared understanding. Turn up your support for this public resource and keep trusted journalism accessible to all.
In response to Hernandez’s claim that his shoulder was dislocated, Olson said in a sworn statement that Hernandez “did not express any displeasure or pain to me.”

ICE officials in Minnesota have said their lawyers analyze release orders for candidates for re-arrest. For example, if the judge ruled the original arrest was warrantless and unlawful, ICE has interpreted that to mean it gets a do-over.

In a Nov. 10 statement to MPR News, an unnamed ICE official wrote: “When appropriate, ICE will address the issues identified by the court and take further action consistent with applicable law and court orders, which can include rearresting an offender.”

An unnamed Department of Homeland Security spokesperson wrote on Oct. 27 that ICE “may seek to rearrest the alien in a way that complies with the judicial decision. To suggest that ICE cannot do this is nothing short of sabotage.”

Hernandez is a 32-year-old man from Mexico, who lives and works in Minnesota. According to court records, he came to the United States in 2024 and overstayed a tourist visa. He’s engaged to a U.S. citizen and expecting a child with her, according to his habeas petition, filed Sept. 3.

U.S. District Judge Jeffrey Bryan wrote a scathing order in response to the re-arrest and required ICE to “immediately” release Hernandez. Bryan wrote that a habeas release order does not preclude the government from ever re-arresting someone, but because ICE officers “immediately swarmed” Hernandez steps outside the Whipple building, he “was not released from custody.”
ICE re-released Hernandez at about 9 a.m. Sept. 25, according to court records.

That same morning, Alejandro Corro Guzmán was instantly re-arrested at the front doors of Whipple. Corro is a 34-year-old man also from Mexico who had a valid work permit and a pending asylum claim when ICE detained him in May. The claim was later denied and an appeal is pending, according to Corro’s lawyer.

Tostrud found Corro and another man who was instantly re-arrested did not make strong enough legal arguments that re-release would remedy the actions ICE took against them.
Corro had previously requested MPR News only refer to him by his first name because he feared retaliation. Now that his habeas case has concluded, Corro agreed his full name could be published.

Now, many immigrants are being denied bond or even the chance at a bond hearing. Many challenge their detention by filing what’s known as a petition for habeas corpus requiring the government to justify why it's holding someone.
In many cases, federal judges are granting habeas petitions and ordering the government to provide a bond hearing or ordering the person’s release outright.

In each of the eight cases confirmed in Minnesota, an immigrant was ordered released by a federal judge. ICE agents brought them from one of the county jails that are paid to hold detainees for ICE to the Whipple building for processing.
The Whipple building is located in Fort Snelling and houses ICE’s St. Paul field office and the immigration court.
The men were told they were being released, signed release papers and were given back their belongings. However, some men reported belongings were missing. Then the men were pointed toward a door.
Sometimes, the men made it steps outside the building’s front doors. Others were brought out a back door or said they didn't make it outside at all before ICE re-arrested them.
Sometimes ICE told the court what happened. Sometimes it didn’t. Some men had lawyers who could quickly alert the court to the re-arrest. Some didn’t.
For example, a Cambodian man named Tha Im was instantly re-arrested on Oct. 19. He is representing himself in court and is still in custody a month later at Kandiyohi County Jail.

extraction.body: Bitcoin fell below $60,000 for the first time since early July as ETF outflows, an AI-stock selloff and rate-hike bets drove its worst month since June 2022. Bitcoin fell below $60,000 on Friday for the first time since early July, market data showed, extending a November selloff that has erased more than a fifth of its value and put it on pace for its worst month since June 2022. The break of a level many traders had treated as a floor was driven by a combination of heavy outflows from US spot bitcoin exchange-traded funds, a rotation into artificial-intelligence stocks after Anthropic's record initial public offering, and expectations of further Federal Reserve rate increases, according to market reports and analysts. On Binance, bitcoin fell 4.79 percent over 24 hours to $59,864.43 late on Friday, while CoinMarketCap's average across more than 20 exchanges showed a 5.05 percent decline, 24.kg reported. Yahoo Finance data showed bitcoin falling as low as $57,957 in late Friday morning trading before recovering to about $58,500 by the afternoon. By early Saturday it had slid further, trading near $56,200. At its Friday price, bitcoin was down more than 20 percent in November, on pace for its worst monthly performance since June 2022 and its eighth-worst month since Yahoo Finance began tracking the asset in September 2014. Bitcoin Magazine reported the price had lost more than half its value from its record above $126,000 set in October 2025. US spot bitcoin ETFs recorded $582.2 million in net withdrawals on Thursday, according to Farside Investors data cited by crypto.news and Decrypt. BlackRock's iShares Bitcoin Trust accounted for $541.1 million, its largest single-day outflow on record. The figure brought net withdrawals to about $3.47 billion across the first 14 US trading sessions of November. Because spot ETFs hold bitcoin directly, net redemptions require funds to sell coins, turning investor withdrawals into market selling. Leveraged traders were hit as well: roughly $727 million in crypto positions were liquidated over 24 hours, about 86 percent of them bullish bets, with more than 151,000 traders liquidated, Decrypt reported citing CoinGlass. The Crypto Fear and Greed Index fell to 9, a reading classified as extreme fear and its lowest since February. Anthropic priced its Nasdaq debut at $83 a share on November 19, raising $81.34 billion in the largest initial public offering on record. The stock opened at $111.50 and closed at $97.17, then fell about 10 percent on Friday, crypto.news reported. Some investors had sold crypto to raise cash for the listing; Bitquery counted roughly $2 billion in Anthropic-linked trading across three Hyperliquid markets from August through November 18. Rate expectations added pressure. Bitcoin Magazine reported that traders saw a roughly 94 percent chance of a Federal Reserve rate increase in December, according to CME Group's FedWatch tool. CoinShares head of research James Butterfill described the slide as "a continuation of the existing bear market" rather than the start of another, with a base case of bitcoin trading between $60,000 and $90,000 through much of 2027. That is a forecast, not a realised outcome. Crypto-linked stocks fell harder than bitcoin. Bitcoin Magazine reported MARA Holdings down about 11 percent, Riot Platforms down 11 percent, CleanSpark down 12 percent and IREN down 12 percent on Friday, while Strategy fell about 7 percent and Coinbase about 3 percent. Onchain analytics firm Glassnode said the average bitcoin holder was only just in profit, with the ratio of market value to realised value, known as MVRV, just above one; a break below would put holders in loss for the first time since early 2023. The selling reached global equities. crypto.news reported that MSCI's world stock index fell for a seventh straight day, its longest streak since 2023, with Taiwan's benchmark down 6.2 percent, South Korea's Kospi down 5.2 percent and Japan's Nikkei down about 5 percent on Friday. US Treasuries rallied, sending the 10-year yield below 5 percent, while the dollar traded near a 20-month high. Prices varied by exchange and time of day, and the figures above are snapshots rather than a single official close. The next checkpoints cited by analysts were the US jobs report on December 4 and the Federal Reserve meeting on December 9, which will shape whether fund outflows and rate pressure ease.
