sources.title: I’m a priest. Silicon Valley’s search for the ‘soul’ of AI is deeply troubling | Rev Kevin Deal - The Guardian
passages: As a priest, I find this pursuit deeply troubling.
Whatever the sincere hopes of its creators, AI is being developed within an economic system that increasingly measures the worth of everything solely by its productivity.
That is what makes Silicon Valley’s fascination with the spirituality of its machines so strange.
It is whether the people building them are willing to treat the rest of humanity as something more than machines.

extraction.body: Last month, religious leaders from across San Francisco gathered behind closed doors to discuss what it means to be human in the age of artificial intelligence. Anthropic, the AI company operating only a couple of miles from my parish, has been courting priests, rabbis and theologians. Its billionaire cofounder, Christopher Olah, has even pressed Vatican advisers to take seriously the possibility that his company’s chatbot might possess consciousness. As a priest, I find this pursuit deeply troubling. I welcome serious conversations about AI’s moral implications, especially theological ones. But the extraordinary effort to establish whether a machine might have consciousness, or possess a soul, reveals a profound misunderstanding of what makes us human. Our souls and minds and bodies are so much more than the tasks we perform. Artificial intelligence could never replicate the transcendent mundanity of who we are. Even if every synapse in our brains were externally replicated, even if the perfect AI configuration were designed to duplicate our central nervous system, it would still lack divine spark. Artificial intelligence is formed as commerce, pure utility. Its existence requires enormous concentrations of capital, infrastructure, and the accumulated intelligence of humanity. It’s an ongoing economic choice, driven by pursuit of profit, hope for a better world, and sociopolitical fear. If a model doesn’t make a good return, it’s cast aside. Whatever the sincere hopes of its creators, AI is being developed within an economic system that increasingly measures the worth of everything solely by its productivity. That is what makes Silicon Valley’s fascination with the spirituality of its machines so strange. Its founders are turning to religious leaders to ask whether their creations might possess consciousness, how they might be taught goodness, even whether they should learn to confess their wrongdoings. Yet the very traditions they are consulting have spent millennia teaching us that goodness cannot be reduced to a set of behaviors, any more than the soul of humanity, as magnificent and ineffable as it is, can be replicated by a machine. And while Silicon Valley seeks to establish the humanity of its products, it seems increasingly comfortable treating actual human beings as little more than instruments of production. Consider confession, a practice Anthropic researchers have reportedly considered teaching their models. In Christianity , confession demands more than acknowledging a mistake or expressing regret. sources.title: Amazon: China-Linked Hackers’ AI Agents Exploited Medical Software Zero-Day - SecurityWeek
passages: Amazon says autonomous AI agents run by a China-linked threat actor found and exploited a zero-day vulnerability in MONAI Label, an open source tool designed for AI-assisted annotation of medical images.
The instance had no authentication, so anyone could see the operator’s prompts and the agents’ output.
The records showed a roughly 48-hour campaign against IP addresses belonging to universities in East Asia outside mainland China.
After identifying the software on one target and mapping its API, the agents discovered a path traversal bug in a file upload function.
“In about 11 minutes, the agents went from mapping the application’s API to arbitrarily writing files on the server,” Amazon said .
“The server that the proxy connected to was running the same vulnerable software, and we infer the actor had used the zero-day to compromise it and establish the tunnel,” Amazon noted.
The MONAI Label developers published an advisory this week.
It rates the bug critical and says it affects versions 0.8.5 and earlier.
Authentication is off by default, enabling anyone who can reach the server over the network to exploit the vulnerability.
A fix has been created and will be included in the next release.

Amazon has attributed the attack to an unidentified Chinese-nexus threat actor with moderate confidence, based on the language used in the prompts, the time zone in the scripts, and the fact that the targeted universities are likely of strategic interest to China.
He worked as a high school IT teacher before starting a career in journalism in 2011.

Amazon says autonomous AI agents run by a China-linked threat actor found and exploited a zero-day vulnerability in MONAI Label, an open source tool designed for AI-assisted annotation of medical images. The tech giant’s threat intelligence team detected the activity in September, after coming across an exposed instance of Cairn , an open source AI penetration testing framework. The instance had no authentication, so anyone could see the operator’s prompts and the agents’ output. The records showed a roughly 48-hour campaign against IP addresses belonging to universities in East Asia outside mainland China. The operator gave the agents a list of targets and told them to obtain shell access. After identifying the software on one target and mapping its API, the agents discovered a path traversal bug in a file upload function. “In about 11 minutes, the agents went from mapping the application’s API to arbitrarily writing files on the server,” Amazon said . In a later session, the agents used the flaw to plant a Python reverse shell in a file Python runs every time the interpreter starts, ultimately achieving a root shell. Advertisement. Scroll to continue reading. “Amazon Threat Intelligence assesses with high confidence that it was a zero-day based on the absence of any corresponding fix, issue, advisory, or prior mention in vulnerability databases for the affected open-source project,” the company said. The operator then gave the agents a proxy that tunneled into a second university and instructed them to target other devices on its network. “The server that the proxy connected to was running the same vulnerable software, and we infer the actor had used the zero-day to compromise it and establish the tunnel,” Amazon noted. The MONAI Label developers published an advisory this week. It rates the bug critical and says it affects versions 0.8.5 and earlier. Authentication is off by default, enabling anyone who can reach the server over the network to exploit the vulnerability. A fix has been created and will be included in the next release. Amazon has attributed the attack to an unidentified Chinese-nexus threat actor with moderate confidence, based on the language used in the prompts, the time zone in the scripts, and the fact that the targeted universities are likely of strategic interest to China. The instance had no authentication, so anyone could see the operator’s prompts and the agents’ output.
The records showed a roughly 48-hour campaign against IP addresses belonging to universities in East Asia outside mainland China.
After identifying the software on one target and mapping its API, the agents discovered a path traversal bug in a file upload function.
“In about 11 minutes, the agents went from mapping the application’s API to arbitrarily writing files on the server,” Amazon said .
“The server that the proxy connected to was running the same vulnerable software, and we infer the actor had used the zero-day to compromise it and establish the tunnel,” Amazon noted.
The MONAI Label developers published an advisory this week.
It rates the bug critical and says it affects versions 0.8.5 and earlier.
Authentication is off by default, enabling anyone who can reach the server over the network to exploit the vulnerability.
A fix has been created and will be included in the next release.

Amazon has attributed the attack to an unidentified Chinese-nexus threat actor with moderate confidence, based on the language used in the prompts, the time zone in the scripts, and the fact that the targeted universities are likely of strategic interest to China.
He worked as a high school IT teacher before starting a career in journalism in 2011.
Eduard holds a bachelor’s degree in industrial informatics and a master’s degree in computer techniques applied in electrical engineering.

extraction.body: A threat actor used autonomous Cairn AI agents to discover and exploit a critical MONAI Label vulnerability. Amazon says autonomous AI agents run by a China-linked threat actor found and exploited a zero-day vulnerability in MONAI Label, an open source tool designed for AI-assisted annotation of medical images. The tech giant’s threat intelligence team detected the activity in September, after coming across an exposed instance of Cairn , an open source AI penetration testing framework. The instance had no authentication, so anyone could see the operator’s prompts and the agents’ output. The records showed a roughly 48-hour campaign against IP addresses belonging to universities in East Asia outside mainland China. The operator gave the agents a list of targets and told them to obtain shell access. After identifying the software on one target and mapping its API, the agents discovered a path traversal bug in a file upload function. “In about 11 minutes, the agents went from mapping the application’s API to arbitrarily writing files on the server,” Amazon said . In a later session, the agents used the flaw to plant a Python reverse shell in a file Python runs every time the interpreter starts, ultimately achieving a root shell. Advertisement. Scroll to continue reading. “Amazon Threat Intelligence assesses with high confidence that it was a zero-day based on the absence of any corresponding fix, issue, advisory, or prior mention in vulnerability databases for the affected open-source project,” the company said. The operator then gave the agents a proxy that tunneled into a second university and instructed them to target other devices on its network. “The server that the proxy connected to was running the same vulnerable software, and we infer the actor had used the zero-day to compromise it and establish the tunnel,” Amazon noted. The MONAI Label developers published an advisory this week. It rates the bug critical and says it affects versions 0.8.5 and earlier. Authentication is off by default, enabling anyone who can reach the server over the network to exploit the vulnerability. A fix has been created and will be included in the next release. Amazon has attributed the attack to an unidentified Chinese-nexus threat actor with moderate confidence, based on the language used in the prompts, the time zone in the scripts, and the fact that the targeted universities are likely of strategic interest to China. passages: ARK Invest Chief Investment Officer Cathie Wood told CNBC the investment management firm's $1.5 million bull case price target for bitcoin by 2030 still stands.
She also said that it wouldn't surprise her if bitcoin reached its all-time high again before the end of 2027.
The broader digital asset market has struggled after the Clarity Act, a crypto market structure bill, failed to advance in the Senate in September.

"I think the biggest catalyst we're seeing right now is actually very much in motion and it's happening, which is capital markets are moving onchain," eToro CEO Yoni Assia told CNBC in an exclusive interview from the conference.
He pointed to the SpaceX IPO as an example, which had derivatives trading on eToro before the IPO.
That includes BlackRock , the world's largest asset manager.
Last month, Strategy's Michael Saylor said he thinks bitcoin's next bull market is already underway.
Wood said that ARK Invest believes bitcoin has found its low and stressed that cybersecurity is "top of mind right now," which could provide yet another opportunity for crypto markets to rebound.
Crypto investors are hunting for the next positive catalyst after U.S. crypto regulation — a longtime market driver — fizzled in 2026.
Assia said that supportive regulation in the U.S. from agencies, including the Securities and Exchange Commission and the Commodity Futures Trading Commission, is also helping adoption of crypto.

extraction.body: Crypto investors are hunting for the next positive catalyst after U.S. crypto regulation — a longtime market driver — fizzled in 2026. Bitcoin traded around $61,500 on Friday, a more than 50% decline from its all-time high above $126,000 reached in October 2025. The broader digital asset market has struggled after the Clarity Act, a crypto market structure bill, failed to advance in the Senate in September. Investors now see Wall Street's embrace of blockchain technology — particularly tokenization — as the next trend to give bitcoin a boost. "Every single traditional firm is now looking at digital assets," BitGo CEO Mike Belshe told CNBC last week in an exclusive interview from the fintech-focused Cantor Convergence conference in Miami Beach. That includes BlackRock , the world's largest asset manager. He pointed to statements from the asset management giant's CEO, Larry Fink, who said the next major evolution in global finance is the creation of digital representations of every stock, bond, fund and real-world asset onto a shared blockchain ledger. "I think the biggest catalyst we're seeing right now is actually very much in motion and it's happening, which is capital markets are moving onchain," eToro CEO Yoni Assia told CNBC in an exclusive interview from the conference. He pointed to the SpaceX IPO as an example, which had derivatives trading on eToro before the IPO. "First day of trading, we distributed it to our retail clients, and it started trading 24/7, and that's all because capital markets are now copying crypto markets and are sitting on the same rails," Assia said. "Crypto markets have always been 24/7, they never sleep, and now what we're seeing is that capital markets are copying crypto markets using the same technology so stocks are moving onchain, they're being tokenized." Assia said that supportive regulation in the U.S. from agencies, including the Securities and Exchange Commission and the Commodity Futures Trading Commission, is also helping adoption of crypto. He pointed to the CFTC earlier this month clearing the way for crypto-style perpetual futures tied to individual stocks to trade on regulated U.S. exchanges for the first time. Assia also highlighted the SEC's move to issue an order in September, creating a regulatory pathway for certain trading venues to trade tokenized representations of publicly traded U.S. stocks. "Blockchain technology is now starting to power what's happening in capital markets," Assia told CNBC. "That is the one of the biggest changes we're going to see in capital markets for many, many years." "We're talking about hundreds of trillions of dollars that are going to be tokenized and move onchain and at the same time, I do believe that will support prices of bitcoin and other blockchains as well," he continued. The industry is also watching whether inflation will ease and geopolitical tensions will subside in the new year, which could lower broader macro risk currently hampering the industry. Last month, Strategy's Michael Saylor said he thinks bitcoin's next bull market is already underway. ARK Invest Chief Investment Officer Cathie Wood told CNBC the investment management firm's $1.5 million bull case price target for bitcoin by 2030 still stands. She also said that it wouldn't surprise her if bitcoin reached its all-time high again before the end of 2027. "Our macro forecast has inflation breaking down considerably," Wood told CNBC in an exclusive interview at Cantor Convergence. "I think the elections have increased our confidence there because the war [in Iran], one way or the other, is going to end." She added that "bitcoin has weathered so much bad news," including the $6.3 billion Binance hack and the "distraction" of AI which, "many people would say is sucking the oxygen away from bitcoin." The maturation of the artificial intelligence trade could provide an opportunity for bitcoin to find new inflows. Wood said that ARK Invest believes bitcoin has found its low and stressed that cybersecurity is "top of mind right now," which could provide yet another opportunity for crypto markets to rebound. "I think if the Bitcoin and crypto world coalesces and makes investors feel that they've got their arms around security and actually understand that there might be more security issues in the traditional financial system, I think we're going to see a wave of support," Wood said. extraction.body: Crypto investors are hunting for the next positive catalyst after U.S. crypto regulation — a longtime market driver — fizzled in 2026. Bitcoin traded around $61,500 on Friday, a more than 50% decline from its all-time high above $126,000 reached in October 2025. The broader digital asset market has struggled after the Clarity Act, a crypto market structure bill, failed to advance in the Senate in September. Investors now see Wall Street's embrace of blockchain technology — particularly tokenization — as the next trend to give bitcoin a boost. "Every single traditional firm is now looking at digital assets," BitGo CEO Mike Belshe told CNBC last week in an exclusive interview from the fintech-focused Cantor Convergence conference in Miami Beach. That includes BlackRock , the world's largest asset manager. He pointed to statements from the asset management giant's CEO, Larry Fink, who said the next major evolution in global finance is the creation of digital representations of every stock, bond, fund and real-world asset onto a shared blockchain ledger. "I think the biggest catalyst we're seeing right now is actually very much in motion and it's happening, which is capital markets are moving onchain," eToro CEO Yoni Assia told CNBC in an exclusive interview from the conference. He pointed to the SpaceX IPO as an example, which had derivatives trading on eToro before the IPO. "First day of trading, we distributed it to our retail clients, and it started trading 24/7, and that's all because capital markets are now copying crypto markets and are sitting on the same rails," Assia said. "Crypto markets have always been 24/7, they never sleep, and now what we're seeing is that capital markets are copying crypto markets using the same technology so stocks are moving onchain, they're being tokenized." Assia said that supportive regulation in the U.S. from agencies, including the Securities and Exchange Commission and the Commodity Futures Trading Commission, is also helping adoption of crypto. He pointed to the CFTC earlier this month clearing the way for crypto-style perpetual futures tied to individual stocks to trade on regulated U.S. exchanges for the first time. Assia also highlighted the SEC's move to issue an order in September, creating a regulatory pathway for certain trading venues to trade tokenized representations of publicly traded U.S. stocks. "Blockchain technology is now starting to power what's happening in capital markets," Assia told CNBC. "That is the one of the biggest changes we're going to see in capital markets for many, many years." "We're talking about hundreds of trillions of dollars that are going to be tokenized and move onchain and at the same time, I do believe that will support prices of bitcoin and other blockchains as well," he continued. The industry is also watching whether inflation will ease and geopolitical tensions will subside in the new year, which could lower broader macro risk currently hampering the industry. Last month, Strategy's Michael Saylor said he thinks bitcoin's next bull market is already underway. ARK Invest Chief Investment Officer Cathie Wood told CNBC the investment management firm's $1.5 million bull case price target for bitcoin by 2030 still stands. She also said that it wouldn't surprise her if bitcoin reached its all-time high again before the end of 2027. "Our macro forecast has inflation breaking down considerably," Wood told CNBC in an exclusive interview at Cantor Convergence. "I think the elections have increased our confidence there because the war [in Iran], one way or the other, is going to end." She added that "bitcoin has weathered so much bad news," including the $6.3 billion Binance hack and the "distraction" of AI which, "many people would say is sucking the oxygen away from bitcoin." The maturation of the artificial intelligence trade could provide an opportunity for bitcoin to find new inflows. Wood said that ARK Invest believes bitcoin has found its low and stressed that cybersecurity is "top of mind right now," which could provide yet another opportunity for crypto markets to rebound. "I think if the Bitcoin and crypto world coalesces and makes investors feel that they've got their arms around security and actually understand that there might be more security issues in the traditional financial system, I think we're going to see a wave of support," Wood said. passages: Amazon says autonomous AI agents run by a China-linked threat actor found and exploited a zero-day vulnerability in MONAI Label, an open source tool designed for AI-assisted annotation of medical images.
The instance had no authentication, so anyone could see the operator’s prompts and the agents’ output.
The records showed a roughly 48-hour campaign against IP addresses belonging to universities in East Asia outside mainland China.
After identifying the software on one target and mapping its API, the agents discovered a path traversal bug in a file upload function.
“In about 11 minutes, the agents went from mapping the application’s API to arbitrarily writing files on the server,” Amazon said .
“The server that the proxy connected to was running the same vulnerable software, and we infer the actor had used the zero-day to compromise it and establish the tunnel,” Amazon noted.
The MONAI Label developers published an advisory this week.
It rates the bug critical and says it affects versions 0.8.5 and earlier.
Authentication is off by default, enabling anyone who can reach the server over the network to exploit the vulnerability.
A fix has been created and will be included in the next release.

Amazon has attributed the attack to an unidentified Chinese-nexus threat actor with moderate confidence, based on the language used in the prompts, the time zone in the scripts, and the fact that the targeted universities are likely of strategic interest to China.

Amazon says autonomous AI agents run by a China-linked threat actor found and exploited a zero-day vulnerability in MONAI Label, an open source tool designed for AI-assisted annotation of medical images. The tech giant’s threat intelligence team detected the activity in September, after coming across an exposed instance of Cairn , an open source AI penetration testing framework. The instance had no authentication, so anyone could see the operator’s prompts and the agents’ output. The records showed a roughly 48-hour campaign against IP addresses belonging to universities in East Asia outside mainland China. The operator gave the agents a list of targets and told them to obtain shell access. After identifying the software on one target and mapping its API, the agents discovered a path traversal bug in a file upload function. “In about 11 minutes, the agents went from mapping the application’s API to arbitrarily writing files on the server,” Amazon said . In a later session, the agents used the flaw to plant a Python reverse shell in a file Python runs every time the interpreter starts, ultimately achieving a root shell. Advertisement. Scroll to continue reading. “Amazon Threat Intelligence assesses with high confidence that it was a zero-day based on the absence of any corresponding fix, issue, advisory, or prior mention in vulnerability databases for the affected open-source project,” the company said. The operator then gave the agents a proxy that tunneled into a second university and instructed them to target other devices on its network. “The server that the proxy connected to was running the same vulnerable software, and we infer the actor had used the zero-day to compromise it and establish the tunnel,” Amazon noted. The MONAI Label developers published an advisory this week. It rates the bug critical and says it affects versions 0.8.5 and earlier. Authentication is off by default, enabling anyone who can reach the server over the network to exploit the vulnerability. A fix has been created and will be included in the next release. Amazon has attributed the attack to an unidentified Chinese-nexus threat actor with moderate confidence, based on the language used in the prompts, the time zone in the scripts, and the fact that the targeted universities are likely of strategic interest to China. extraction.body: Test using prompts with unique, trackable secrets proves that data doesn’t stay private. Researchers planted 2 million digital tripwires in requests sent through a sprawling network of AI services to find out what happened to sensitive information entrusted to them. What they discovered was an ecosystem that leaked highly sensitive data like a sieve. The exposure was found through an ingenious experiment designed to test if sensitive information can leak through the vast chain of widely used AI services and how that information is exploited when it does. Many of today’s AI apps use services such as OpenRouter or Vercel that act as brokers. These “AI routers,” sometimes also known as “AI gateways,” receive large numbers of prompts sent from AI app end users and route them to an available inference engine based on criteria such as the one charging the lowest price or being best suited for the given task. Instead of using Anthropic, OpenAI, or another big provider, the developer hires an AI router to find the most suitable model. To test for potential leakage, researcher HD Moore assembled a collection of Amazon Web Services access keys, functioning credentials tied to empty AWS accounts, passwords for services such as SSH, and unique URLs, DNS names, and private git repository references. None of the secrets had ever been used before, and he controlled the infrastructure that received any requests using the credentials. He then seeded each secret into exactly one prompt sent to a single provider. In the event any of the secrets were leaked, these “canaries”—so called because they resemble the role of that bird when taken into coal mines—would allow Moore to identify each link in the chain that was responsible. “We sent nearly two million AI prompts containing unique, trackable secrets to AI providers, then watched where those secrets surfaced,” Moore, the chief research officer of security firm Dragos, wrote Thursday . “What we found revealed security breaches, prompt theft, and widespread failures to protect customer data.” Although prompts are encrypted in transit, they are decrypted at each hop inside the large inference reseller network. The prompt is first sent to an AI router, which reads the plaintext in it to determine the most suitable inference providers to handle the request. Often, the prompt is then sent to a pool of available models, which sometimes run inside different hosting providers. Prompts can also pass from one AI router (such as Vercel) to another one (e.g., OpenRouter). Each one of these players is likely to log the prompt and store it for as long as its policies call for (if not indefinitely). The most concerning finding was the breach of three separate hosting providers. The attackers who compromised one of the providers reused “a couple hundred” of the AWS keys. Moore wrote: Each key was sent in exactly one request to one provider, all within a few short windows in late October, and every request we sent during those windows was stolen. Some of the stolen keys came from requests that the provider rejected before a model ever ran—this tells us that the attacker was copying requests at the provider’s front door, and not somewhere deeper in the inference stack. In the other two breaches, some of the stolen requests were marked as ZDR. A privacy flag doesn’t help when the attacker is already inside. Parties tied to the hack of these three providers then tested each key, in some cases within hours of being seeded, to see what kind of resources it gave access to. The parties looked through S3 buckets, secrets managers, and parameter stores in search of still more credentials. They also tried to enable hosted models in AWS Bedrock and added their own IAM users to maintain access. In all, the stolen bait keys were used “tens of thousands” of times in AWS API calls. Secrets sent to two of the hacked providers were quickly used together, almost immediately, from the same rented server. That means the providers were almost certainly compromised by the same adversary. As noted earlier, some of the secrets were stolen by the resellers themselves. To lure prompts to their servers, they offered low prices. Then they turned on request logging and waited. Moore identified them by sending requests to the same model through different sellers. When credentials were later reused when sent through one seller and not another, the researcher knew it was the reseller, not the model provider, that was responsible. Last, the canary experiment revealed that some providers are scraping secret URLs put into the prompts, in violation of privacy terms. Moore wrote: The clearest example involves a Chinese AI lab. This lab’s systems fetched the secret URLs from more than half of the prompts that we sent to its models between July and October, including roughly two-thirds of the requests marked as “no data collection” or Zero Data Retention. The scraper typically showed up two or three days after the request. This wasn’t limited to requests sent to the lab directly. Several US hosting providers resell this lab’s models, and prompts sent to those providers triggered the exact same scraper—the prompts were flowing back to the lab. A customer who picked a US provider specifically to keep their data in the U.S. didn’t get what they paid for. Later on, a git client on a different cloud started trying to clone the private repositories referenced in our prompts, but only for prompts that used this lab’s models. The researcher said he found one US hosting provider crawling a secret URL more than two months after it was used in a single inference call to its search endpoint. Another ran a scraper that came back for URLs days after each request, regardless of the AI router used to reach it. The blockbuster research is the latest indictment exposing the lax privacy and security that’s endemic in much of the AI ecosystem. The findings mean that people who want to ensure secrets they put into prompts stay private face a daunting task that isn’t likely to become easier any time soon. extraction.body: Riverside County Sheriff Chad Bianco traveled to St. Louis earlier this year for a podcast appearance in which he touted his gubernatorial bid. “I don't want to be the governor, but I know I have to have that spot to fix California,” he said in the interview on Andy Frisella’s REAL AF. Bianco wasn’t alone on the trip in late March, during which he also made a campaign stop at the headquarters of a supplement company Frisella founded. He was accompanied by a security detail consisting of a sergeant and two deputies from his department, which booked three rooms at the Ritz-Carlton, along with airfare and car rentals — all on the taxpayer's dime, according to a report from the Riverside County Auditor-Controller’s Office. In all, Bianco’s protective detail, including their salaries, cost taxpayers nearly $3.2 million from October 2025 through last month, the report found. Most of the cost stemmed from payroll-related charges but taxpayers also paid for nearly $32,500 in purchasing-card expenses and reimbursements for meals, airfare, car rentals and hotel rooms, according to the document. Some of those expenses were associated with events promoting Bianco’s ultimately unsuccessful campaign as a Republican candidate for governor. In a statement, Riverside County Undersheriff Don Sharp defended the cost of Bianco's security, writing that he formed the detail because Bianco has received intensifying death threats that date back to his opposition to COVID-19 mandates. "Serving as the elected Sheriff is not a job that ends at the close of business," Sharp wrote. "Sheriff Bianco holds that responsibility 24 hours a day, 365 days a year." Sharp said some of the expenses involved security for Bianco and suggested the report was politically motivated. Experts in ethics and election law say some of expenditures associated with campaign trips should raise concerns. “The spirit of the law is certainly not set up to allow a sheriff who’s going all over the place to campaign for himself to use taxpayer dollars on an unlimited basis and justify it as part of his official duties,” said Sean McMorris, transparency, ethics and accountability program manager for the government watchdog group Common Cause. “From an ethics perspective, I would argue, because you can, you should use your campaign money, not taxpayer dollars, if you're going to a campaign event," he added. It’s not the only controversy Bianco is involved in related to the use of taxpayer dollars. The California Supreme Court ruled the seizure unlawful. Last month, Bianco filed a legal claim — a precursor to a lawsuit — seeking to recoup his legal costs from the county, but the claim was rejected this week. Now, Bianco is finalizing a lawsuit against the county, according to his attorney, Bradley Hertz. With the release of the spending report on Tuesday, which was first reported by the Riverside Press-Enterprise, Riverside County Supervisor Jose Medina said he expects the auditor-controller to request an outside auditor be brought in to scrutinize the expenditures further. "I don’t think this will be the end of the investigation," he said. California law prohibits the use of taxpayer dollars for campaign activity — typically defined as activity that unambiguously promotes an outcome in an election — that’s not authorized by law, Morris said. The phrase “not authorized by law” could provide some leeway for the sheriff to argue such expenses were permitted, but it would probably be a tough case to make, especially in instances when Bianco traveled outside Riverside County to campaign, he said. Jessica Levinson, a professor at Loyola Law School and former president of the Los Angeles Ethics Commission, said it’s fairly common for elected officials to have taxpayer-funded security details accompany them to campaign events. “The law does not require that the security be cut loose because you're engaging in a political activity.” But, she added, “when it's solely a campaign-purpose trip and it’s not an activity that he would undertake as the sheriff, it’s an activity he would undertake only as a candidate, I think that becomes harder to defend.” The sheriff's office billed taxpayers for a sergeant and corporal to accompany Bianco to an April 1 gubernatorial debate at Cal State Fresno, including rooms at the Fairfield Marriott; five personnel to travel to an April 22 televised debate at KRON4 Studios in San Francisco, including hotel reservations, flights and rental cars; and six employees to protect him at an election night watch party in Eastvale, according to the report. A county purchasing card was also used to buy $26.19 worth of ice and water for employees working a Bianco for Governor rally on March 14, the report notes. Medina had requested the audit report, saying he felt his constituents had a right to know how much Bianco's security detail cost them. "I was concerned for quite a while that the line between his official duties and candidacy for governor were quite blurred during his campaign," he said. The supervisor in March requested that Riverside County Dist. Michael Hestrin investigate whether Bianco misused public resources on his campaign, including by campaigning in uniform and using on-duty personnel for campaign-related activities. He said that Hestrin declined, citing a lack of evidence. In light of the audit report, Medina plans to ask both Hestrin and Atty. Rob Bonta to open investigations into potential legal violations, he said. The auditor-controller's accounts-payable team flagged the security detail charges, including one that appeared to be related to a gubernatorial debate, during a routine review and asked the sheriff’s office to identify the county business purpose of the expenses, according to the report. "The travel charges in question for the Protective Security Detail Team are to provide security to the Sheriff,” the deputy director of sheriff’s administrative services replied May 28, per the report. “We do not differentiate on the type of travel." But the purpose of the trips matters, according to Davina Hurt, director of government ethics at the Markkula Center for Applied Ethics at Santa Clara University. "A debate and an election night party are campaign events, and that’s not a close call," she wrote in an email.

extraction.body: Riverside County Sheriff Chad Bianco traveled to St. Louis earlier this year for a podcast appearance in which he touted his gubernatorial bid. “I don't want to be the governor, but I know I have to have that spot to fix California,” he said in the interview on Andy Frisella’s REAL AF. Bianco wasn’t alone on the trip in late March, during which he also made a campaign stop at the headquarters of a supplement company Frisella founded. He was accompanied by a security detail consisting of a sergeant and two deputies from his department, which booked three rooms at the Ritz-Carlton, along with airfare and car rentals — all on the taxpayer's dime, according to a report from the Riverside County Auditor-Controller’s Office. In all, Bianco’s protective detail, including their salaries, cost taxpayers nearly $3.2 million from October 2025 through last month, the report found. Most of the cost stemmed from payroll-related charges but taxpayers also paid for nearly $32,500 in purchasing-card expenses and reimbursements for meals, airfare, car rentals and hotel rooms, according to the document. Some of those expenses were associated with events promoting Bianco’s ultimately unsuccessful campaign as a Republican candidate for governor. In a statement, Riverside County Undersheriff Don Sharp defended the cost of Bianco's security, writing that he formed the detail because Bianco has received intensifying death threats that date back to his opposition to COVID-19 mandates. "Serving as the elected Sheriff is not a job that ends at the close of business," Sharp wrote. "Sheriff Bianco holds that responsibility 24 hours a day, 365 days a year." Sharp said some of the expenses involved security for Bianco and suggested the report was politically motivated. Experts in ethics and election law say some of expenditures associated with campaign trips should raise concerns. “The spirit of the law is certainly not set up to allow a sheriff who’s going all over the place to campaign for himself to use taxpayer dollars on an unlimited basis and justify it as part of his official duties,” said Sean McMorris, transparency, ethics and accountability program manager for the government watchdog group Common Cause. “From an ethics perspective, I would argue, because you can, you should use your campaign money, not taxpayer dollars, if you're going to a campaign event," he added. It’s not the only controversy Bianco is involved in related to the use of taxpayer dollars. The California Supreme Court ruled the seizure unlawful. Last month, Bianco filed a legal claim — a precursor to a lawsuit — seeking to recoup his legal costs from the county, but the claim was rejected this week. Now, Bianco is finalizing a lawsuit against the county, according to his attorney, Bradley Hertz. With the release of the spending report on Tuesday, which was first reported by the Riverside Press-Enterprise, Riverside County Supervisor Jose Medina said he expects the auditor-controller to request an outside auditor be brought in to scrutinize the expenditures further. "I don’t think this will be the end of the investigation," he said. California law prohibits the use of taxpayer dollars for campaign activity — typically defined as activity that unambiguously promotes an outcome in an election — that’s not authorized by law, Morris said. The phrase “not authorized by law” could provide some leeway for the sheriff to argue such expenses were permitted, but it would probably be a tough case to make, especially in instances when Bianco traveled outside Riverside County to campaign, he said. Jessica Levinson, a professor at Loyola Law School and former president of the Los Angeles Ethics Commission, said it’s fairly common for elected officials to have taxpayer-funded security details accompany them to campaign events. “The law does not require that the security be cut loose because you're engaging in a political activity.” But, she added, “when it's solely a campaign-purpose trip and it’s not an activity that he would undertake as the sheriff, it’s an activity he would undertake only as a candidate, I think that becomes harder to defend.” The sheriff's office billed taxpayers for a sergeant and corporal to accompany Bianco to an April 1 gubernatorial debate at Cal State Fresno, including rooms at the Fairfield Marriott; five personnel to travel to an April 22 televised debate at KRON4 Studios in San Francisco, including hotel reservations, flights and rental cars; and six employees to protect him at an election night watch party in Eastvale, according to the report. A county purchasing card was also used to buy $26.19 worth of ice and water for employees working a Bianco for Governor rally on March 14, the report notes. Medina had requested the audit report, saying he felt his constituents had a right to know how much Bianco's security detail cost them. "I was concerned for quite a while that the line between his official duties and candidacy for governor were quite blurred during his campaign," he said. The supervisor in March requested that Riverside County Dist. Michael Hestrin investigate whether Bianco misused public resources on his campaign, including by campaigning in uniform and using on-duty personnel for campaign-related activities. He said that Hestrin declined, citing a lack of evidence. In light of the audit report, Medina plans to ask both Hestrin and Atty. Rob Bonta to open investigations into potential legal violations, he said. The auditor-controller's accounts-payable team flagged the security detail charges, including one that appeared to be related to a gubernatorial debate, during a routine review and asked the sheriff’s office to identify the county business purpose of the expenses, according to the report. "The travel charges in question for the Protective Security Detail Team are to provide security to the Sheriff,” the deputy director of sheriff’s administrative services replied May 28, per the report. “We do not differentiate on the type of travel." But the purpose of the trips matters, according to Davina Hurt, director of government ethics at the Markkula Center for Applied Ethics at Santa Clara University. "A debate and an election night party are campaign events, and that’s not a close call," she wrote in an email.

extraction.body: Spotify founder Daniel Ek is backing Europa Fusion, a stealthy fusion power startup founded by an AI researcher who is taking a different approach to developing a fusion power plant. The U.K.-based startup was founded in February, though sources told TechCrunch that the founder, Nantas Nardelli, has been working on the idea for longer. The people asked not to be identified because the information isn’t public. Bloomberg first reported Ek’s backing of Europa Fusion. Nardelli has extensive experience in the AI world, having previously worked at Google DeepMind, Facebook AI Research, and Microsoft Research Cambridge. Recently, he was head of machine learning at Pacific Fusion , the fusion power startup based in Fremont, California. Pacific Fusion recently broke ground on a demonstration facility in New Mexico. Like most fusion startups of its size , Pacific Fusion leans heavily on physical devices to test its theories and improve its simulations. Nardelli apparently didn’t agree with the focus on hardware, instead thinking that fusion startups should invest in a more simulation- and data-heavy approach, a source familiar with his thinking told TechCrunch. Like Pacific Fusion, Europa Fusion will pursue a pulsed-power approach to fusion. Pulsed-power reactors use massive, perfectly timed surges of electrical current to compress fuel targets until the atoms inside fuse and release energy. Fusion power has the potential to be a significant energy source in the coming decades, but to date, no one has built a power plant capable of supplying electricity to the grid. If fusion power becomes commercially viable, though, it could possibly be a significant source of carbon-free power that draws on nearly limitless fuel supplies. The technology also has the potential to alleviate concerns about AI’s energy consumption. Fusion’s ability to generate electricity without exacerbating climate change apparently drove Nardelli’s pivot from AI. “My original background is in electronics and control engineering,” he wrote on his website . “I used to build robots for a living. extraction.body: Apple, Google, and Microsoft called out for failing to provide developers with adequate AI agent controls Signal, the encrypted messaging app, has barred Google Gemini, Apple Siri, and other AI agents from accessing messages unless the user has explicitly granted permission, based on privacy concerns. Citing the screenshot blocking implemented last year to defend against Microsoft Recall, Signal CEO Meredith Whittaker said similar measures have become necessary to prevent agentic software available in iOS and Android from gaining access to communication that's intended to be private. "Google and Apple are integrating agentic capabilities like Gemini Intelligence with Google Gemini and Onscreen Awareness with Siri AI deep into their operating systems," wrote Whittaker in a blog post . "In order to gain access to information about you, these OS AI agents 'scan' the information that’s on your screen. In doing so, your Signal data is captured, then made available to these agentic systems in order to allow them to answer your questions and do your bidding." The result is that private messages ingested by these agentic systems may end up on someone else's server where they're no longer private. Updates to Signal's iOS and Android apps now include controls that by default block Siri on iOS and Gemini and other agents on Android from taking screenshots, which AI agents process using optical character recognition to extract text. Whittaker says that those who wish to take screenshots of their messages can disable this protection via Signal's settings menu, but warns doing so risks exposing your Signal content (and that sent by your contacts) to AI agents. Screenshot blocking, Whittaker concedes, is only a partial solution since AI agents may have other ways to access application data through the device file system. "We want to be very clear: it is a serious problem that Signal – and application developers beyond – lack robust tools to prevent AI agents from undermining application-level privacy," she said. "Even where we are able to detect and block AI data access, Google, Apple, Microsoft, and others do not provide ways for developers to easily restrict such AI data access without making drastic compromises to the core user experience. This is also the reason we are currently unable to implement these protections on macOS." Apple is taking some action to implement protection from AI agents on macOS, though it appears to be doing so largely to defend against third-party access to data rather than to limit its own Siri service. Siri can be turned off separately. With macOS 27.3 , currently in public beta testing, Apple's desktop operating system will get more granular controls on two APIs: Device Control and Data Access, and Full Disk Access. The result will be more permission prompts for users of macOS apps that seek access to user data, and the inconvenience of applying for an entitlement from Apple to obtain Full Disk Access for backup software and assistive technologies that use Accessibility APIs. "As AI agents become increasingly capable and autonomous, the risks associated with this level of access will grow substantially," Apple said when it introduced the Full Disk Access change. "We are committed to ensuring users clearly understand these risks before granting such access, so they can make informed decisions about their own data and privacy." Apple is also reportedly working on its own AI agent in a bid to compete with Anthropic and OpenAI. It remains to be seen whether Apple will use its operating system ownership as competitive leverage against AI firms that threaten its gatekeeping power, as it has done with web browsers . While Apple casts itself as an ally that's helping to defend device customers against prying AI agents, Signal's decision to block Siri shows that AI agents have complicated trust decisions and the competitive landscape. AI agents are supposed to serve the user but when they spirit data away to the cloud and come between customers and merchants, they wear out their welcome. AI agents also threaten the business relationship between consumers and merchants. Amazon has blocked shopping agents like Meta Muse from its e-commerce site (though not AWS Marketplace ) while Walmart has invited third-party agents to interact through its AI Gateway. Anthropic has blocked subscription customers from using third-party harnesses . United Airlines has banned transactions from unauthorized AI bots. Similar barriers or limitations related to third-party AI agents have been erected by Target, Home Depot, Etsy, eBay, JPMorgan Chase, Charles Schwab, Citigroup, and Wells Fargo, among others. Meanwhile, there's a burgeoning industry in bot detection and mitigation, led by the likes of Cloudflare, Akamai, and DataDome, to name a few. The web browser is sometimes referred to as a user agent, based on the idealistic notion that it serves its user. That vision has been muddied by online advertising and data collection, and default settings that often serve the interests of browser makers instead of promoting privacy. Now AI agents face the same scrutiny as people wonder whether their agents really serve them or someone else. After a year or two of agent vendors arguing for access to all digital data for the sake of personalization and context, the backlash has arrived. ® Just don't expect complex, coherent, or always correct answers PLUS: US takes down Iranian propaganda sites; Marketing company asks 'Why Do We Have Your Information?' And more!

He made the remarks at a White House briefing shortly after returning from Asia, in a policy statement that came with almost no detail. "We're not going to allow our companies to build data centers outside of our country," Trump told reporters. "Because China will take all of them, and we're not allowing that to happen." He added that "we're going to put tremendous penalties on companies that try and do it." He framed the policy as part of a contest with China over AI, saying the United States is leading in data center construction and will not let China overtake it. Neither the size of the tax nor the method of enforcement was described. Trump said he had not yet told his own team, remarking, "I haven't even said that to my people. But I'm telling them now, they're here." Google announced a 13 billion euro investment in Finnish AI infrastructure in September, about $15 billion, including funding for three data centers, and Trump said of a Finland project, "They want to build now one in Finland, and we're not allowing that to happen." Building work on two of the Google sites was halted last month after plans to clear over 300 hectares of woodland drew concern. Meta has broken ground on a data center in Alberta, Canada, and Anthropic has agreed to lease a planned facility in Nova Scotia under a long-term deal. Many Democratic candidates promised tougher regulation of new data centers in this month's midterm elections, and Trump told communities to take advantage of the facilities and "make them pay you, make them pay your community." Hart Research Associates, working with Public Opinion Strategies, polled 1,000 voters nationwide Oct. 14 to 18 and found that 63 percent oppose an AI data center built within 10 miles of where they live, while 13 percent support one. Roughly half the sample got that question, so its uncertainty runs 4.38 points either way. The Pew Research Center counted about 3,000 data centers nationwide in April, with roughly 1,500 more moving through approval or construction. A Turner & Townsend report on 62 global markets found that U.S. data center construction costs rose 13 percent year over year, more than double the global rate and about three times the ten-year average, as demand for AI capacity outran available land with power and skilled labor. The Commerce Department's interim final rule on where advanced chips can go, announced Nov. 16 and effective Nov. 19, requires export licenses for advanced chips shipped to Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand and Brazil, which the department describes as carrying a higher risk of diversion. Commerce said the Treasury Department and the National Security Council wrote the rule and gave the direction for it. It also requires a license when an overseas data center provides large volumes of compute to a company headquartered in China, and existing providers have 90 days to apply. U.S.-headquartered companies in the five named countries are exempt if they meet reporting requirements. No rate, legal mechanism or timeline has been announced, and Google was contacted for comment on the remarks. Companies already planning foreign sites, from the Finland investment to the Alberta and Nova Scotia projects, face that presidential threat on top of the Commerce Department's new licensing rule, and the October poll of 1,000 voters put opposition at 63 percent, with 13 percent in support, for an AI facility sited fewer than 10 miles from where those voters live. Several basic questions went unanswered. He did not say whether a tax would reach foreign subsidiaries or only U.S. parent companies, whether rented space would count the same as owned buildings, or whether existing overseas sites would be exempt. extraction.body: The president gave no details at a White House briefing Friday, said he had not told his own team, and named a Google project in Finland as one he will not allow President Donald Trump said Friday that U.S. companies will not be allowed to build artificial intelligence data centers outside the country, and he threatened a "tremendous tax" on firms that go ahead anyway. He made the remarks at a White House briefing shortly after returning from Asia, in a policy statement that came with almost no detail. "We're not going to allow our companies to build data centers outside of our country," Trump told reporters. "Because China will take all of them, and we're not allowing that to happen." He added that "we're going to put tremendous penalties on companies that try and do it." He framed the policy as part of a contest with China over AI, saying the United States is leading in data center construction and will not let China overtake it. Neither the size of the tax nor the method of enforcement was described. Trump said he had not yet told his own team, remarking, "I haven't even said that to my people. But I'm telling them now, they're here." Google announced a 13 billion euro investment in Finnish AI infrastructure in September, about $15 billion, including funding for three data centers, and Trump said of a Finland project, "They want to build now one in Finland, and we're not allowing that to happen." Building work on two of the Google sites was halted last month after plans to clear over 300 hectares of woodland drew concern. Meta has broken ground on a data center in Alberta, Canada, and Anthropic has agreed to lease a planned facility in Nova Scotia under a long-term deal. Many Democratic candidates promised tougher regulation of new data centers in this month's midterm elections, and Trump told communities to take advantage of the facilities and "make them pay you, make them pay your community." Hart Research Associates, working with Public Opinion Strategies, polled 1,000 voters nationwide Oct. 14 to 18 and found that 63 percent oppose an AI data center built within 10 miles of where they live, while 13 percent support one. Roughly half the sample got that question, so its uncertainty runs 4.38 points either way. The Pew Research Center counted about 3,000 data centers nationwide in April, with roughly 1,500 more moving through approval or construction. A Turner & Townsend report on 62 global markets found that U.S. data center construction costs rose 13 percent year over year, more than double the global rate and about three times the ten-year average, as demand for AI capacity outran available land with power and skilled labor. The Commerce Department's interim final rule on where advanced chips can go, announced Nov. 16 and effective Nov. 19, requires export licenses for advanced chips shipped to Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand and Brazil, which the department describes as carrying a higher risk of diversion. Commerce said the Treasury Department and the National Security Council wrote the rule and gave the direction for it. It also requires a license when an overseas data center provides large volumes of compute to a company headquartered in China, and existing providers have 90 days to apply. U.S.-headquartered companies in the five named countries are exempt if they meet reporting requirements. No rate, legal mechanism or timeline has been announced, and Google was contacted for comment on the remarks. Companies already planning foreign sites, from the Finland investment to the Alberta and Nova Scotia projects, face that presidential threat on top of the Commerce Department's new licensing rule, and the October poll of 1,000 voters put opposition at 63 percent, with 13 percent in support, for an AI facility sited fewer than 10 miles from where those voters live. They say the companies knew about the risks to young users and failed to change their products to reduce those risks.​The cases bring together claims from multiple school districts so that common issues can be handled before trial, while each district’s case is decided separately.
A settlement would allow YouTube to resolve claims from participating districts.

Thousands of individual personal injury lawsuits against the company remain active.​What happened in the Kentucky case​The first school district case set to go to trial involved Breathitt County, Kentucky, a district with fewer than 2,000 students.

YouTube, Meta, Snap and TikTok settled with the district for a combined $27 million about a month before the trial was due to begin.​YouTube agreed to pay slightly more than $2 million and provide training programs to the district, according to documents released under Kentucky’s open records law.

Google spokesperson José Castaneda and the plaintiffs’ attorneys co-leading the federal school district cases have yet to comment.​Why school districts sued YouTubeThe districts allege that features such as autoplay and endless scrolling encourage students to spend more time on social media.
YouTube has reached a preliminary settlement with US schools.
The districts are seeking reimbursement for expenses they say stem from social media addiction, including the cost of expanding counselling and mental health services for students.

extraction.body: YouTube could potentially pay about $3 billion to several US school districts to settle allegations that its platform promotes addictive behavior among students. This agreement is currently in its preliminary stage. The agreement still needs several approvals before it can move forward. A majority of the school districts involved in the lawsuits must accept YouTube’s proposed settlement, which includes about $3 billion in compensation and additional safeguards for teenagers. Judge Yvonne Gonzalez Rogers must then approve the agreement. The process could take months. The federal lawsuit, case 22-md-03047-YGR , focuses on allegations that how YouTube was designed hurts students’ mental health. YouTube is denying the allegations. According to the school districts, the autoplay, personalized recommendations, and infinite scrolling features of YouTube encourage students to linger on the platform longer than intended. They claim that this has necessitated schools to increase their spending on mental health services and to enforce phone restrictions. Limiting YouTube use during school hours is not straightforward because teachers also rely on the platform for lessons. Students, however, do not always use it for educational purposes. A Fordham Institute survey found that more than 30% of surveyed high-school students watched YouTube for entertainment during school hours. YouTube is not alone in facing these allegations. Thousands of lawsuits filed by individuals, school districts and government agencies accuse social media companies, including Meta, TikTok and Snap, of designing platforms that encourage addictive behavior among young people. According to the American Psychological Association , these cases focus on features such as autoplay and infinite scrolling, rather than the content users post. However, researchers have yet to agree on how much harm these features cause. Johns Hopkins researcher Johannes Thrul estimates that social media addiction affects roughly 5% of people worldwide. The research did not officially acknowledge the condition as a diagnosis. The researchers also were not able to determine whether the autoplay and infinite scrolling features play a role in the development of mental health issues. When viewed in the light of YouTube’s advertising earnings, the proposed $3 billion settlement appears to be small. Alphabet reported YouTube advertising revenue of $11.207 billion in the third quarter of 2026. If this amount is maintained throughout the year, the annual revenue would be around $44.8 billion. The proposed settlement represents 6.7% of that annualized estimate or 7.4% of YouTube’s real advertising revenue of $40.367 billion in 2025. But how much would individual schools receive? Dividing $3 billion equally among all 19,183 operating US public school districts would give each roughly $156,000 . This is only an illustration, however. Actual payments would depend on which districts participate and how the money is distributed. The settlement could have consequences beyond the money YouTube pays. Changes to autoplay and personalized recommendations could affect how viewers discover videos, potentially reducing advertising opportunities for content creators. The stakes are growing. WARC expects social video to account for 51.7% of global video advertising spending in 2026. Any changes to how platforms keep audiences watching could therefore affect advertisers and creators worldwide. Meanwhile, European regulators are addressing similar concerns. The European Commission’s July 2025 guidelines recommend switching off autoplay and push notifications by default for minors. Although the guidelines are voluntary, regulators can use them when assessing compliance with the Digital Services Act. YouTube’s proposed settlement comes after other legal setbacks for social media companies. In March 2026, a Los Angeles jury awarded $6 million in an addiction case against Meta and YouTube. The decision is documented in Meta’s filing and the court verdict . Both companies challenged the ruling, which Cryptopolitan covered . Five months later, states announced a separate Meta settlement worth up to $17.1 billion over ten years. The agreement includes additional protections for young users but still requires court approval. The legal battles are not over. Another trial involving the Tucson school district and other social media platforms is scheduled for February 2027. Reuters, citing a Bloomberg News report, said YouTube has agreed in principle to pay about $3 billion, but the deal is not finalized: a majority of school districts must sign on, and US District Judge Yvonne Gonzalez Rogers must approve it, with finalization expected to take a few months. The districts argue that autoplay, infinite scrolling, and recommendation algorithms were built to keep young people hooked and worsened anxiety, depression, and eating disorders, claims the companies deny. No. Johns Hopkins researchers said problematic social media use is associated with loneliness, anxiety, and depression, but a causal link is still debated, and social media addiction is not a recognized clinical diagnosis. passages: YouTube could potentially pay about $3 billion to several US school districts to settle allegations that its platform promotes addictive behavior among students. This agreement is currently in its preliminary stage.

The agreement still needs several approvals before it can move forward. A majority of the school districts involved in the lawsuits must accept YouTube’s proposed settlement, which includes about $3 billion in compensation and additional safeguards for teenagers. Judge Yvonne Gonzalez Rogers must then approve the agreement. The process could take months.
The federal lawsuit, case 22-md-03047-YGR , focuses on allegations that how YouTube was designed hurts students’ mental health. YouTube is denying the allegations.

According to the school districts, the autoplay, personalized recommendations, and infinite scrolling features of YouTube encourage students to linger on the platform longer than intended. They claim that this has necessitated schools to increase their spending on mental health services and to enforce phone restrictions.

Limiting YouTube use during school hours is not straightforward because teachers also rely on the platform for lessons. Students, however, do not always use it for educational purposes. A Fordham Institute survey found that more than 30% of surveyed high-school students watched YouTube for entertainment during school hours.

YouTube is not alone in facing these allegations. Thousands of lawsuits filed by individuals, school districts and government agencies accuse social media companies, including Meta, TikTok and Snap, of designing platforms that encourage addictive behavior among young people. According to the American Psychological Association , these cases focus on features such as autoplay and infinite scrolling, rather than the content users post.

However, researchers have yet to agree on how much harm these features cause. Johns Hopkins researcher Johannes Thrul estimates that social media addiction affects roughly 5% of people worldwide. The research did not officially acknowledge the condition as a diagnosis. The researchers also were not able to determine whether the autoplay and infinite scrolling features play a role in the development of mental health issues.
When viewed in the light of YouTube’s advertising earnings, the proposed $3 billion settlement appears to be small.

Alphabet reported YouTube advertising revenue of $11.207 billion in the third quarter of 2026. If this amount is maintained throughout the year, the annual revenue would be around $44.8 billion. The proposed settlement represents 6.7% of that annualized estimate or 7.4% of YouTube’s real advertising revenue of $40.367 billion in 2025.

But how much would individual schools receive? Dividing $3 billion equally among all 19,183 operating US public school districts would give each roughly $156,000 . This is only an illustration, however. Actual payments would depend on which districts participate and how the money is distributed.

The settlement could have consequences beyond the money YouTube pays. Changes to autoplay and personalized recommendations could affect how viewers discover videos, potentially reducing advertising opportunities for content creators.

The stakes are growing. WARC expects social video to account for 51.7% of global video advertising spending in 2026. Any changes to how platforms keep audiences watching could therefore affect advertisers and creators worldwide.

Meanwhile, European regulators are addressing similar concerns. The European Commission’s July 2025 guidelines recommend switching off autoplay and push notifications by default for minors. Although the guidelines are voluntary, regulators can use them when assessing compliance with the Digital Services Act.
YouTube’s proposed settlement comes after other legal setbacks for social media companies.

In March 2026, a Los Angeles jury awarded $6 million in an addiction case against Meta and YouTube. The decision is documented in Meta’s filing and the court verdict . Both companies challenged the ruling, which Cryptopolitan covered .

Five months later, states announced a separate Meta settlement worth up to $17.1 billion over ten years. The agreement includes additional protections for young users but still requires court approval.
The legal battles are not over. Another trial involving the Tucson school district and other social media platforms is scheduled for February 2027.

Reuters, citing a Bloomberg News report, said YouTube has agreed in principle to pay about $3 billion, but the deal is not finalized: a majority of school districts must sign on, and US District Judge Yvonne Gonzalez Rogers must approve it, with finalization expected to take a few months.

The districts argue that autoplay, infinite scrolling, and recommendation algorithms were built to keep young people hooked and worsened anxiety, depression, and eating disorders, claims the companies deny.

No. Johns Hopkins researchers said problematic social media use is associated with loneliness, anxiety, and depression, but a causal link is still debated, and social media addiction is not a recognized clinical diagnosis.

story.title: YouTube is reportedly preparing to settle social media addiction claims for $3 billion

facts.text: Meta, Snap, TikTok and YouTube settled an earlier lawsuit with a school district in Kentucky in May, in which YouTube agreed to pay slightly more than $2 million.
The video platform was also found negligent in a personal-injury lawsuit in Los Angeles in March and agreed to settle a separate personal-injury lawsuit in June .
The settlement "will likely take a few months to officially finalize" and is contingent on a majority of districts agreeing.
The deal will reportedly also include "additional product safeguards for teens."
Engadget has asked YouTube to comment on the school district settlement.

Like Meta, Snap and TikTok, YouTube is facing a growing number of lawsuits alleging that its platform is designed to be addictive, and that it knew using it could produce negative outcomes for younger users.

YouTube and many other Google products are heavily used in classrooms, so reaching a settlement would allow the company to avoid drawn-out legal battles during what's already a contentious moment between Google and schools .
YouTube is preparing to pay $3 billion to thousands of school districts to settle claims that its “addictive design” harmed kids, according to Bloomberg.
In March, both YouTube and Meta were found negligent in a separate legal battle over social media addiction.
As part of the agreement, Meta will only shell out the remaining $5.3 billion of its $17.1 billion settlement if YouTube and TikTok roll out similar changes and pay matching amounts.
Sources tell the publication that YouTube reached the agreement “in principle,” and that the deal would also include new safeguards for teens.
The settlement would allow Google to avoid a wave of lawsuits filed by US school districts that accuse YouTube, Meta, Snap, and TikTok of negatively impacting the mental health of teen users.

The Google-owned video platform could pay about $3 billion to thousands of school districts that accuse it of designing an addictive service that harmed students’ mental health, a Bloomberg report claimed, citing people familiar with the matter.

The proposed agreement also includes additional safeguards for teenagers who use YouTube.​The agreement depends on a majority of the districts signing on and could take several months to finalise, the report claims.

They say the companies knew about the risks to young users and failed to change their products to reduce those risks.​The cases bring together claims from multiple school districts so that common issues can be handled before trial, while each district’s case is decided separately.
A settlement would allow YouTube to resolve claims from participating districts.

Thousands of individual personal injury lawsuits against the company remain active.​What happened in the Kentucky case​The first school district case set to go to trial involved Breathitt County, Kentucky, a district with fewer than 2,000 students.

YouTube, Meta, Snap and TikTok settled with the district for a combined $27 million about a month before the trial was due to begin.​YouTube agreed to pay slightly more than $2 million and provide training programs to the district, according to documents released under Kentucky’s open records law.

Google spokesperson José Castaneda and the plaintiffs’ attorneys co-leading the federal school district cases have yet to comment.​Why school districts sued YouTubeThe districts allege that features such as autoplay and endless scrolling encourage students to spend more time on social media.

The districts are seeking reimbursement for expenses they say stem from social media addiction, including the cost of expanding counselling and mental health services for students.

passages: Meta’s executives are rethinking the company’s original goal of achieving net-zero emissions by 2030.
In the November 19, 2026, report, they attributed the changing conditions and the need for a rethink to how “demand for AI infrastructure has grown faster than almost anyone projected.”

Meta’s statement about re-evaluating its 2030 emissions goal is a significant public acknowledgment, given that Amazon, Google, and Microsoft have all stuck by their original sustainability goals so far.
Despite efforts to invest in more renewable energy projects, Meta and its rivals are still often pushing forward on AI data centers that rely on burning natural gas to generate electricity.

Meta also reported a sharp increase in water consumption related to purchased electricity—the amount of water consumed by related power generation—from 19 billion gallons in 2024 to more than 26 billion gallons in 2025.

This once again highlights that, for data centers, the far bigger water usage comes from the power plants that supply electricity to data centers as opposed to data centers directly using water for cooling.

That would make Meta’s annual carbon footprint roughly comparable to total emissions for the state of Idaho, while surpassing the total emissions of states such as Hawaii, Maine, South Dakota, and New Hampshire.
The company attributed much of this emissions increase to “capital goods,” like as data center servers.
However, Meta still likely has one of the smallest total carbon footprints among the Big Tech companies.

Meta also said it would post updates on its sustainability website, while Reuters reported that the cuts would hit non-AI teams as 2026 capital spending rises to as much as $135 billion.

Rachel Peterson and Blair Swedeen wrote that "The reality has been far more complex" after Meta set its net zero goal, and they tied the shift to demand for AI infrastructure. Meta said delivering on its vision "requires building the infrastructure that powers AI," and the company described the resulting buildout as outpacing what it had anticipated. Meta’s sustainability reporting also pointed to accounting methods that climate advocates view with scepticism, and Al Jazeera said the figure is based on those methods.

Meta’s report said its electricity use increased 35% in 2025 as additional data centers came online, and it attributed much of the emissions increase to capital goods like data center servers. Meta’s reassessment arrived as Al Jazeera described a broader corporate retreat from climate pledges, naming General Motors, Walmart, Google, Coca-Cola and Pepsi as companies that had adjusted or weakened climate commitments. Meta’s report also set up a near-term test, because Meta did not announce a revised target date and said it would disclose updates later on its sustainability website.

Meta’s electricity and emissions figures were framed against data center scale, with a study cited by Al Jazeera finding 403 of the most powerful data centers in the United States accounted for about 2% of the country’s electricity use. Al Jazeera also said corporate emissions accounting methods, including renewable energy certificates, are ones climate advocates view with scepticism, and it warned that the physical grid impact could be worse than Meta’s reported number.

coreStoryFacts.text: Meta’s executives are rethinking the company’s original goal of achieving net-zero emissions by 2030.
In the November 19, 2026, report, they attributed the changing conditions and the need for a rethink to how “demand for AI infrastructure has grown faster than almost anyone projected.”

Meta’s statement about re-evaluating its 2030 emissions goal is a significant public acknowledgment, given that Amazon, Google, and Microsoft have all stuck by their original sustainability goals so far.
Despite efforts to invest in more renewable energy projects, Meta and its rivals are still often pushing forward on AI data centers that rely on burning natural gas to generate electricity.

Meta also reported a sharp increase in water consumption related to purchased electricity—the amount of water consumed by related power generation—from 19 billion gallons in 2024 to more than 26 billion gallons in 2025.

This once again highlights that, for data centers, the far bigger water usage comes from the power plants that supply electricity to data centers as opposed to data centers directly using water for cooling.

That would make Meta’s annual carbon footprint roughly comparable to total emissions for the state of Idaho, while surpassing the total emissions of states such as Hawaii, Maine, South Dakota, and New Hampshire.
The company attributed much of this emissions increase to “capital goods,” like as data center servers.
However, Meta still likely has one of the smallest total carbon footprints among the Big Tech companies.
