facts.text: Meta’s executives are rethinking the company’s original goal of achieving net-zero emissions by 2030.
In the November 19, 2026, report, they attributed the changing conditions and the need for a rethink to how “demand for AI infrastructure has grown faster than almost anyone projected.”

Meta’s statement about re-evaluating its 2030 emissions goal is a significant public acknowledgment, given that Amazon, Google, and Microsoft have all stuck by their original sustainability goals so far.
Despite efforts to invest in more renewable energy projects, Meta and its rivals are still often pushing forward on AI data centers that rely on burning natural gas to generate electricity.

Meta also reported a sharp increase in water consumption related to purchased electricity—the amount of water consumed by related power generation—from 19 billion gallons in 2024 to more than 26 billion gallons in 2025.

This once again highlights that, for data centers, the far bigger water usage comes from the power plants that supply electricity to data centers as opposed to data centers directly using water for cooling.

That would make Meta’s annual carbon footprint roughly comparable to total emissions for the state of Idaho, while surpassing the total emissions of states such as Hawaii, Maine, South Dakota, and New Hampshire.
The company attributed much of this emissions increase to “capital goods,” like as data center servers.
However, Meta still likely has one of the smallest total carbon footprints among the Big Tech companies.
Meta Platforms is reportedly reassessing its commitment to achieving net-zero carbon emissions by 2030, as highlighted by recent record emissions stemming from AI data center operations.
The company had initially set a comprehensive net-zero target in 2020, covering both its operations and supply chain.
However, the increased demand for AI-related data centers has led to a 45% rise in emissions, prompting a reevaluation of its timeline and interim goals.
This reassessment does not mean a withdrawal from its overall sustainability ambitions but indicates that the current pathway might need revision.
Observers will be closely monitoring any legislative developments in Oklahoma, where discussions around a data center moratorium are ongoing.
Key actors, such as the Oklahoma Legislature and Governor Kevin Stitt, could influence the outcome.
The market’s response to these developments could provide insights into the evolving landscape of environmental regulations surrounding data centers.

Meta reported that its net emissions rose 45% in 2025 to 11.8 million tonnes of carbon dioxide equivalent, and the report was signed by Rachel Peterson and Blair Swedeen.
Meta reconsiders 2030 net-zero goal amid record emissions from AI data centers
Meta said delivering on its vision "requires building the infrastructure that powers AI," and the company described the resulting buildout as outpacing what it had anticipated.

Meta reevaluates its 2030 zero-emissions target amid the rise of artificial intelligence
Meta’s report said its electricity use increased 35% in 2025 as additional data centers came online, and it attributed much of the emissions increase to capital goods like data center servers.
Meta’s executives said they anticipated steady growth and falling clean energy costs when they set the goal, but they said the broader system did not enable progress at the pace they envisioned.

extraction.body: Meta is “re-evaluating” 2030 sustainability goals. Will others follow? Meta’s executives are rethinking the company’s original goal of achieving net-zero emissions by 2030. That revelation in Meta’s latest sustainability report comes as the company reported a record percentage increase in greenhouse gas emissions that exceeds any other Big Tech competitor racing to build new AI data centers. The company’s 2026 sustainability report claims that “our long-term ambitions haven’t changed, but our operating environment has,” according to an introduction from Rachel Peterson, vice president of data centers at Meta, and Blair Swedeen, global head of net zero and sustainability at Meta. In the November 19, 2026, report, they attributed the changing conditions and the need for a rethink to how “demand for AI infrastructure has grown faster than almost anyone projected.” “We are re-evaluating our timelines, sequencing, and interim milestones—including the 2030 timeframe for our net zero emissions goal and our near-term intensity targets—so our approach reflects current operating realities while keeping progress transparent year over year,” Peterson and Swedeen wrote in the report. Meta’s statement about re-evaluating its 2030 emissions goal is a significant public acknowledgment, given that Amazon, Google, and Microsoft have all stuck by their original sustainability goals so far. But all the companies have acknowledged challenges in balancing their original sustainability goals against the breakneck buildout of hyperscale data centers . Despite efforts to invest in more renewable energy projects, Meta and its rivals are still often pushing forward on AI data centers that rely on burning natural gas to generate electricity. Meta’s report described the company’s total emissions as surging from 15.6 million metric tonnes of carbon dioxide equivalent in 2024 to more than 21.7 million metric tonnes in 2025. That would make Meta’s annual carbon footprint roughly comparable to total emissions for the state of Idaho, while surpassing the total emissions of states such as Hawaii, Maine, South Dakota, and New Hampshire. The company attributed much of this emissions increase to “capital goods,” like as data center servers. That also represents a nearly 40 percent increase in Meta’s carbon footprint between 2024 and 2025, which is the highest percentage year-over-year increase for total emissions reported by any of the four major US tech giants. For comparison, Microsoft reported a 25 percent increase in its overall carbon footprint, Google reported an 18 percent increase, and Amazon’s report described a 16 percent increase between 2024 and 2025. However, Meta still likely has one of the smallest total carbon footprints among the Big Tech companies. Meta’s approach to achieving net-zero emissions has included developing new renewable energy projects to match emissions and using carbon removal technology. But even when factoring in such efforts, Meta still reported net emissions increasing from more than 8.1 million metric tonnes to more than 11.8 million metric tonnes for 2025. That represents a 45 percent increase. From a water consumption standpoint , Meta reported progress in reducing facility consumption from 825 million gallons in 2024 to 790 million gallons in 2025. Yet that positive trend is tempered by the fact that Meta also described an increase in water consumption from “areas with water stress,” rising from 198 million gallons in 2024 to 246 million gallons in 2025. Meta also reported a sharp increase in water consumption related to purchased electricity—the amount of water consumed by related power generation—from 19 billion gallons in 2024 to more than 26 billion gallons in 2025. This once again highlights that, for data centers, the far bigger water usage comes from the power plants that supply electricity to data centers as opposed to data centers directly using water for cooling. Still, some minor credit is due. The publication Data Center Dynamics pointed out that “Meta is the only hyperscaler to report indirect water use, a growing concern as data centers shift to closed-loop cooling systems that, despite using less water at source, require more electricity to run.” It would very much be in the public interest for other Big Tech companies to follow suit on the reporting front—and public pressure continues to build after the AI backlash impact on US midterm election results. Meta’s executives are rethinking the company’s original goal of achieving net-zero emissions by 2030. That revelation in Meta’s latest sustainability report comes as the company reported a record percentage increase in greenhouse gas emissions that exceeds any other Big Tech competitor racing to build new AI data centers.

The company’s 2026 sustainability report claims that “our long-term ambitions haven’t changed, but our operating environment has,” according to an introduction from Rachel Peterson, vice president of data centers at Meta, and Blair Swedeen, global head of net zero and sustainability at Meta. In the November 19, 2026, report, they attributed the changing conditions and the need for a rethink to how “demand for AI infrastructure has grown faster than almost anyone projected.”

“We are re-evaluating our timelines, sequencing, and interim milestones—including the 2030 timeframe for our net zero emissions goal and our near-term intensity targets—so our approach reflects current operating realities while keeping progress transparent year over year,” Peterson and Swedeen wrote in the report.

Meta’s statement about re-evaluating its 2030 emissions goal is a significant public acknowledgment, given that Amazon, Google, and Microsoft have all stuck by their original sustainability goals so far.

But all the companies have acknowledged challenges in balancing their original sustainability goals against the breakneck buildout of hyperscale data centers . Despite efforts to invest in more renewable energy projects, Meta and its rivals are still often pushing forward on AI data centers that rely on burning natural gas to generate electricity.
Meta’s report described the company’s total emissions as surging from 15.6 million metric tonnes of carbon dioxide equivalent in 2024 to more than 21.7 million metric tonnes in 2025.

That would make Meta’s annual carbon footprint roughly comparable to total emissions for the state of Idaho, while surpassing the total emissions of states such as Hawaii, Maine, South Dakota, and New Hampshire. The company attributed much of this emissions increase to “capital goods,” like as data center servers.

That also represents a nearly 40 percent increase in Meta’s carbon footprint between 2024 and 2025, which is the highest percentage year-over-year increase for total emissions reported by any of the four major US tech giants.

For comparison, Microsoft reported a 25 percent increase in its overall carbon footprint, Google reported an 18 percent increase, and Amazon’s report described a 16 percent increase between 2024 and 2025. However, Meta still likely has one of the smallest total carbon footprints among the Big Tech companies.
Meta’s approach to achieving net-zero emissions has included developing new renewable energy projects to match emissions and using carbon removal technology.

But even when factoring in such efforts, Meta still reported net emissions increasing from more than 8.1 million metric tonnes to more than 11.8 million metric tonnes for 2025. That represents a 45 percent increase.
From a water consumption standpoint , Meta reported progress in reducing facility consumption from 825 million gallons in 2024 to 790 million gallons in 2025.

Yet that positive trend is tempered by the fact that Meta also described an increase in water consumption from “areas with water stress,” rising from 198 million gallons in 2024 to 246 million gallons in 2025.

Meta also reported a sharp increase in water consumption related to purchased electricity—the amount of water consumed by related power generation—from 19 billion gallons in 2024 to more than 26 billion gallons in 2025. This once again highlights that, for data centers, the far bigger water usage comes from the power plants that supply electricity to data centers as opposed to data centers directly using water for cooling.

Still, some minor credit is due. The publication Data Center Dynamics pointed out that “Meta is the only hyperscaler to report indirect water use, a growing concern as data centers shift to closed-loop cooling systems that, despite using less water at source, require more electricity to run.”

It would very much be in the public interest for other Big Tech companies to follow suit on the reporting front—and public pressure continues to build after the AI backlash impact on US midterm election results.

story.title: Meta reconsiders 2030 net-zero goal amid record emissions from AI data centers

facts.text: Meta’s executives are rethinking the company’s original goal of achieving net-zero emissions by 2030.
In the November 19, 2026, report, they attributed the changing conditions and the need for a rethink to how “demand for AI infrastructure has grown faster than almost anyone projected.”

Meta’s statement about re-evaluating its 2030 emissions goal is a significant public acknowledgment, given that Amazon, Google, and Microsoft have all stuck by their original sustainability goals so far.
Despite efforts to invest in more renewable energy projects, Meta and its rivals are still often pushing forward on AI data centers that rely on burning natural gas to generate electricity.

Meta also reported a sharp increase in water consumption related to purchased electricity—the amount of water consumed by related power generation—from 19 billion gallons in 2024 to more than 26 billion gallons in 2025.

This once again highlights that, for data centers, the far bigger water usage comes from the power plants that supply electricity to data centers as opposed to data centers directly using water for cooling.

That would make Meta’s annual carbon footprint roughly comparable to total emissions for the state of Idaho, while surpassing the total emissions of states such as Hawaii, Maine, South Dakota, and New Hampshire.
The company attributed much of this emissions increase to “capital goods,” like as data center servers.
However, Meta still likely has one of the smallest total carbon footprints among the Big Tech companies.
Meta Platforms is reportedly reassessing its commitment to achieving net-zero carbon emissions by 2030, as highlighted by recent record emissions stemming from AI data center operations.
The company had initially set a comprehensive net-zero target in 2020, covering both its operations and supply chain.
However, the increased demand for AI-related data centers has led to a 45% rise in emissions, prompting a reevaluation of its timeline and interim goals.
This reassessment does not mean a withdrawal from its overall sustainability ambitions but indicates that the current pathway might need revision.
Observers will be closely monitoring any legislative developments in Oklahoma, where discussions around a data center moratorium are ongoing.
Key actors, such as the Oklahoma Legislature and Governor Kevin Stitt, could influence the outcome.
The market’s response to these developments could provide insights into the evolving landscape of environmental regulations surrounding data centers.

sources.title: Bitcoin suffered identical sell-off pattern ahead of Anthropic, SpaceX IPOs — what happens next? - CNBC
passages: Bitcoin has suffered nearly identical sell-offs ahead of two of the biggest public offerings this year, leaving investors wondering if competing demand for investor capital could be weighing on the cryptocurrency and perhaps delaying its recovery.
The price of the bitcoin dropped 22.7% in the 30 days before Anthropic's IPO and fell 22.3% in the month leading up to SpaceX's June 12 listing.
"Liquidity events can elevate correlations across asset classes quickly," Matthew Sheffield, chief investment officer at the ether treasury firm Sharplink , told CNBC.
"The first 15 min of [Thursday's] Anthropic IPO put that on full display.
Tech stocks, value stocks, oil, gold, crypto all sold off as traders sold assets to buy shares in the secondary market."
Bitcoin's next critical test is between $60,000 and $62,000, according to Nicolai Sondergaard, a research analyst at Nansen.
Throughout November, bitcoin has been struggling from a combination of dollar strength, institutional selling, and ongoing leveraged bitcoin liquidations.
Still, the post-IPO price action may offer a data point in understanding where bitcoin's price goes next.
With Anthropic now public, investors are watching to see whether bitcoin and ether find a floor, and if institutional demand returns.

"[After] the SpaceX IPO, bitcoin didn't truly find its final bottom until after the IPO was completed, and it didn't actually reverse the downtrend until 70 days later," said Matt Cole, CEO and chairman of Strive Asset Management , a bitcoin treasury firm.
Bitcoin is in the early stages of forming a bottom, according to Cole.

Retail fear is elevated amid recent outages, quantum concerns and other short-term uncertainties, but bitcoin should continue to benefit from macro forces like rising debt and weakening fiat currencies, which should drive price higher, he said.

The price of the bitcoin dropped 22.7% in the 30 days before Anthropic's IPO and fell 22.3% in the month leading up to SpaceX's June 12 listing. Ether declined 25.3% in the 30 days preceding Anthropic's debut, and 28% in the same window ahead of SpaceX. "Liquidity events can elevate correlations across asset classes quickly," Matthew Sheffield, chief investment officer at the ether treasury firm Sharplink , told CNBC. "The first 15 min of [Thursday's] Anthropic IPO put that on full display. Tech stocks, value stocks, oil, gold, crypto all sold off as traders sold assets to buy shares in the secondary market." "Stores of value function as such over long horizons, but in the short term are still liquidity driven," Sheffield said. "We saw this in early Covid when the market fled to cash. Stock, bonds, commodities ... it didn't matter, you were being sold for cash." While investors appear to be rotating capital out of crypto to make room for history-making IPO investments, that can't be said with precise certainty. Crypto has also been under pressure from ETF outflows, leverage, macro uncertainty and broader risk-off sentiment. Still, the post-IPO price action may offer a data point in understanding where bitcoin's price goes next. With Anthropic now public, investors are watching to see whether bitcoin and ether find a floor, and if institutional demand returns. "[After] the SpaceX IPO, bitcoin didn't truly find its final bottom until after the IPO was completed, and it didn't actually reverse the downtrend until 70 days later," said Matt Cole, CEO and chairman of Strive Asset Management , a bitcoin treasury firm. "My view is that [for] bitcoin, the most likely scenario is that it chops around here." The expiration of IPO allocation restrictions can influence the timing of capital flows into digital assets, Sheffield said. "Post SpaceX we saw the wealth effect in full force," Sheffield said. "Many brokers make traders wait 15-30 days before they are allowed to flip shares they received as allocations. … If you went long ETH versus SpaceX on the day of the IPO, on day 31 was when you would have become profitable." Bitcoin's next critical test is between $60,000 and $62,000, according to Nicolai Sondergaard, a research analyst at Nansen. On Friday, it was sitting at about $62,000. As of Friday, bitcoin was hovering at the upper end of a critical $60,000 to $62,000 support range. Its next move could determine whether it can stabilize or if it will face another leg lower and revisit its July low of $57,737.35. Throughout November, bitcoin has been struggling from a combination of dollar strength, institutional selling, and ongoing leveraged bitcoin liquidations. The declines began in late October, as concerns over artificial intelligence valuations and spending fueled a broad tech sell-off. They were compounded by the $6.3 billion Binance hack and weakening institutional ETF demand. Bitcoin is in the early stages of forming a bottom, according to Cole. Retail fear is elevated amid recent outages, quantum concerns and other short-term uncertainties, but bitcoin should continue to benefit from macro forces like rising debt and weakening fiat currencies, which should drive price higher, he said. "Capital markets are open, … retail fears are high, and when you combine those things it's much more likely to be a dip-buying opportunity across the board, including bitcoin, than the start of a great financial crisis," said Cole. "It'll likely age as a volatile time to consider allocating to risk, not the opposite." "The winter for bitcoin is basically at the end, but after winter does not come summer, it comes early spring," he added. "Anytime anyone's been around early spring, what you notice is it gets really cold still, it still rains – it's not necessarily great weather, and I think that's the environment we're in for bitcoin." passages: Bitcoin and ether both experienced sharp sell-offs in the weeks leading up to Anthropic's public debut, mirroring almost exactly the same pattern that played out before SpaceX went public earlier this year.

With Anthropic closing its first trading day up 17% at $97.17, crypto analysts are now watching to see if digital assets find a floor or if the liquidity drain deepens as more AI unicorns prepare to go public.
As Anthropic priced its IPO at $83, topping its expected range on surging institutional demand, bitcoin slid from recent highs while ether underperformed even more dramatically.

The identical sell-off pattern before both the SpaceX and Anthropic IPOs reveals an uncomfortable truth about institutional crypto holdings: they're being used as a liquidity pool to fund hot tech allocations.
Anthropic's debut certainly commanded attention.
If the SpaceX-Anthropic pattern holds, crypto investors should watch for a potential stabilization phase over the next week or two, followed by a test of whether institutional buyers return.

What makes this pattern particularly concerning for crypto advocates is that it suggests digital assets are being treated as secondary holdings, something to liquidate when "real" opportunities like AI IPOs emerge.

extraction.body: Bitcoin and ether just traced the same sharp sell-off pattern that preceded SpaceX's blockbuster IPO earlier this year, raising urgent questions about whether institutional money is abandoning crypto for hot tech listings. With Anthropic closing its first trading day up 17% at $97.17, crypto analysts are now watching to see if digital assets find a floor or if the liquidity drain deepens as more AI unicorns prepare to go public. The crypto market just delivered an eerie sense of déjà vu. Bitcoin and ether both experienced sharp sell-offs in the weeks leading up to Anthropic's public debut, mirroring almost exactly the same pattern that played out before SpaceX went public earlier this year. The correlation is raising uncomfortable questions for crypto bulls about whether institutional money views digital assets as a liquidity source to fund allocations in hot tech IPOs. As Anthropic priced its IPO at $83, topping its expected range on surging institutional demand, bitcoin slid from recent highs while ether underperformed even more dramatically. The pattern matches what happened in the lead-up to SpaceX's listing, when both cryptocurrencies shed double-digit percentages before finding support only after the IPO priced. When a massive IPO looms, institutional investors appear to be liquidating portions of their crypto holdings to free up capital for new allocations. It's a liquidity rotation that hits hardest in the two to three weeks before pricing, precisely when underwriters are locking in final commitments from large buyers. Anthropic's debut certainly commanded attention. But here's where it gets interesting for crypto traders. After SpaceX priced its IPO, bitcoin and ether both stabilized within days and then mounted modest recoveries over the following weeks. The theory goes that once institutional allocations are locked and IPO euphoria fades, some of that capital rotates back into crypto as investors rebalance portfolios. With Anthropic's first trading day in the books and the initial pop already priced in, crypto markets are testing whether they can find a floor. Bitcoin has shown some signs of stabilization, though trading volumes remain thin, suggesting many institutional players are still on the sidelines. What makes this pattern particularly concerning for crypto advocates is that it suggests digital assets are being treated as secondary holdings, something to liquidate when "real" opportunities like AI IPOs emerge. That's a far cry from the narrative of bitcoin as digital gold or a portfolio hedge that trades independently of traditional markets. The institutional demand picture is murkier than it was during previous crypto rallies. While bitcoin ETFs have attracted steady inflows this year, the pace has slowed considerably. Meanwhile, the pipeline of major tech IPOs remains robust, with several AI and enterprise software unicorns reportedly preparing listings for early 2027. If the SpaceX-Anthropic pattern holds, crypto investors should watch for a potential stabilization phase over the next week or two, followed by a test of whether institutional buyers return. The key variable is whether another blockbuster IPO gets announced soon, which could trigger a repeat of the cycle. Some crypto analysts argue the sell-off is actually healthy, shaking out weak hands and establishing clearer support levels. Others worry it exposes how dependent crypto markets have become on the same institutional money that chases every hot tech trend. The difference in perspective often comes down to whether you view crypto as a mature asset class or still an emerging one fighting for legitimacy. Bitcoin is hovering near technical support levels that held during previous corrections, while ether faces a more uncertain picture given its underperformance. Trading desks report that institutional inquiry has picked up slightly since Anthropic's debut, but no one is ready to call a bottom yet. The broader implication is that crypto's fate may be more intertwined with the tech IPO calendar than many investors realized. As long as venture-backed unicorns keep going public at premium valuations, institutional investors may continue using crypto as a source of liquidity to fund those allocations. That's not necessarily bearish long-term, but it does suggest crypto markets could face periodic pressure whenever the IPO window heats up. The identical sell-off pattern before both the SpaceX and Anthropic IPOs reveals an uncomfortable truth about institutional crypto holdings: they're being used as a liquidity pool to fund hot tech allocations. Whether bitcoin and ether can establish a floor now that Anthropic's debut is complete will signal if the SpaceX playbook repeats, with capital gradually rotating back into digital assets. But with more AI unicorns eyeing 2027 listings, crypto investors may need to accept that their markets are now tethered to the tech IPO calendar in ways that challenge the independence narrative. The next few weeks will show if institutional demand returns or if crypto faces another cycle of liquidation as the next blockbuster listing approaches.

"Stores of value function as such over long horizons, but in the short term are still liquidity driven," Sheffield said. "We saw this in early Covid when the market fled to cash. Stock, bonds, commodities ... it didn't matter, you were being sold for cash." While investors appear to be rotating capital out of crypto to make room for history-making IPO investments, that can't be said with precise certainty. Crypto has also been under pressure from ETF outflows, leverage, macro uncertainty and broader risk-off sentiment. Still, the post-IPO price action may offer a data point in understanding where bitcoin's price goes next. With Anthropic now public, investors are watching to see whether bitcoin and ether find a floor, and if institutional demand returns. "[After] the SpaceX IPO, bitcoin didn't truly find its final bottom until after the IPO was completed, and it didn't actually reverse the downtrend until 70 days later," said Matt Cole, CEO and chairman of Strive Asset Management , a bitcoin treasury firm. "My view is that [for] bitcoin, the most likely scenario is that it chops around here." The expiration of IPO allocation restrictions can influence the timing of capital flows into digital assets, Sheffield said. "Post SpaceX we saw the wealth effect in full force," Sheffield said. "Many brokers make traders wait 15-30 days before they are allowed to flip shares they received as allocations. … If you went long ETH versus SpaceX on the day of the IPO, on day 31 was when you would have become profitable." Bitcoin's next critical test is between $60,000 and $62,000, according to Nicolai Sondergaard, a research analyst at Nansen. On Friday, it was sitting at about $62,000. As of Friday, bitcoin was hovering at the upper end of a critical $60,000 to $62,000 support range. Its next move could determine whether it can stabilize or if it will face another leg lower and revisit its July low of $57,737.35. Throughout November, bitcoin has been struggling from a combination of dollar strength, institutional selling, and ongoing leveraged bitcoin liquidations. The declines began in late October, as concerns over artificial intelligence valuations and spending fueled a broad tech sell-off. They were compounded by the $6.3 billion Binance hack and weakening institutional ETF demand. Bitcoin is in the early stages of forming a bottom, according to Cole. Retail fear is elevated amid recent outages, quantum concerns and other short-term uncertainties, but bitcoin should continue to benefit from macro forces like rising debt and weakening fiat currencies, which should drive price higher, he said. "Capital markets are open, … retail fears are high, and when you combine those things it's much more likely to be a dip-buying opportunity across the board, including bitcoin, than the start of a great financial crisis," said Cole. "It'll likely age as a volatile time to consider allocating to risk, not the opposite." "The winter for bitcoin is basically at the end, but after winter does not come summer, it comes early spring," he added. "Anytime anyone's been around early spring, what you notice is it gets really cold still, it still rains – it's not necessarily great weather, and I think that's the environment we're in for bitcoin." Bitcoin's next critical test is between $60,000 and $62,000, according to Nicolai Sondergaard, a research analyst at Nansen. On Friday, it was sitting at about $62,000.

As of Friday, bitcoin was hovering at the upper end of a critical $60,000 to $62,000 support range. Its next move could determine whether it can stabilize or if it will face another leg lower and revisit its July low of $57,737.35.

Throughout November, bitcoin has been struggling from a combination of dollar strength, institutional selling, and ongoing leveraged bitcoin liquidations. The declines began in late October, as concerns over artificial intelligence valuations and spending fueled a broad tech sell-off. They were compounded by the $6.3 billion Binance hack and weakening institutional ETF demand.

Bitcoin is in the early stages of forming a bottom, according to Cole. Retail fear is elevated amid recent outages, quantum concerns and other short-term uncertainties, but bitcoin should continue to benefit from macro forces like rising debt and weakening fiat currencies, which should drive price higher, he said.

"Capital markets are open, … retail fears are high, and when you combine those things it's much more likely to be a dip-buying opportunity across the board, including bitcoin, than the start of a great financial crisis," said Cole. "It'll likely age as a volatile time to consider allocating to risk, not the opposite."

"The winter for bitcoin is basically at the end, but after winter does not come summer, it comes early spring," he added. "Anytime anyone's been around early spring, what you notice is it gets really cold still, it still rains – it's not necessarily great weather, and I think that's the environment we're in for bitcoin."

That is an almost identical dip the OG crypto recorded around the time of the SpaceX IPO in June, and given that it then went on a run that took it above $80,000, some market watchers are wondering whether the same can happen again. The comparisons were made in a November 19 post on X by CryptosRus, who shared a chart measuring peak-to-trough losses across the weeks before each company’s stock market debut. It showed that before SpaceX w ent public around June 12, BTC’s price had dropped by almost 29% from a peak close to $83,000 in early May to near $59,000 in the first week of June. After that, the asset made a recovery, eventually going as high as $87,000 in September. Something similar is also happening ahead of the Anthropic listing. After Bitcoin went to $87,400 on September 21, it started a steady decline that has it changing hands just above $63,000 at the time of writing, representing a drawdown of nearly 28% across 8 weeks. “Same setup, same opportunity,” CryptosRus wrote, suggesting that the earlier recovery could offer a reference point for the current market. That BTC drop near $63,000 triggered liquidations approaching $500 million, with positions worth more than $100 million wiped out in one hour. Data from CoinGecko shows the asset is nearly 2% lower than 24 hours ago, with the losses stretching to just over 14% across seven days and 21% in the last two weeks. In the previous month, the number one cryptocurrency has seen its price drop by almost 23%, while the plunge year-on-year stands at around 30%. The timing of the asset’s weakness and the Anthropic IPO prompted speculation that investors may have been moving their capital into AI companies. With Anthropic closing its first trading day up 17% at $97.17, crypto analysts are now watching to see if digital assets find a floor or if the liquidity drain deepens as more AI unicorns prepare to go public. The crypto market just delivered an eerie sense of déjà vu. Bitcoin and ether both experienced sharp sell-offs in the weeks leading up to Anthropic's public debut, mirroring almost exactly the same pattern that played out before SpaceX went public earlier this year. The correlation is raising uncomfortable questions for crypto bulls about whether institutional money views digital assets as a liquidity source to fund allocations in hot tech IPOs. As Anthropic priced its IPO at $83, topping its expected range on surging institutional demand, bitcoin slid from recent highs while ether underperformed even more dramatically. The pattern matches what happened in the lead-up to SpaceX's listing, when both cryptocurrencies shed double-digit percentages before finding support only after the IPO priced. When a massive IPO looms, institutional investors appear to be liquidating portions of their crypto holdings to free up capital for new allocations. It's a liquidity rotation that hits hardest in the two to three weeks before pricing, precisely when underwriters are locking in final commitments from large buyers. Anthropic's debut certainly commanded attention. But here's where it gets interesting for crypto traders. After SpaceX priced its IPO, bitcoin and ether both stabilized within days and then mounted modest recoveries over the following weeks. The theory goes that once institutional allocations are locked and IPO euphoria fades, some of that capital rotates back into crypto as investors rebalance portfolios. With Anthropic's first trading day in the books and the initial pop already priced in, crypto markets are testing whether they can find a floor. Bitcoin has shown some signs of stabilization, though trading volumes remain thin, suggesting many institutional players are still on the sidelines. What makes this pattern particularly concerning for crypto advocates is that it suggests digital assets are being treated as secondary holdings, something to liquidate when "real" opportunities like AI IPOs emerge. That's a far cry from the narrative of bitcoin as digital gold or a portfolio hedge that trades independently of traditional markets. The institutional demand picture is murkier than it was during previous crypto rallies. While bitcoin ETFs have attracted steady inflows this year, the pace has slowed considerably. Meanwhile, the pipeline of major tech IPOs remains robust, with several AI and enterprise software unicorns reportedly preparing listings for early 2027. If the SpaceX-Anthropic pattern holds, crypto investors should watch for a potential stabilization phase over the next week or two, followed by a test of whether institutional buyers return. The key variable is whether another blockbuster IPO gets announced soon, which could trigger a repeat of the cycle. Some crypto analysts argue the sell-off is actually healthy, shaking out weak hands and establishing clearer support levels. Others worry it exposes how dependent crypto markets have become on the same institutional money that chases every hot tech trend. The difference in perspective often comes down to whether you view crypto as a mature asset class or still an emerging one fighting for legitimacy. Bitcoin is hovering near technical support levels that held during previous corrections, while ether faces a more uncertain picture given its underperformance. Trading desks report that institutional inquiry has picked up slightly since Anthropic's debut, but no one is ready to call a bottom yet. The broader implication is that crypto's fate may be more intertwined with the tech IPO calendar than many investors realized. As long as venture-backed unicorns keep going public at premium valuations, institutional investors may continue using crypto as a source of liquidity to fund those allocations. That's not necessarily bearish long-term, but it does suggest crypto markets could face periodic pressure whenever the IPO window heats up. The identical sell-off pattern before both the SpaceX and Anthropic IPOs reveals an uncomfortable truth about institutional crypto holdings: they're being used as a liquidity pool to fund hot tech allocations. Whether bitcoin and ether can establish a floor now that Anthropic's debut is complete will signal if the SpaceX playbook repeats, with capital gradually rotating back into digital assets. But with more AI unicorns eyeing 2027 listings, crypto investors may need to accept that their markets are now tethered to the tech IPO calendar in ways that challenge the independence narrative. The next few weeks will show if institutional demand returns or if crypto faces another cycle of liquidation as the next blockbuster listing approaches.

story.title: Bitcoin suffered identical sell-off pattern ahead of Anthropic, SpaceX IPOs — what happens next? - CNBC

facts.text: Bitcoin has suffered nearly identical sell-offs ahead of two of the biggest public offerings this year, leaving investors wondering if competing demand for investor capital could be weighing on the cryptocurrency and perhaps delaying its recovery.
The price of the bitcoin dropped 22.7% in the 30 days before Anthropic's IPO and fell 22.3% in the month leading up to SpaceX's June 12 listing.
"Liquidity events can elevate correlations across asset classes quickly," Matthew Sheffield, chief investment officer at the ether treasury firm Sharplink , told CNBC.
"The first 15 min of [Thursday's] Anthropic IPO put that on full display.
Tech stocks, value stocks, oil, gold, crypto all sold off as traders sold assets to buy shares in the secondary market."
Bitcoin's next critical test is between $60,000 and $62,000, according to Nicolai Sondergaard, a research analyst at Nansen.
Throughout November, bitcoin has been struggling from a combination of dollar strength, institutional selling, and ongoing leveraged bitcoin liquidations.
Still, the post-IPO price action may offer a data point in understanding where bitcoin's price goes next.
With Anthropic now public, investors are watching to see whether bitcoin and ether find a floor, and if institutional demand returns.

"[After] the SpaceX IPO, bitcoin didn't truly find its final bottom until after the IPO was completed, and it didn't actually reverse the downtrend until 70 days later," said Matt Cole, CEO and chairman of Strive Asset Management , a bitcoin treasury firm.
Bitcoin is in the early stages of forming a bottom, according to Cole.

Retail fear is elevated amid recent outages, quantum concerns and other short-term uncertainties, but bitcoin should continue to benefit from macro forces like rising debt and weakening fiat currencies, which should drive price higher, he said.
Anthropic began trading on the Nasdaq Global Select Market under the ticker symbol 'ANT' on the 19th (local time).
The company announced that it completed both its public and private offerings on the 20th.
The public offering consisted of 1.127 billion shares at $83 per share, totaling approximately $93.5 billion.
Including the private placement, the total funding reached approximately $119.5 billion.
According to CNBC, Bitcoin's price fell 22.7% in the 30 days prior to the Anthropic listing, and it dropped 22.3% in the month leading up to the SpaceX listing on June 12th.
Ethereum also saw similar selling pressure in the cryptocurrency market ahead of the two major IPOs, declining 25.3% and 28% during the respective periods.
He views Bitcoin as being in the early stages of forming a bottom and believes the market is likely to repeat fluctuations for the time being.
The timing of when lock-up periods on IPO-allocated shares expire could also impact capital flows.

The SpaceX IPO documentation includes a structure where share sale restrictions vary by existing shareholder, and some holdings become eligible for trading in stages following future earnings releases.
Analysts suggest that when large IPOs occur, the correlation across asset markets can rise sharply as investors sell existing assets to buy newly listed stocks.

Matthew Sheffield, Chief Investment Officer at Sharplink, cited the simultaneous sell-off of tech stocks, value stocks, oil, gold, and cryptocurrencies during the first 15 minutes of Anthropic's listing as an example of such capital movement.
He noted that even assets that function as stores of value in the long term are influenced by cash liquidity in the short term.

Other factors cited for the recent weakness in cryptocurrency include fund outflows from exchange-traded funds, the liquidation of leveraged positions, macroeconomic uncertainty, and risk-aversion sentiment.
Nicolai Søndergaard, a research analyst at Nansen, identified $60,000 to $62,000 as the next critical test range for Bitcoin.
However, he compared Bitcoin's recovery phase to "early spring" right after the end of deep winter, explaining that sharp cold snaps and rain could still occur during the rebound process.
Something similar is also happening ahead of the Anthropic listing.
After Bitcoin went to $87,400 on September 21, it started a steady decline that has it changing hands just above $63,000 at the time of writing, representing a drawdown of nearly 28% across 8 weeks.
Bitcoin (BTC) has fallen by approximately 28% from its September peak ahead of Anthropic’s Nasdaq debut on November 19.

Most of the discounts below are promoted as Black Friday deals, but we’ve also included a few that aren’t technically part of the shopping event but have “coincidentally” dropped in price in the last week or so. Black Friday isn’t until November 27th, however, so some prices could fall further in the coming days. Read our review. * The second-gen AirPods Max are down to $419 ($130 off) at Amazon, which is $19 shy of their best price to date (Best Buy and Target also have them for about $10 more). Like the original, Apple’s latest over-ear headphones feature a luxurious build consisting of aluminum, steel, and a mesh fabric, but they offer better sound and noise cancellation. Amazon also has the pink headphones on sale for $79.99, while other colors are $20 more at both retailers. The headphones are a noticeable improvement over their predecessor, delivering more detailed sound and support for lossless audio. Read our review. * The Beats Studio Buds Plus are down to around $89.95 ($80 off) at Amazon, Best Buy, and Target, nearly matching their lowest price to date. It has a smaller screen and a slower chip than the newer model, and it lacks an OLED screen, the Acoustic Display, and water resistance. Still, it’s a great option for reading and everyday use that’s currently more affordable than its $699 successor, with support for Apple Intelligence and the Apple Pencil Pro.

passages: Zscaler shares surged 18% in extended trading on Friday after Bloomberg reported that CrowdStrike is in talks to buy the cybersecurity vendor.
Shares of CrowdStrike shares fell more than 8%.
The talks between the two companies are ongoing, Bloomberg reported, citing sources familiar in the matter.
CrowdStrike declined to comment on the report.
Zscaler didn't immediately respond to CNBC's request for comment.
CrowdStrike has been one of the big cybersecurity winners in the artificial intelligence boom, with its stock about doubling in value this year, lifting its market cap to $235 billion.
Along with CrowdStrike, Palo Alto Networks has seen its business boom as businesses race to upgrade their networks in the AI era.
Palo Alto closed Friday at a nearly $282 billion market cap.
CrowdStrike's deals to this point have been on the smaller side.The company announced plans earlier this month to acquire agentic observability platform Fiddler AI and AI trust platform Dreadnode.

relevantPassages.text: Zscaler shares surged 18% in extended trading on Friday after Bloomberg reported that CrowdStrike is in talks to buy the cybersecurity vendor.
Shares of CrowdStrike shares fell more than 8%.
The talks between the two companies are ongoing, Bloomberg reported, citing sources familiar in the matter.
CrowdStrike declined to comment on the report.
Zscaler didn't immediately respond to CNBC's request for comment.
CrowdStrike has been one of the big cybersecurity winners in the artificial intelligence boom, with its stock about doubling in value this year, lifting its market cap to $235 billion.
Along with CrowdStrike, Palo Alto Networks has seen its business boom as businesses race to upgrade their networks in the AI era.
Palo Alto closed Friday at a nearly $282 billion market cap.
CrowdStrike's deals to this point have been on the smaller side.The company announced plans earlier this month to acquire agentic observability platform Fiddler AI and AI trust platform Dreadnode.

extraction.body: Bloomberg reported on November 20, 2026, that CrowdStrike was in ongoing talks to acquire Zscaler, citing people familiar with the matter, in a report carried by CNBC . Zscaler shares rose 18% in extended trading following the report, while CrowdStrike shares fell more than 8%. No acquisition agreement has been announced. CrowdStrike declined to comment on the report, and Zscaler did not immediately respond to a request for comment. CNBC put CrowdStrike’s market capitalization at $235 billion after its stock roughly doubled during 2026, while Zscaler’s was about $32 billion after a 13% decline during the year. A completed transaction would rank among cybersecurity’s largest, CNBC said. Its comparisons were Google’s $32 billion acquisition of Wiz in 2025, Cisco’s roughly $28 billion purchase of Splunk in 2024 and Palo Alto Networks’ $25 billion acquisition of CyberArk in 2026. Zscaler’s September 2, 2026 partnership announcement details an existing technical relationship between the companies. The expanded partnership is intended to automate security workflows and support real-time, adaptive Zero Trust enforcement by connecting CrowdStrike’s detection and response with Zscaler’s access controls. Zscaler said a planned integration using the OpenID Shared Signals Framework, an industry-standard method for sharing risk context, would let Falcon continuously evaluate user risk and pass that context to Zscaler’s Adaptive Access Engine. When suspicious endpoint behavior is detected, Zscaler can then automatically adjust access to match the current risk posture. The companies are also developing a native Falcon Foundry application built on Zscaler OneAPI. Planned functions include triggering Zscaler enforcement from Charlotte Agentic SOAR, CrowdStrike’s security automation interface, and supporting end-to-end automated remediation without middleware, connectors or separate infrastructure. Zscaler said network-event and AI-event logs are designed to stream into Falcon Next-Gen SIEM , CrowdStrike’s security-event management platform, where they can be correlated with Falcon endpoint, identity and cloud data. The combined telemetry is designed to help analysts reconstruct multi-stage attacks across domains. The AI telemetry includes AI-application interactions, risky chatbot prompts and policy violations, placing AI-specific risks alongside network and user activity in a unified investigation interface. Under the partnership plan, CrowdStrike would also expand Project QuiltWorks, an industry coalition focused on frontier AI risk, to include Zscaler . Zscaler cautioned that unreleased services and features covered by the announcement remained in development and subject to change. On November 3, 2026, CrowdStrike announced a definitive agreement to acquire Fiddler AI to add pre-deployment evaluation, continuous agent observability and explainability to Falcon. A separate agreement to acquire Dreadnode would add automated pre-deployment security testing of AI models, applications and agents. Both proposed acquisitions were expected to close in CrowdStrike’s fourth quarter of fiscal 2027, subject to customary closing conditions. The reported talks sit on top of an existing integration roadmap rather than a relationship built from scratch. The open question is whether that roadmap remains a partner integration or becomes part of a single company; for now, the documented product work and the reported transaction are at different stages, with several of the partnership’s features still in development. sources.title: CrowdStrike is in talks to buy Zscaler, and only one stock liked the news - Startup Fortune
passages: CrowdStrike is in talks to acquire Zscaler, Bloomberg and Reuters reported on Friday, November 20, with Reuters putting its story out at 4:46 pm Eastern.
Both outlets cited people familiar with the discussions, which Reuters described as ongoing.
Neither company had commented when Reuters asked, and nothing has been announced.
Reuters was explicit that no deal is guaranteed and that the talks could end without an agreement.
Zscaler already carries a market value of about $33.5 billion, so a premium would push any CrowdStrike offer past $30 billion.
Zscaler jumped 17% and CrowdStrike fell 8%, according to Reuters.
Frankly, the fit looks better on a slide than it may in practice.

Zscaler and CrowdStrike aren't strangers: they've run a partnership for years, covering product integrations, threat-intelligence sharing and automated response, and customers who want both can already get both.
If the combination works only because it's a single invoice, the premium is hard to defend.
If it works because one team can finally write detection logic that sees the laptop and the network connection in the same data set, that's worth paying for.
CrowdStrike built its name on Falcon, a platform that began with endpoint protection, the software on laptops and servers, and has since grown into identity and cloud security through acquisitions.
What it has never had is a strong network-security product.
Zscaler sells exactly that: cloud-delivered zero-trust access, which decides who and what gets onto a company's applications and network before any traffic moves.
CrowdStrike posted strong fiscal first-quarter 2027 results and announced a four-for-one stock split, but the market reaction showed how high expectations have become for AI-linked software stocks.

The company is making a more concrete AI security case, but investors now want proof in growth, margins and guidance. - why AI security stocks face higher valuation standards - how CrowdStrike's strong earnings disappointed AI-focused investors
Reuters noted the purchase would close CrowdStrike's biggest gap and put it in more direct competition with platform vendors such as Palo Alto Networks.

Large companies have been cutting the number of security vendors they pay, and a buyer that can offer endpoint, identity, cloud and network from one contract has an easier sale than one that has to say "and for the network, call someone else."
That split is the oldest pattern in deal-making.
The target's holders get paid a premium, the buyer's holders get handed the bill and the integration risk.
An 8% drop in a company CrowdStrike's size wipes out a lot of value in a few hours, which is the market saying it wants to see the price and the plan before it believes in either.

There's also the question of what else is in play. Reuters framed the talks as part of a wider push to consolidate in the security software sector, and the news arrived in the middle of a broader tech selloff, which makes a buyer's shares an awkward currency. Whether CrowdStrike would pay in cash, in stock or in some mix hasn't been reported.

For now, the facts are thin and the reaction is not. Two outlets say talks are underway, neither company has confirmed them, and the stocks have already moved by double digits and high single digits. extraction.body: 'Agents kept adapting for nearly a full day without human direction,' Amazon CISO said Suspected Chinese spies deployed AI agents which worked autonomously to find a zero-day in an open source application and then abuse the flaw to break into university networks, gaining full control of a server, according to Amazon CISO CJ Moses. The China-linked attacker used Cairn, an open source, penetration-testing framework that has become increasingly popular with cybercriminals who use the AI tool to carry out multi-stage intrusions with no human assistance . In this case, the agents found and exploited a zero-day MONAI Label, an open-source medical imaging AI application. Amazon notified the project's maintainers of the vulnerability, and they released a fix and a security advisory . On September 10, Amazon's Threat Intelligence Team found a server with a publicly hosted instance of Cairn that provided visibility into the campaign targeting universities in East Asia, outside Mainland China, Moses said in a Friday report shared with The Register . The campaign occurred over a period of 48 hours beginning on September 8, and the prompts were written in Simplified Chinese, with timestamps in executed scripts configured to China Standard Time. Before the AI agents found and exploited the zero day, however, they tried to break into another university’s Redis server over about 16 hours and 148 sequential actions, including abusing Redis's replication feature to load unauthorized code, escaping its scripting sandbox, writing to its configuration files, and corrupting its memory. None of these were successful, and when those actions failed, the agents also attempted a Log4Shell injection against a different service, a server-side request forgery (SSRF) attack against a vulnerability in a co-located Qdrant instance, and several credential sprays against PostgreSQL, SSH, and other tools. Meanwhile, a separate operation running for more than 6 hours targeted a university GPU server with another credential-spray attack, compiling a list of 80 real user names found across the school’s public websites, academic papers and other documents. "Neither operation succeeded, yet together they show that the agents kept adapting for nearly a full day without human direction," Moses wrote. Then the AI agents found the zero-day path traversal vulnerability in MONAI Label, and this time they were able to gain access to the server. "The agents identified the application's framework, mapped its API endpoints, and found an upload endpoint with a filename parameter," Moses wrote. They tested that parameter for path traversal, and the parameter was vulnerable. In about 11 minutes, the agents went from mapping the application’s API to arbitrarily writing files on the server." Later, the agents abused the same flaw to execute a Python reverse shell running as root. In another session, after the agents discovered the zero-day, the human operator provided them with a proxy that tunneled into a second university network, and connected to a server running the same vulnerable code. Amazon's discovery follows an earlier report by Gambit Security's threat intelligence team that also documented a Chinese operator using Cairn to carry out at least 105 attacks, and managing to compromise, "to varying degrees," at least 27 companies. This campaign also occurred in September. In addition to Cairn, the attacker used two other open source AI harnesses to steal credit card records and other sensitive data from a Fortune 500 hospitality company, a major US airline, a large private US industrial supplies distributor, and a US online fashion retailer, and other companies. "Together, these cases show that this autonomous AI agent framework is being adopted in both espionage and criminal operations," Moses wrote. ® Just don't expect complex, coherent, or always correct answers Pre-digital tech can't be transformed and automated Like a parent disciplining a misbehaving child, PHP’s annual update clamps down on loose default behaviors to curb malicious hacker horseplay. In this case, the agents found and exploited a zero-day MONAI Label, an open-source medical imaging AI application. Amazon notified the project's maintainers of the vulnerability, and they released a fix and a security advisory .

On September 10, Amazon's Threat Intelligence Team found a server with a publicly hosted instance of Cairn that provided visibility into the campaign targeting universities in East Asia, outside Mainland China, Moses said in a Friday report shared with The Register .
The campaign occurred over a period of 48 hours beginning on September 8, and the prompts were written in Simplified Chinese, with timestamps in executed scripts configured to China Standard Time.

Before the AI agents found and exploited the zero day, however, they tried to break into another university’s Redis server over about 16 hours and 148 sequential actions, including abusing Redis's replication feature to load unauthorized code, escaping its scripting sandbox, writing to its configuration files, and corrupting its memory.

None of these were successful, and when those actions failed, the agents also attempted a Log4Shell injection against a different service, a server-side request forgery (SSRF) attack against a vulnerability in a co-located Qdrant instance, and several credential sprays against PostgreSQL, SSH, and other tools.

Meanwhile, a separate operation running for more than 6 hours targeted a university GPU server with another credential-spray attack, compiling a list of 80 real user names found across the school’s public websites, academic papers and other documents.
"Neither operation succeeded, yet together they show that the agents kept adapting for nearly a full day without human direction," Moses wrote.
Then the AI agents found the zero-day path traversal vulnerability in MONAI Label, and this time they were able to gain access to the server.

"The agents identified the application's framework, mapped its API endpoints, and found an upload endpoint with a filename parameter," Moses wrote. They tested that parameter for path traversal, and the parameter was vulnerable. In about 11 minutes, the agents went from mapping the application’s API to arbitrarily writing files on the server."
Later, the agents abused the same flaw to execute a Python reverse shell running as root.

In another session, after the agents discovered the zero-day, the human operator provided them with a proxy that tunneled into a second university network, and connected to a server running the same vulnerable code.

Amazon's discovery follows an earlier report by Gambit Security's threat intelligence team that also documented a Chinese operator using Cairn to carry out at least 105 attacks, and managing to compromise, "to varying degrees," at least 27 companies.

This campaign also occurred in September. In addition to Cairn, the attacker used two other open source AI harnesses to steal credit card records and other sensitive data from a Fortune 500 hospitality company, a major US airline, a large private US industrial supplies distributor, and a US online fashion retailer, and other companies.
"Together, these cases show that this autonomous AI agent framework is being adopted in both espionage and criminal operations," Moses wrote. ®

extraction.body: Amazon's security chief is urging defenders to let machines respond to attacks automatically, after AI agents operating without step-by-step human direction discovered an unknown software flaw and used it to take over a university server. The agents, run through an open-source penetration-testing framework called Cairn, spent nearly two full days probing university networks in East Asia before breaking through, according to a report published Friday by CJ Moses, chief information security officer at Amazon Integrated Security. The activity was detected on Sept. 10, and the intrusions began two days earlier. Moses wrote that an agent capable of finding and exploiting a zero-day within minutes "completes its activity faster than many security operations centers can manually triage an alert." His prescription: organizations should lean on high-confidence detections that trigger automatic containment, with humans watching the results rather than signing off on every step. The breakthrough came against MONAI Label, an open-source application for medical imaging AI. The agents identified the software's framework, mapped its API endpoints and located an upload function that accepted a filename parameter. They then tested that parameter for path traversal, a technique that lets an attacker write files outside the directory an application is supposed to use. Within roughly 11 minutes of mapping the API, the agents could write files anywhere on the server, the report said. In a later session they planted a Python reverse shell in sitecustomize.py, a file Python loads at startup, and obtained root, the highest level of access on the machine. Amazon said it assessed with high confidence that the bug was a zero-day because no patch, advisory or prior public mention existed. The company alerted the project's maintainers, who issued a fix; a GitHub advisory published Nov. 18 rates the path traversal flaw as critical. The operator behind the campaign also pointed the agents at a second university network through a proxy, where a server ran the same vulnerable code. Amazon believes the same flaw was used to compromise that machine and open the tunnel. Before the zero-day fell, the agents made two sustained attempts that did not succeed, and the contrast illustrates how much machine speed has changed the economics of intrusion. Against the Redis in-memory database, which was exposed without a password, the agents tried to abuse replication to inject rogue code, escape the scripting sandbox, rewrite configuration files and corrupt memory. They also fired a Log4Shell exploit at another service on the same host, used a server-side request forgery flaw in a co-located Qdrant database to map the internal Docker network, and sprayed credentials at SSH, PostgreSQL and other services. On the GPU server, they assembled a list of about 80 real usernames from faculty directories, lab sites, archived pages and published papers before running their credential attack. Moses noted that the agents "ran continuously for 16 hours without breaks, sleep, or working-hour constraints." Amazon tied the campaign to a China-linked operator with moderate confidence, citing prompts written in Simplified Chinese, scripts configured to China Standard Time and targets of likely strategic interest to Beijing. Because the victims were not AWS customers, the company passed word through a government partner. The Cairn framework has surfaced in other investigations. Gambit Security's threat intelligence team documented a Chinese operator using it in at least 105 attacks that compromised 27 companies to varying degrees, including a Fortune 500 hospitality company, a major U.S. airline, a large private industrial supplies distributor and an online fashion retailer. Google researchers said on Nov. 17 that they had found Cairn in intrusions at American aerospace companies. Moses said the cases together show the framework is being picked up for both espionage and financial crime. The disclosure lands as defenders debate how much autonomy to hand to security tooling. Moses' argument is that the alternative to automated response is a human queue that an agent can outrun. Security teams that wait for an analyst to confirm each alert are, in effect, giving an intruder a head start measured in minutes, and the MONAI Label episode shows that window is now wide enough to go from first contact to full control of a server. For software maintainers, the case is a reminder that open-source projects serving specialized fields such as medical imaging can sit inside university and hospital networks without anyone watching their upload endpoints. The flaw is now public and patched, but Amazon's account suggests the agents found it by probing, not by reading code, which means similar gaps elsewhere may be discovered the same way. The China-linked attacker used Cairn, an open source, penetration-testing framework that has become increasingly popular with cybercriminals who use the AI tool to carry out multi-stage intrusions with no human assistance .

In this case, the agents found and exploited a zero-day MONAI Label, an open-source medical imaging AI application. Amazon notified the project's maintainers of the vulnerability, and they released a fix and a security advisory .

On September 10, Amazon's Threat Intelligence Team found a server with a publicly hosted instance of Cairn that provided visibility into the campaign targeting universities in East Asia, outside Mainland China, Moses said in a Friday report shared with The Register .
The campaign occurred over a period of 48 hours beginning on September 8, and the prompts were written in Simplified Chinese, with timestamps in executed scripts configured to China Standard Time.

Before the AI agents found and exploited the zero day, however, they tried to break into another university’s Redis server over about 16 hours and 148 sequential actions, including abusing Redis's replication feature to load unauthorized code, escaping its scripting sandbox, writing to its configuration files, and corrupting its memory.

None of these were successful, and when those actions failed, the agents also attempted a Log4Shell injection against a different service, a server-side request forgery (SSRF) attack against a vulnerability in a co-located Qdrant instance, and several credential sprays against PostgreSQL, SSH, and other tools.

Meanwhile, a separate operation running for more than 6 hours targeted a university GPU server with another credential-spray attack, compiling a list of 80 real user names found across the school’s public websites, academic papers and other documents.
"Neither operation succeeded, yet together they show that the agents kept adapting for nearly a full day without human direction," Moses wrote.
Then the AI agents found the zero-day path traversal vulnerability in MONAI Label, and this time they were able to gain access to the server.

"The agents identified the application's framework, mapped its API endpoints, and found an upload endpoint with a filename parameter," Moses wrote. They tested that parameter for path traversal, and the parameter was vulnerable. In about 11 minutes, the agents went from mapping the application’s API to arbitrarily writing files on the server."
Later, the agents abused the same flaw to execute a Python reverse shell running as root.

In another session, after the agents discovered the zero-day, the human operator provided them with a proxy that tunneled into a second university network, and connected to a server running the same vulnerable code.

Amazon's discovery follows an earlier report by Gambit Security's threat intelligence team that also documented a Chinese operator using Cairn to carry out at least 105 attacks, and managing to compromise, "to varying degrees," at least 27 companies.

This campaign also occurred in September. In addition to Cairn, the attacker used two other open source AI harnesses to steal credit card records and other sensitive data from a Fortune 500 hospitality company, a major US airline, a large private US industrial supplies distributor, and a US online fashion retailer, and other companies.
"Together, these cases show that this autonomous AI agent framework is being adopted in both espionage and criminal operations," Moses wrote. ®

relevantPassages.text: On September 10, Amazon's Threat Intelligence Team found a server with a publicly hosted instance of Cairn that provided visibility into the campaign targeting universities in East Asia, outside Mainland China, Moses said in a Friday report shared with The Register .

Before the AI agents found and exploited the zero day, however, they tried to break into another university’s Redis server over about 16 hours and 148 sequential actions, including abusing Redis's replication feature to load unauthorized code, escaping its scripting sandbox, writing to its configuration files, and corrupting its memory.

Meanwhile, a separate operation running for more than 6 hours targeted a university GPU server with another credential-spray attack, compiling a list of 80 real user names found across the school’s public websites, academic papers and other documents.
"The agents identified the application's framework, mapped its API endpoints, and found an upload endpoint with a filename parameter," Moses wrote.

None of these were successful, and when those actions failed, the agents also attempted a Log4Shell injection against a different service, a server-side request forgery (SSRF) attack against a vulnerability in a co-located Qdrant instance, and several credential sprays against PostgreSQL, SSH, and other tools.
PLUS: China upgrades smartphone surveillance tools; Ring eases anti-snooping stance; and more

The China-linked attacker used Cairn, an open source, penetration-testing framework that has become increasingly popular with cybercriminals who use the AI tool to carry out multi-stage intrusions with no human assistance .
Later, the agents abused the same flaw to execute a Python reverse shell running as root.

The activity was detected on Sept. 10, and the intrusions began two days earlier. Moses wrote that an agent capable of finding and exploiting a zero-day within minutes "completes its activity faster than many security operations centers can manually triage an alert." His prescription: organizations should lean on high-confidence detections that trigger automatic containment, with humans watching the results rather than signing off on every step. The breakthrough came against MONAI Label, an open-source application for medical imaging AI. The agents identified the software's framework, mapped its API endpoints and located an upload function that accepted a filename parameter. They then tested that parameter for path traversal, a technique that lets an attacker write files outside the directory an application is supposed to use. Within roughly 11 minutes of mapping the API, the agents could write files anywhere on the server, the report said. In a later session they planted a Python reverse shell in sitecustomize.py, a file Python loads at startup, and obtained root, the highest level of access on the machine. Amazon said it assessed with high confidence that the bug was a zero-day because no patch, advisory or prior public mention existed. The company alerted the project's maintainers, who issued a fix; a GitHub advisory published Nov. 18 rates the path traversal flaw as critical. The operator behind the campaign also pointed the agents at a second university network through a proxy, where a server ran the same vulnerable code. Amazon believes the same flaw was used to compromise that machine and open the tunnel. Before the zero-day fell, the agents made two sustained attempts that did not succeed, and the contrast illustrates how much machine speed has changed the economics of intrusion. Against the Redis in-memory database, which was exposed without a password, the agents tried to abuse replication to inject rogue code, escape the scripting sandbox, rewrite configuration files and corrupt memory. They also fired a Log4Shell exploit at another service on the same host, used a server-side request forgery flaw in a co-located Qdrant database to map the internal Docker network, and sprayed credentials at SSH, PostgreSQL and other services. On the GPU server, they assembled a list of about 80 real usernames from faculty directories, lab sites, archived pages and published papers before running their credential attack. Before the AI agents found and exploited the zero day, however, they tried to break into another university’s Redis server over about 16 hours and 148 sequential actions, including abusing Redis's replication feature to load unauthorized code, escaping its scripting sandbox, writing to its configuration files, and corrupting its memory.

Meanwhile, a separate operation running for more than 6 hours targeted a university GPU server with another credential-spray attack, compiling a list of 80 real user names found across the school’s public websites, academic papers and other documents.
"The agents identified the application's framework, mapped its API endpoints, and found an upload endpoint with a filename parameter," Moses wrote.

Later, the agents abused the same flaw to execute a Python reverse shell running as root.

Amazon said it assessed with high confidence that the bug was a zero-day because no patch, advisory or prior public mention existed.

Amazon's security chief is urging defenders to let machines respond to attacks automatically, after AI agents operating without step-by-step human direction discovered an unknown software flaw and used it to take over a university server.

For software maintainers, the case is a reminder that open-source projects serving specialized fields such as medical imaging can sit inside university and hospital networks without anyone watching their upload endpoints.
The flaw is now public and patched, but Amazon's account suggests the agents found it by probing, not by reading code, which means similar gaps elsewhere may be discovered the same way.
Once added, BigGo Finance appears first in Google Search Top Stories, so you get the broadest, most up-to-the-minute, and most comprehensive global financial news first.

The agents, run through an open-source penetration-testing framework called Cairn, spent nearly two full days probing university networks in East Asia before breaking through, according to a report published Friday by CJ Moses, chief information security officer at Amazon Integrated Security.
Before the zero-day fell, the agents made two sustained attempts that did not succeed, and the contrast illustrates how much machine speed has changed the economics of intrusion.
The agents identified the software's framework, mapped its API endpoints and located an upload function that accepted a filename parameter.

The China-linked attacker used Cairn, an open source, penetration-testing framework that has become increasingly popular with cybercriminals who use the AI tool to carry out multi-stage intrusions with no human assistance .
Those failures do not erase the successful intrusion.
Amazon recommends high-confidence detections and automated responses where appropriate, with people overseeing the results.
Automation can help defenders move faster, but a poorly chosen automatic action can also interrupt a legitimate service.
Plan and test it against the systems you actually operate.
