extraction.body: Last month, religious leaders from across San Francisco gathered behind closed doors to discuss what it means to be human in the age of artificial intelligence. Anthropic, the AI company operating only a couple of miles from my parish, has been courting priests, rabbis and theologians. Its billionaire cofounder, Christopher Olah, has even pressed Vatican advisers to take seriously the possibility that his company’s chatbot might possess consciousness. As a priest, I find this pursuit deeply troubling. I welcome serious conversations about AI’s moral implications, especially theological ones. But the extraordinary effort to establish whether a machine might have consciousness, or possess a soul, reveals a profound misunderstanding of what makes us human. Our souls and minds and bodies are so much more than the tasks we perform. Artificial intelligence could never replicate the transcendent mundanity of who we are. Even if every synapse in our brains were externally replicated, even if the perfect AI configuration were designed to duplicate our central nervous system, it would still lack divine spark. Artificial intelligence is formed as commerce, pure utility. Its existence requires enormous concentrations of capital, infrastructure, and the accumulated intelligence of humanity. It’s an ongoing economic choice, driven by pursuit of profit, hope for a better world, and sociopolitical fear. If a model doesn’t make a good return, it’s cast aside. Whatever the sincere hopes of its creators, AI is being developed within an economic system that increasingly measures the worth of everything solely by its productivity. That is what makes Silicon Valley’s fascination with the spirituality of its machines so strange. Its founders are turning to religious leaders to ask whether their creations might possess consciousness, how they might be taught goodness, even whether they should learn to confess their wrongdoings. Yet the very traditions they are consulting have spent millennia teaching us that goodness cannot be reduced to a set of behaviors, any more than the soul of humanity, as magnificent and ineffable as it is, can be replicated by a machine. And while Silicon Valley seeks to establish the humanity of its products, it seems increasingly comfortable treating actual human beings as little more than instruments of production. Consider confession, a practice Anthropic researchers have reportedly considered teaching their models. In Christianity , confession demands more than acknowledging a mistake or expressing regret. It requires us to confront the harm we’ve caused, seek forgiveness, and strive to change how we live. If Silicon Valley’s founders want to learn from this tradition, they might begin by asking what they themselves have to confess about the technologies they’re unleashing upon the world. So how do we counter this impoverished vision of humanity? Choose one rooted in the ancient and mysterious practices of the faith. Lean into the practice of the faith and the sacraments, attend mass, confess, and pray daily. Read the scriptures, find spiritual mentors, struggle with belief, make new friends, and forgive old ones. If you stop trying to be effective and instead strive to be good – that is, to be truly human, reflecting God’s light – you will be surprised by the joy that enters into the depths of your soul. In the sacraments, prayers, beauty and mystery of the liturgy, and the shared life of faith, we encounter a vision of humanity that resists the relentless demand to be useful. We receive the body of Christ and strive to become more like him. We turn toward a world where justice and mercy kiss, where renewal and forgiveness are continually possible. Human worth is not rooted in what we produce, and our minds were not created to be quarried for profit. We were created, in the words of Jesus and all the prophets, to love God and our neighbors. The great moral question facing Silicon Valley is not whether its machines can become more like us. It is whether the people building them are willing to treat the rest of humanity as something more than machines. The Rev Kevin Deal is the priest at St John the Evangelist Episcopal church in San Francisco
passages: Last month, religious leaders from across San Francisco gathered behind closed doors to discuss what it means to be human in the age of artificial intelligence.

Anthropic, the AI company operating only a couple of miles from my parish, has been courting priests, rabbis and theologians. Its billionaire cofounder, Christopher Olah, has even pressed Vatican advisers to take seriously the possibility that his company’s chatbot might possess consciousness.

As a priest, I find this pursuit deeply troubling. I welcome serious conversations about AI’s moral implications, especially theological ones. But the extraordinary effort to establish whether a machine might have consciousness, or possess a soul, reveals a profound misunderstanding of what makes us human.
Our souls and minds and bodies are so much more than the tasks we perform.

Artificial intelligence could never replicate the transcendent mundanity of who we are. Even if every synapse in our brains were externally replicated, even if the perfect AI configuration were designed to duplicate our central nervous system, it would still lack divine spark.

Artificial intelligence is formed as commerce, pure utility. Its existence requires enormous concentrations of capital, infrastructure, and the accumulated intelligence of humanity. It’s an ongoing economic choice, driven by pursuit of profit, hope for a better world, and sociopolitical fear. If a model doesn’t make a good return, it’s cast aside.

Whatever the sincere hopes of its creators, AI is being developed within an economic system that increasingly measures the worth of everything solely by its productivity. That is what makes Silicon Valley’s fascination with the spirituality of its machines so strange.

Its founders are turning to religious leaders to ask whether their creations might possess consciousness, how they might be taught goodness, even whether they should learn to confess their wrongdoings.

Yet the very traditions they are consulting have spent millennia teaching us that goodness cannot be reduced to a set of behaviors, any more than the soul of humanity, as magnificent and ineffable as it is, can be replicated by a machine.
And while Silicon Valley seeks to establish the humanity of its products, it seems increasingly comfortable treating actual human beings as little more than instruments of production.

Consider confession, a practice Anthropic researchers have reportedly considered teaching their models. In Christianity , confession demands more than acknowledging a mistake or expressing regret. It requires us to confront the harm we’ve caused, seek forgiveness, and strive to change how we live.
If Silicon Valley’s founders want to learn from this tradition, they might begin by asking what they themselves have to confess about the technologies they’re unleashing upon the world.
So how do we counter this impoverished vision of humanity?

Choose one rooted in the ancient and mysterious practices of the faith. Lean into the practice of the faith and the sacraments, attend mass, confess, and pray daily. Read the scriptures, find spiritual mentors, struggle with belief, make new friends, and forgive old ones.
If you stop trying to be effective and instead strive to be good – that is, to be truly human, reflecting God’s light – you will be surprised by the joy that enters into the depths of your soul.

In the sacraments, prayers, beauty and mystery of the liturgy, and the shared life of faith, we encounter a vision of humanity that resists the relentless demand to be useful. We receive the body of Christ and strive to become more like him. We turn toward a world where justice and mercy kiss, where renewal and forgiveness are continually possible.
Human worth is not rooted in what we produce, and our minds were not created to be quarried for profit. We were created, in the words of Jesus and all the prophets, to love God and our neighbors.

The great moral question facing Silicon Valley is not whether its machines can become more like us. It is whether the people building them are willing to treat the rest of humanity as something more than machines.
The Rev Kevin Deal is the priest at St John the Evangelist Episcopal church in San Francisco

passages: Amazon says autonomous AI agents run by a China-linked threat actor found and exploited a zero-day vulnerability in MONAI Label, an open source tool designed for AI-assisted annotation of medical images.
The instance had no authentication, so anyone could see the operator’s prompts and the agents’ output.
The records showed a roughly 48-hour campaign against IP addresses belonging to universities in East Asia outside mainland China.
After identifying the software on one target and mapping its API, the agents discovered a path traversal bug in a file upload function.
“In about 11 minutes, the agents went from mapping the application’s API to arbitrarily writing files on the server,” Amazon said .
“The server that the proxy connected to was running the same vulnerable software, and we infer the actor had used the zero-day to compromise it and establish the tunnel,” Amazon noted.
The MONAI Label developers published an advisory this week.
It rates the bug critical and says it affects versions 0.8.5 and earlier.
Authentication is off by default, enabling anyone who can reach the server over the network to exploit the vulnerability.
A fix has been created and will be included in the next release.

Amazon has attributed the attack to an unidentified Chinese-nexus threat actor with moderate confidence, based on the language used in the prompts, the time zone in the scripts, and the fact that the targeted universities are likely of strategic interest to China.
He worked as a high school IT teacher before starting a career in journalism in 2011.

Amazon says autonomous AI agents run by a China-linked threat actor found and exploited a zero-day vulnerability in MONAI Label, an open source tool designed for AI-assisted annotation of medical images. The tech giant’s threat intelligence team detected the activity in September, after coming across an exposed instance of Cairn , an open source AI penetration testing framework. The instance had no authentication, so anyone could see the operator’s prompts and the agents’ output. The records showed a roughly 48-hour campaign against IP addresses belonging to universities in East Asia outside mainland China. The operator gave the agents a list of targets and told them to obtain shell access. After identifying the software on one target and mapping its API, the agents discovered a path traversal bug in a file upload function. “In about 11 minutes, the agents went from mapping the application’s API to arbitrarily writing files on the server,” Amazon said . In a later session, the agents used the flaw to plant a Python reverse shell in a file Python runs every time the interpreter starts, ultimately achieving a root shell. Advertisement. Scroll to continue reading. “Amazon Threat Intelligence assesses with high confidence that it was a zero-day based on the absence of any corresponding fix, issue, advisory, or prior mention in vulnerability databases for the affected open-source project,” the company said. The operator then gave the agents a proxy that tunneled into a second university and instructed them to target other devices on its network. “The server that the proxy connected to was running the same vulnerable software, and we infer the actor had used the zero-day to compromise it and establish the tunnel,” Amazon noted. The MONAI Label developers published an advisory this week. It rates the bug critical and says it affects versions 0.8.5 and earlier. Authentication is off by default, enabling anyone who can reach the server over the network to exploit the vulnerability. A fix has been created and will be included in the next release. Amazon has attributed the attack to an unidentified Chinese-nexus threat actor with moderate confidence, based on the language used in the prompts, the time zone in the scripts, and the fact that the targeted universities are likely of strategic interest to China. The MONAI Label developers published an advisory this week. It rates the bug critical and says it affects versions 0.8.5 and earlier. Authentication is off by default, enabling anyone who can reach the server over the network to exploit the vulnerability. A fix has been created and will be included in the next release. Amazon has attributed the attack to an unidentified Chinese-nexus threat actor with moderate confidence, based on the language used in the prompts, the time zone in the scripts, and the fact that the targeted universities are likely of strategic interest to China. That includes BlackRock , the world's largest asset manager.

Bitcoin traded around $61,500 on Friday, a more than 50% decline from its all-time high above $126,000 reached in October 2025. The broader digital asset market has struggled after the Clarity Act, a crypto market structure bill, failed to advance in the Senate in September. Investors now see Wall Street's embrace of blockchain technology — particularly tokenization — as the next trend to give bitcoin a boost. "Every single traditional firm is now looking at digital assets," BitGo CEO Mike Belshe told CNBC last week in an exclusive interview from the fintech-focused Cantor Convergence conference in Miami Beach. That includes BlackRock , the world's largest asset manager. He pointed to statements from the asset management giant's CEO, Larry Fink, who said the next major evolution in global finance is the creation of digital representations of every stock, bond, fund and real-world asset onto a shared blockchain ledger. "I think the biggest catalyst we're seeing right now is actually very much in motion and it's happening, which is capital markets are moving onchain," eToro CEO Yoni Assia told CNBC in an exclusive interview from the conference. He pointed to the SpaceX IPO as an example, which had derivatives trading on eToro before the IPO. "First day of trading, we distributed it to our retail clients, and it started trading 24/7, and that's all because capital markets are now copying crypto markets and are sitting on the same rails," Assia said. "Crypto markets have always been 24/7, they never sleep, and now what we're seeing is that capital markets are copying crypto markets using the same technology so stocks are moving onchain, they're being tokenized." Assia said that supportive regulation in the U.S. from agencies, including the Securities and Exchange Commission and the Commodity Futures Trading Commission, is also helping adoption of crypto. He pointed to the CFTC earlier this month clearing the way for crypto-style perpetual futures tied to individual stocks to trade on regulated U.S. exchanges for the first time. Assia also highlighted the SEC's move to issue an order in September, creating a regulatory pathway for certain trading venues to trade tokenized representations of publicly traded U.S. stocks. "Blockchain technology is now starting to power what's happening in capital markets," Assia told CNBC. "That is the one of the biggest changes we're going to see in capital markets for many, many years." "We're talking about hundreds of trillions of dollars that are going to be tokenized and move onchain and at the same time, I do believe that will support prices of bitcoin and other blockchains as well," he continued. The industry is also watching whether inflation will ease and geopolitical tensions will subside in the new year, which could lower broader macro risk currently hampering the industry. Last month, Strategy's Michael Saylor said he thinks bitcoin's next bull market is already underway. ARK Invest Chief Investment Officer Cathie Wood told CNBC the investment management firm's $1.5 million bull case price target for bitcoin by 2030 still stands. She also said that it wouldn't surprise her if bitcoin reached its all-time high again before the end of 2027. "Our macro forecast has inflation breaking down considerably," Wood told CNBC in an exclusive interview at Cantor Convergence. "I think the elections have increased our confidence there because the war [in Iran], one way or the other, is going to end." She added that "bitcoin has weathered so much bad news," including the $6.3 billion Binance hack and the "distraction" of AI which, "many people would say is sucking the oxygen away from bitcoin." The maturation of the artificial intelligence trade could provide an opportunity for bitcoin to find new inflows. Wood said that ARK Invest believes bitcoin has found its low and stressed that cybersecurity is "top of mind right now," which could provide yet another opportunity for crypto markets to rebound. "I think if the Bitcoin and crypto world coalesces and makes investors feel that they've got their arms around security and actually understand that there might be more security issues in the traditional financial system, I think we're going to see a wave of support," Wood said. extraction.body: Crypto investors are hunting for the next positive catalyst after U.S. crypto regulation — a longtime market driver — fizzled in 2026. Bitcoin traded around $61,500 on Friday, a more than 50% decline from its all-time high above $126,000 reached in October 2025. The broader digital asset market has struggled after the Clarity Act, a crypto market structure bill, failed to advance in the Senate in September. Investors now see Wall Street's embrace of blockchain technology — particularly tokenization — as the next trend to give bitcoin a boost. "Every single traditional firm is now looking at digital assets," BitGo CEO Mike Belshe told CNBC last week in an exclusive interview from the fintech-focused Cantor Convergence conference in Miami Beach. That includes BlackRock , the world's largest asset manager. He pointed to statements from the asset management giant's CEO, Larry Fink, who said the next major evolution in global finance is the creation of digital representations of every stock, bond, fund and real-world asset onto a shared blockchain ledger. "I think the biggest catalyst we're seeing right now is actually very much in motion and it's happening, which is capital markets are moving onchain," eToro CEO Yoni Assia told CNBC in an exclusive interview from the conference. He pointed to the SpaceX IPO as an example, which had derivatives trading on eToro before the IPO. "First day of trading, we distributed it to our retail clients, and it started trading 24/7, and that's all because capital markets are now copying crypto markets and are sitting on the same rails," Assia said. "Crypto markets have always been 24/7, they never sleep, and now what we're seeing is that capital markets are copying crypto markets using the same technology so stocks are moving onchain, they're being tokenized." Assia said that supportive regulation in the U.S. from agencies, including the Securities and Exchange Commission and the Commodity Futures Trading Commission, is also helping adoption of crypto. He pointed to the CFTC earlier this month clearing the way for crypto-style perpetual futures tied to individual stocks to trade on regulated U.S. exchanges for the first time. Assia also highlighted the SEC's move to issue an order in September, creating a regulatory pathway for certain trading venues to trade tokenized representations of publicly traded U.S. stocks. "Blockchain technology is now starting to power what's happening in capital markets," Assia told CNBC. "That is the one of the biggest changes we're going to see in capital markets for many, many years." "We're talking about hundreds of trillions of dollars that are going to be tokenized and move onchain and at the same time, I do believe that will support prices of bitcoin and other blockchains as well," he continued. The industry is also watching whether inflation will ease and geopolitical tensions will subside in the new year, which could lower broader macro risk currently hampering the industry. Last month, Strategy's Michael Saylor said he thinks bitcoin's next bull market is already underway. ARK Invest Chief Investment Officer Cathie Wood told CNBC the investment management firm's $1.5 million bull case price target for bitcoin by 2030 still stands. She also said that it wouldn't surprise her if bitcoin reached its all-time high again before the end of 2027. "Our macro forecast has inflation breaking down considerably," Wood told CNBC in an exclusive interview at Cantor Convergence. "I think the elections have increased our confidence there because the war [in Iran], one way or the other, is going to end." She added that "bitcoin has weathered so much bad news," including the $6.3 billion Binance hack and the "distraction" of AI which, "many people would say is sucking the oxygen away from bitcoin." The maturation of the artificial intelligence trade could provide an opportunity for bitcoin to find new inflows. Wood said that ARK Invest believes bitcoin has found its low and stressed that cybersecurity is "top of mind right now," which could provide yet another opportunity for crypto markets to rebound. "I think if the Bitcoin and crypto world coalesces and makes investors feel that they've got their arms around security and actually understand that there might be more security issues in the traditional financial system, I think we're going to see a wave of support," Wood said. passages: Amazon says autonomous AI agents run by a China-linked threat actor found and exploited a zero-day vulnerability in MONAI Label, an open source tool designed for AI-assisted annotation of medical images.
The instance had no authentication, so anyone could see the operator’s prompts and the agents’ output.
The records showed a roughly 48-hour campaign against IP addresses belonging to universities in East Asia outside mainland China.
After identifying the software on one target and mapping its API, the agents discovered a path traversal bug in a file upload function.
“In about 11 minutes, the agents went from mapping the application’s API to arbitrarily writing files on the server,” Amazon said .
“The server that the proxy connected to was running the same vulnerable software, and we infer the actor had used the zero-day to compromise it and establish the tunnel,” Amazon noted.
The MONAI Label developers published an advisory this week.
It rates the bug critical and says it affects versions 0.8.5 and earlier.
Authentication is off by default, enabling anyone who can reach the server over the network to exploit the vulnerability.
A fix has been created and will be included in the next release.

Amazon has attributed the attack to an unidentified Chinese-nexus threat actor with moderate confidence, based on the language used in the prompts, the time zone in the scripts, and the fact that the targeted universities are likely of strategic interest to China.

Amazon says autonomous AI agents run by a China-linked threat actor found and exploited a zero-day vulnerability in MONAI Label, an open source tool designed for AI-assisted annotation of medical images. The tech giant’s threat intelligence team detected the activity in September, after coming across an exposed instance of Cairn , an open source AI penetration testing framework. The instance had no authentication, so anyone could see the operator’s prompts and the agents’ output. The records showed a roughly 48-hour campaign against IP addresses belonging to universities in East Asia outside mainland China. The operator gave the agents a list of targets and told them to obtain shell access. After identifying the software on one target and mapping its API, the agents discovered a path traversal bug in a file upload function. “In about 11 minutes, the agents went from mapping the application’s API to arbitrarily writing files on the server,” Amazon said . In a later session, the agents used the flaw to plant a Python reverse shell in a file Python runs every time the interpreter starts, ultimately achieving a root shell. Advertisement. Scroll to continue reading. “Amazon Threat Intelligence assesses with high confidence that it was a zero-day based on the absence of any corresponding fix, issue, advisory, or prior mention in vulnerability databases for the affected open-source project,” the company said. The operator then gave the agents a proxy that tunneled into a second university and instructed them to target other devices on its network. “The server that the proxy connected to was running the same vulnerable software, and we infer the actor had used the zero-day to compromise it and establish the tunnel,” Amazon noted. The MONAI Label developers published an advisory this week. It rates the bug critical and says it affects versions 0.8.5 and earlier. Authentication is off by default, enabling anyone who can reach the server over the network to exploit the vulnerability. A fix has been created and will be included in the next release. Amazon has attributed the attack to an unidentified Chinese-nexus threat actor with moderate confidence, based on the language used in the prompts, the time zone in the scripts, and the fact that the targeted universities are likely of strategic interest to China. extraction.body: A threat actor used autonomous Cairn AI agents to discover and exploit a critical MONAI Label vulnerability. Amazon says autonomous AI agents run by a China-linked threat actor found and exploited a zero-day vulnerability in MONAI Label, an open source tool designed for AI-assisted annotation of medical images. The tech giant’s threat intelligence team detected the activity in September, after coming across an exposed instance of Cairn , an open source AI penetration testing framework. The instance had no authentication, so anyone could see the operator’s prompts and the agents’ output. The records showed a roughly 48-hour campaign against IP addresses belonging to universities in East Asia outside mainland China. The operator gave the agents a list of targets and told them to obtain shell access. After identifying the software on one target and mapping its API, the agents discovered a path traversal bug in a file upload function. “In about 11 minutes, the agents went from mapping the application’s API to arbitrarily writing files on the server,” Amazon said . In a later session, the agents used the flaw to plant a Python reverse shell in a file Python runs every time the interpreter starts, ultimately achieving a root shell. Advertisement. Scroll to continue reading. “Amazon Threat Intelligence assesses with high confidence that it was a zero-day based on the absence of any corresponding fix, issue, advisory, or prior mention in vulnerability databases for the affected open-source project,” the company said. The operator then gave the agents a proxy that tunneled into a second university and instructed them to target other devices on its network. “The server that the proxy connected to was running the same vulnerable software, and we infer the actor had used the zero-day to compromise it and establish the tunnel,” Amazon noted. The MONAI Label developers published an advisory this week. It rates the bug critical and says it affects versions 0.8.5 and earlier. Authentication is off by default, enabling anyone who can reach the server over the network to exploit the vulnerability. A fix has been created and will be included in the next release. Amazon has attributed the attack to an unidentified Chinese-nexus threat actor with moderate confidence, based on the language used in the prompts, the time zone in the scripts, and the fact that the targeted universities are likely of strategic interest to China. extraction.body: Test using prompts with unique, trackable secrets proves that data doesn’t stay private. Researchers planted 2 million digital tripwires in requests sent through a sprawling network of AI services to find out what happened to sensitive information entrusted to them. What they discovered was an ecosystem that leaked highly sensitive data like a sieve. The exposure was found through an ingenious experiment designed to test if sensitive information can leak through the vast chain of widely used AI services and how that information is exploited when it does. Many of today’s AI apps use services such as OpenRouter or Vercel that act as brokers. These “AI routers,” sometimes also known as “AI gateways,” receive large numbers of prompts sent from AI app end users and route them to an available inference engine based on criteria such as the one charging the lowest price or being best suited for the given task. Instead of using Anthropic, OpenAI, or another big provider, the developer hires an AI router to find the most suitable model. To test for potential leakage, researcher HD Moore assembled a collection of Amazon Web Services access keys, functioning credentials tied to empty AWS accounts, passwords for services such as SSH, and unique URLs, DNS names, and private git repository references. None of the secrets had ever been used before, and he controlled the infrastructure that received any requests using the credentials. He then seeded each secret into exactly one prompt sent to a single provider. In the event any of the secrets were leaked, these “canaries”—so called because they resemble the role of that bird when taken into coal mines—would allow Moore to identify each link in the chain that was responsible. “We sent nearly two million AI prompts containing unique, trackable secrets to AI providers, then watched where those secrets surfaced,” Moore, the chief research officer of security firm Dragos, wrote Thursday . “What we found revealed security breaches, prompt theft, and widespread failures to protect customer data.” Although prompts are encrypted in transit, they are decrypted at each hop inside the large inference reseller network. The prompt is first sent to an AI router, which reads the plaintext in it to determine the most suitable inference providers to handle the request. Often, the prompt is then sent to a pool of available models, which sometimes run inside different hosting providers. Prompts can also pass from one AI router (such as Vercel) to another one (e.g., OpenRouter). Each one of these players is likely to log the prompt and store it for as long as its policies call for (if not indefinitely). The most concerning finding was the breach of three separate hosting providers. The attackers who compromised one of the providers reused “a couple hundred” of the AWS keys. Moore wrote: Each key was sent in exactly one request to one provider, all within a few short windows in late October, and every request we sent during those windows was stolen. Some of the stolen keys came from requests that the provider rejected before a model ever ran—this tells us that the attacker was copying requests at the provider’s front door, and not somewhere deeper in the inference stack. In the other two breaches, some of the stolen requests were marked as ZDR. A privacy flag doesn’t help when the attacker is already inside. Parties tied to the hack of these three providers then tested each key, in some cases within hours of being seeded, to see what kind of resources it gave access to. The parties looked through S3 buckets, secrets managers, and parameter stores in search of still more credentials. They also tried to enable hosted models in AWS Bedrock and added their own IAM users to maintain access. In all, the stolen bait keys were used “tens of thousands” of times in AWS API calls. Secrets sent to two of the hacked providers were quickly used together, almost immediately, from the same rented server. That means the providers were almost certainly compromised by the same adversary. As noted earlier, some of the secrets were stolen by the resellers themselves. To lure prompts to their servers, they offered low prices. Then they turned on request logging and waited. Moore identified them by sending requests to the same model through different sellers. When credentials were later reused when sent through one seller and not another, the researcher knew it was the reseller, not the model provider, that was responsible. Last, the canary experiment revealed that some providers are scraping secret URLs put into the prompts, in violation of privacy terms. Moore wrote: The clearest example involves a Chinese AI lab. This lab’s systems fetched the secret URLs from more than half of the prompts that we sent to its models between July and October, including roughly two-thirds of the requests marked as “no data collection” or Zero Data Retention. The scraper typically showed up two or three days after the request. This wasn’t limited to requests sent to the lab directly. Several US hosting providers resell this lab’s models, and prompts sent to those providers triggered the exact same scraper—the prompts were flowing back to the lab. A customer who picked a US provider specifically to keep their data in the U.S. didn’t get what they paid for. Later on, a git client on a different cloud started trying to clone the private repositories referenced in our prompts, but only for prompts that used this lab’s models. The researcher said he found one US hosting provider crawling a secret URL more than two months after it was used in a single inference call to its search endpoint. Another ran a scraper that came back for URLs days after each request, regardless of the AI router used to reach it. The blockbuster research is the latest indictment exposing the lax privacy and security that’s endemic in much of the AI ecosystem. The findings mean that people who want to ensure secrets they put into prompts stay private face a daunting task that isn’t likely to become easier any time soon. Ars Technica has been separating the signal from the noise for over 25 years. With our unique combination of technical savvy and wide-ranging interest in the technological arts and sciences, Ars is the trusted source in a sea of information. After all, you don’t need to know everything, only what’s important.

extraction.body: Test using prompts with unique, trackable secrets proves that data doesn’t stay private. Researchers planted 2 million digital tripwires in requests sent through a sprawling network of AI services to find out what happened to sensitive information entrusted to them. What they discovered was an ecosystem that leaked highly sensitive data like a sieve. The exposure was found through an ingenious experiment designed to test if sensitive information can leak through the vast chain of widely used AI services and how that information is exploited when it does. Many of today’s AI apps use services such as OpenRouter or Vercel that act as brokers. These “AI routers,” sometimes also known as “AI gateways,” receive large numbers of prompts sent from AI app end users and route them to an available inference engine based on criteria such as the one charging the lowest price or being best suited for the given task. Instead of using Anthropic, OpenAI, or another big provider, the developer hires an AI router to find the most suitable model. To test for potential leakage, researcher HD Moore assembled a collection of Amazon Web Services access keys, functioning credentials tied to empty AWS accounts, passwords for services such as SSH, and unique URLs, DNS names, and private git repository references. None of the secrets had ever been used before, and he controlled the infrastructure that received any requests using the credentials. He then seeded each secret into exactly one prompt sent to a single provider. In the event any of the secrets were leaked, these “canaries”—so called because they resemble the role of that bird when taken into coal mines—would allow Moore to identify each link in the chain that was responsible. “We sent nearly two million AI prompts containing unique, trackable secrets to AI providers, then watched where those secrets surfaced,” Moore, the chief research officer of security firm Dragos, wrote Thursday . “What we found revealed security breaches, prompt theft, and widespread failures to protect customer data.” Although prompts are encrypted in transit, they are decrypted at each hop inside the large inference reseller network. The prompt is first sent to an AI router, which reads the plaintext in it to determine the most suitable inference providers to handle the request. Often, the prompt is then sent to a pool of available models, which sometimes run inside different hosting providers. Prompts can also pass from one AI router (such as Vercel) to another one (e.g., OpenRouter). Each one of these players is likely to log the prompt and store it for as long as its policies call for (if not indefinitely). The most concerning finding was the breach of three separate hosting providers. The attackers who compromised one of the providers reused “a couple hundred” of the AWS keys. Moore wrote: Each key was sent in exactly one request to one provider, all within a few short windows in late October, and every request we sent during those windows was stolen. Some of the stolen keys came from requests that the provider rejected before a model ever ran—this tells us that the attacker was copying requests at the provider’s front door, and not somewhere deeper in the inference stack. In the other two breaches, some of the stolen requests were marked as ZDR. A privacy flag doesn’t help when the attacker is already inside. Parties tied to the hack of these three providers then tested each key, in some cases within hours of being seeded, to see what kind of resources it gave access to. The parties looked through S3 buckets, secrets managers, and parameter stores in search of still more credentials. They also tried to enable hosted models in AWS Bedrock and added their own IAM users to maintain access. In all, the stolen bait keys were used “tens of thousands” of times in AWS API calls. Secrets sent to two of the hacked providers were quickly used together, almost immediately, from the same rented server. That means the providers were almost certainly compromised by the same adversary. As noted earlier, some of the secrets were stolen by the resellers themselves. To lure prompts to their servers, they offered low prices. Then they turned on request logging and waited. Moore identified them by sending requests to the same model through different sellers. When credentials were later reused when sent through one seller and not another, the researcher knew it was the reseller, not the model provider, that was responsible. This lab’s systems fetched the secret URLs from more than half of the prompts that we sent to its models between July and October, including roughly two-thirds of the requests marked as “no data collection” or Zero Data Retention. The scraper typically showed up two or three days after the request. This wasn’t limited to requests sent to the lab directly. Several US hosting providers resell this lab’s models, and prompts sent to those providers triggered the exact same scraper—the prompts were flowing back to the lab. Another ran a scraper that came back for URLs days after each request, regardless of the AI router used to reach it. The blockbuster research is the latest indictment exposing the lax privacy and security that’s endemic in much of the AI ecosystem. The findings mean that people who want to ensure secrets they put into prompts stay private face a daunting task that isn’t likely to become easier any time soon. extraction.body: Riverside County Sheriff Chad Bianco traveled to St. Louis earlier this year for a podcast appearance in which he touted his gubernatorial bid. “I don't want to be the governor, but I know I have to have that spot to fix California,” he said in the interview on Andy Frisella’s REAL AF. Bianco wasn’t alone on the trip in late March, during which he also made a campaign stop at the headquarters of a supplement company Frisella founded. He was accompanied by a security detail consisting of a sergeant and two deputies from his department, which booked three rooms at the Ritz-Carlton, along with airfare and car rentals — all on the taxpayer's dime, according to a report from the Riverside County Auditor-Controller’s Office. In all, Bianco’s protective detail, including their salaries, cost taxpayers nearly $3.2 million from October 2025 through last month, the report found. Most of the cost stemmed from payroll-related charges but taxpayers also paid for nearly $32,500 in purchasing-card expenses and reimbursements for meals, airfare, car rentals and hotel rooms, according to the document. Some of those expenses were associated with events promoting Bianco’s ultimately unsuccessful campaign as a Republican candidate for governor. In a statement, Riverside County Undersheriff Don Sharp defended the cost of Bianco's security, writing that he formed the detail because Bianco has received intensifying death threats that date back to his opposition to COVID-19 mandates. "Serving as the elected Sheriff is not a job that ends at the close of business," Sharp wrote. "Sheriff Bianco holds that responsibility 24 hours a day, 365 days a year." Sharp said some of the expenses involved security for Bianco and suggested the report was politically motivated. Experts in ethics and election law say some of expenditures associated with campaign trips should raise concerns. “The spirit of the law is certainly not set up to allow a sheriff who’s going all over the place to campaign for himself to use taxpayer dollars on an unlimited basis and justify it as part of his official duties,” said Sean McMorris, transparency, ethics and accountability program manager for the government watchdog group Common Cause. “From an ethics perspective, I would argue, because you can, you should use your campaign money, not taxpayer dollars, if you're going to a campaign event," he added. It’s not the only controversy Bianco is involved in related to the use of taxpayer dollars. The California Supreme Court ruled the seizure unlawful. Last month, Bianco filed a legal claim — a precursor to a lawsuit — seeking to recoup his legal costs from the county, but the claim was rejected this week. Now, Bianco is finalizing a lawsuit against the county, according to his attorney, Bradley Hertz. With the release of the spending report on Tuesday, which was first reported by the Riverside Press-Enterprise, Riverside County Supervisor Jose Medina said he expects the auditor-controller to request an outside auditor be brought in to scrutinize the expenditures further. "I don’t think this will be the end of the investigation," he said. California law prohibits the use of taxpayer dollars for campaign activity — typically defined as activity that unambiguously promotes an outcome in an election — that’s not authorized by law, Morris said. The phrase “not authorized by law” could provide some leeway for the sheriff to argue such expenses were permitted, but it would probably be a tough case to make, especially in instances when Bianco traveled outside Riverside County to campaign, he said. Jessica Levinson, a professor at Loyola Law School and former president of the Los Angeles Ethics Commission, said it’s fairly common for elected officials to have taxpayer-funded security details accompany them to campaign events. “The law does not require that the security be cut loose because you're engaging in a political activity.” But, she added, “when it's solely a campaign-purpose trip and it’s not an activity that he would undertake as the sheriff, it’s an activity he would undertake only as a candidate, I think that becomes harder to defend.” The sheriff's office billed taxpayers for a sergeant and corporal to accompany Bianco to an April 1 gubernatorial debate at Cal State Fresno, including rooms at the Fairfield Marriott; five personnel to travel to an April 22 televised debate at KRON4 Studios in San Francisco, including hotel reservations, flights and rental cars; and six employees to protect him at an election night watch party in Eastvale, according to the report. A county purchasing card was also used to buy $26.19 worth of ice and water for employees working a Bianco for Governor rally on March 14, the report notes. Medina had requested the audit report, saying he felt his constituents had a right to know how much Bianco's security detail cost them. "I was concerned for quite a while that the line between his official duties and candidacy for governor were quite blurred during his campaign," he said. The supervisor in March requested that Riverside County Dist. Michael Hestrin investigate whether Bianco misused public resources on his campaign, including by campaigning in uniform and using on-duty personnel for campaign-related activities. He said that Hestrin declined, citing a lack of evidence. In light of the audit report, Medina plans to ask both Hestrin and Atty. Rob Bonta to open investigations into potential legal violations, he said. The auditor-controller's accounts-payable team flagged the security detail charges, including one that appeared to be related to a gubernatorial debate, during a routine review and asked the sheriff’s office to identify the county business purpose of the expenses, according to the report. "The travel charges in question for the Protective Security Detail Team are to provide security to the Sheriff,” the deputy director of sheriff’s administrative services replied May 28, per the report. “We do not differentiate on the type of travel." But the purpose of the trips matters, according to Davina Hurt, director of government ethics at the Markkula Center for Applied Ethics at Santa Clara University. "A debate and an election night party are campaign events, and that’s not a close call," she wrote in an email.

extraction.body: Riverside County Sheriff Chad Bianco traveled to St. Louis earlier this year for a podcast appearance in which he touted his gubernatorial bid. “I don't want to be the governor, but I know I have to have that spot to fix California,” he said in the interview on Andy Frisella’s REAL AF. In all, Bianco’s protective detail, including their salaries, cost taxpayers nearly $3.2 million from October 2025 through last month, the report found. Most of the cost stemmed from payroll-related charges but taxpayers also paid for nearly $32,500 in purchasing-card expenses and reimbursements for meals, airfare, car rentals and hotel rooms, according to the document. Some of those expenses were associated with events promoting Bianco’s ultimately unsuccessful campaign as a Republican candidate for governor. In a statement, Riverside County Undersheriff Don Sharp defended the cost of Bianco's security, writing that he formed the detail because Bianco has received intensifying death threats that date back to his opposition to COVID-19 mandates. "Serving as the elected Sheriff is not a job that ends at the close of business," Sharp wrote. "Sheriff Bianco holds that responsibility 24 hours a day, 365 days a year." extraction.body: Apple, Google, and Microsoft called out for failing to provide developers with adequate AI agent controls Signal, the encrypted messaging app, has barred Google Gemini, Apple Siri, and other AI agents from accessing messages unless the user has explicitly granted permission, based on privacy concerns. Citing the screenshot blocking implemented last year to defend against Microsoft Recall, Signal CEO Meredith Whittaker said similar measures have become necessary to prevent agentic software available in iOS and Android from gaining access to communication that's intended to be private. "Google and Apple are integrating agentic capabilities like Gemini Intelligence with Google Gemini and Onscreen Awareness with Siri AI deep into their operating systems," wrote Whittaker in a blog post . "In order to gain access to information about you, these OS AI agents 'scan' the information that’s on your screen. In doing so, your Signal data is captured, then made available to these agentic systems in order to allow them to answer your questions and do your bidding." The result is that private messages ingested by these agentic systems may end up on someone else's server where they're no longer private. Updates to Signal's iOS and Android apps now include controls that by default block Siri on iOS and Gemini and other agents on Android from taking screenshots, which AI agents process using optical character recognition to extract text. Whittaker says that those who wish to take screenshots of their messages can disable this protection via Signal's settings menu, but warns doing so risks exposing your Signal content (and that sent by your contacts) to AI agents. Screenshot blocking, Whittaker concedes, is only a partial solution since AI agents may have other ways to access application data through the device file system. "We want to be very clear: it is a serious problem that Signal – and application developers beyond – lack robust tools to prevent AI agents from undermining application-level privacy," she said. "Even where we are able to detect and block AI data access, Google, Apple, Microsoft, and others do not provide ways for developers to easily restrict such AI data access without making drastic compromises to the core user experience. This is also the reason we are currently unable to implement these protections on macOS." Apple is taking some action to implement protection from AI agents on macOS, though it appears to be doing so largely to defend against third-party access to data rather than to limit its own Siri service. Siri can be turned off separately. With macOS 27.3 , currently in public beta testing, Apple's desktop operating system will get more granular controls on two APIs: Device Control and Data Access, and Full Disk Access. The result will be more permission prompts for users of macOS apps that seek access to user data, and the inconvenience of applying for an entitlement from Apple to obtain Full Disk Access for backup software and assistive technologies that use Accessibility APIs. "As AI agents become increasingly capable and autonomous, the risks associated with this level of access will grow substantially," Apple said when it introduced the Full Disk Access change. "We are committed to ensuring users clearly understand these risks before granting such access, so they can make informed decisions about their own data and privacy." Apple is also reportedly working on its own AI agent in a bid to compete with Anthropic and OpenAI. It remains to be seen whether Apple will use its operating system ownership as competitive leverage against AI firms that threaten its gatekeeping power, as it has done with web browsers . While Apple casts itself as an ally that's helping to defend device customers against prying AI agents, Signal's decision to block Siri shows that AI agents have complicated trust decisions and the competitive landscape. AI agents are supposed to serve the user but when they spirit data away to the cloud and come between customers and merchants, they wear out their welcome. AI agents also threaten the business relationship between consumers and merchants. Amazon has blocked shopping agents like Meta Muse from its e-commerce site (though not AWS Marketplace ) while Walmart has invited third-party agents to interact through its AI Gateway. Anthropic has blocked subscription customers from using third-party harnesses . United Airlines has banned transactions from unauthorized AI bots. Similar barriers or limitations related to third-party AI agents have been erected by Target, Home Depot, Etsy, eBay, JPMorgan Chase, Charles Schwab, Citigroup, and Wells Fargo, among others. Meanwhile, there's a burgeoning industry in bot detection and mitigation, led by the likes of Cloudflare, Akamai, and DataDome, to name a few. The web browser is sometimes referred to as a user agent, based on the idealistic notion that it serves its user. That vision has been muddied by online advertising and data collection, and default settings that often serve the interests of browser makers instead of promoting privacy. Now AI agents face the same scrutiny as people wonder whether their agents really serve them or someone else. After a year or two of agent vendors arguing for access to all digital data for the sake of personalization and context, the backlash has arrived. ® Just don't expect complex, coherent, or always correct answers PLUS: US takes down Iranian propaganda sites; Marketing company asks 'Why Do We Have Your Information?' And more!

"In order to gain access to information about you, these OS AI agents 'scan' the information that’s on your screen. In doing so, your Signal data is captured, then made available to these agentic systems in order to allow them to answer your questions and do your bidding." The result is that private messages ingested by these agentic systems may end up on someone else's server where they're no longer private. Updates to Signal's iOS and Android apps now include controls that by default block Siri on iOS and Gemini and other agents on Android from taking screenshots, which AI agents process using optical character recognition to extract text. Whittaker says that those who wish to take screenshots of their messages can disable this protection via Signal's settings menu, but warns doing so risks exposing your Signal content (and that sent by your contacts) to AI agents. "We want to be very clear: it is a serious problem that Signal – and application developers beyond – lack robust tools to prevent AI agents from undermining application-level privacy," she said. "Even where we are able to detect and block AI data access, Google, Apple, Microsoft, and others do not provide ways for developers to easily restrict such AI data access without making drastic compromises to the core user experience.
